metadata.summary: This guideline addresses screening, diagnosis, severity assessment, treatment, and follow-up of diabetic retinopathy and diabetic macular edema in people with diabetes mellitus. It covers systemic risk-factor management, retinal imaging, intravitreal treatment, laser surgery, and vitrectomy, while emphasizing coordination of care and individualized clinical decisions.

target_population: Women with diabetes who are planning pregnancy or are pregnant
therapeutic_areas: Healthy diet, exercise, and weight control

toxicities.event: Infectious endophthalmitis
toxicities.incidence: For intravitreal injections, 0.019% to 0.09% in clinical trial settings.
prevention: Use topical povidone iodine for intravitreal injections; omission has been associated with an unacceptably high risk of endophthalmitis.
Do not routinely use antibiotic eye drops before or after intravitreal injections: they do not lower endophthalmitis risk and increase antibiotic resistance in ocular flora.

toxicities.event: Ocular hemorrhage
Sustained elevated IOP
toxicities.incidence: In the intravitreal triamcinolone acetonide group, about 30% of eyes had an IOP increase above 10 mmHg from baseline. In MEAD, approximately one third of patients receiving the dexamethasone implant had an IOP increase requiring treatment during the study. In PALADIN, IOP rose to more than 30 mmHg in 10.89% of fluocinolone acetonide implant-treated eyes; the rate of incisional surgery attributable to steroid use was 1.49%. In FAME at 3 years, incisional glaucoma surgery occurred in 4.8% of implant recipients versus 0.5% of sham recipients.
recognition: Increased IOP measured during examination.

management.actions: Treat the IOP increase; MEAD reports this requirement without specifying a treatment protocol.

prevention: The fluocinolone acetonide implant is approved for patients previously treated with corticosteroids without an IOP rise.

toxicities.event: Cataract development or progression
associated_therapies: Panretinal photocoagulation surgery (scatter) for severe NPDR or PDR
toxicities.incidence: In the intravitreal triamcinolone acetonide group, half of phakic eyes underwent cataract surgery within 2 years. In MEAD, cataract-related adverse events occurred in 67.9% of phakic eyes receiving the dexamethasone implant versus 20.4% receiving sham treatment. In FAME at 3 years, cataract extraction occurred in 80.0% of phakic eyes receiving the fluocinolone acetonide implant versus 27.3% receiving sham.
prevention: Because cataract progression and elevated IOP are concerns, intravitreal corticosteroids are generally used as second-line agents for DME, particularly in phakic patients.

toxicities.event: Intraocular inflammation and retinal vasculitis
toxicities.incidence: In KESTREL, intraocular inflammation occurred in 3.7% with brolucizumab 6 mg, including 0.5% with retinal vasculitis, versus 0.5% with aflibercept 2 mg. In KITE, intraocular inflammation was 1.7% in each of the brolucizumab 6-mg and aflibercept 2-mg arms, with no retinal vasculitis reported. In YOSEMITE and RHINE, intraocular inflammation excluding endophthalmitis occurred in 1.3% of pooled faricimab groups versus 0.6% of the aflibercept group.
recognition: Occlusive retinal vasculitis has been reported after intravitreal brolucizumab injection.
Intravitreal injections can also produce noninfectious inflammatory reactions.

toxicities.event: Possible systemic arterial thromboembolic and cardiovascular events
toxicities.incidence: In pooled RISE and RIDE analyses at 2 years, ATE occurred in 7.2% (18 of 250) with 0.5-mg ranibizumab, 5.6% (14 of 250) with 0.3-mg ranibizumab, and 5.2% (13 of 250) with control; stroke occurred in 3.2% (8 of 250), 1.2% (3 of 250), and 1.6% (4 of 250), respectively. At 3 years, ATE occurred in 10.4% (26 of 249) with 0.5-mg ranibizumab and 10.8% (27 of 250) with 0.3-mg ranibizumab; stroke occurred in 4.8% (12 of 249) and 2.0% (5 of 250), respectively. In YOSEMITE and RHINE, reported ATE from baseline to week 100 occurred in 5% (64 of 1,262) with faricimab and 5% (32 of 625) with aflibercept 2 mg. Reported thromboembolic events from baseline to week 100 occurred in 6.4% (37 of 578) in the combined aflibercept 8 mg group versus 4.2% (12 of 287) in the control group. In PHOTON through week 48, reported ATE occurred in 3.1% (15 of 491 patients) in the combined aflibercept 8-mg groups versus 3.6% (6 of 167 patients) with aflibercept 2 mg.
recognition: The potential systemic arterial thromboembolic risk of anti-VEGF treatment remains theoretical, and clinical trial findings are inconclusive.
A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis found no increase in major cardiovascular events with intravitreal anti-VEGF agents.

toxicities.event: Possible mortality associated with intravitreal anti-VEGF treatment
toxicities.incidence: In pooled RISE and RIDE analyses during the first 2 years, fatalities occurred in 4.4% (11 of 250) with 0.5 mg ranibizumab, 2.8% (7 of 250) with 0.3-mg ranibizumab, and 1.2% (3 of 250) with control. Over 3 years, fatalities occurred in 6.4% (16 of 249) with 0.5-mg ranibizumab and 4.4% (11 of 250) with 0.3-mg ranibizumab. A systematic review found marginal evidence of an association between anti-VEGF treatment intensity and mortality in the DME subgroup (incidence rate ratio 1.17; 95% CI, 1.02–1.33, P = 0.03).
recognition: A causal relationship between the deaths in RISE and RIDE and intravitreal VEGF inhibitors cannot be excluded.
A 2023 Cochrane review reported no increased mortality risk but could not rule out a clinically relevant increase because certainty of evidence was low to very low.

Another meta-analysis suggested a possible modest increase in death and cerebrovascular events with monthly treatment for 2 years; a 2021 review found increased mortality among patients with DR despite finding no increase in major cardiovascular events.

toxicities.event: Retinal traction or tractional retinal detachment
recognition: Severe PDR may develop traction after an anti-VEGF injection, or existing traction may progress.
Protocol S found no statistically significant difference in tractional retinal detachment rates between anti-VEGF and PRP.

toxicities.event: Other injection-related ocular injury
toxicities.incidence: Retinal detachment, cataract formation, injury to zonules or capsules, and sustained elevated IOP are described as rare.
recognition: Retinal detachment
Damage to zonules or capsules
Capsular tear

toxicities.event: Anterior-chamber implant migration and corneal edema
recognition: Migration from the posterior to the anterior chamber has occurred predominantly in aphakic eyes, pseudophakic eyes with an open posterior capsule, and pseudophakic eyes with disrupted lens zonules.
The dexamethasone implant can cause endothelial injury and corneal edema through chemical toxicity or mechanical trauma.

The fluocinolone acetonide implant can mechanically injure the corneal endothelium and raise IOP when located in the anterior chamber; corneal edema is less common than with the dexamethasone implant.

management.severity: Anterior-chamber migration of the dexamethasone implant with risk of corneal decompensation
management.actions: Urgently remove or reposition the implant to avoid corneal decompensation and keratoplasty.

management.severity: Anterior-chamber migration of the fluocinolone acetonide implant

toxicities.event: Central or paracentral visual impairment after focal laser photocoagulation
associated_therapies: Focal laser photocoagulation surgery for DME
recognition: An initially transient reduction in central vision may occur.
Burns near the fovea, particularly large or confluent burns, may produce paracentral scotomas.
An inadvertent foveal burn can produce a permanent central scotoma.
prevention: Discuss treatment adverse effects and risks before surgery.

The recommended modified ETDRS technique uses less intense laser energy, greater spacing than a grid, direct targeting of microaneurysms, and avoidance of foveal vasculature within at least 500 µm of the macular center.

toxicities.event: Laser-scar enlargement, choroidal neovascularization, or subretinal fibrosis
associated_therapies: Focal laser photocoagulation surgery for DME
toxicities.incidence: Subretinal fibrosis with choroidal neovascularization is described as rare.
recognition: Laser scars may expand over many years.
Subretinal fibrosis with choroidal neovascularization may be associated with permanent central vision loss.
More severe subretinal hard exudates and elevated serum lipids before treatment are associated with subretinal fibrosis apart from choroidal neovascularization.
prevention: Arrange a post-treatment assessment within 3 to 4 months of laser surgery.

toxicities.event: Macular edema and transient central visual loss after PRP
associated_therapies: Panretinal photocoagulation surgery (scatter) for severe NPDR or PDR
recognition: Macular edema may worsen after PRP and temporarily reduce central vision.
prevention: Assess for macular edema before PRP and discuss visual risks with the patient.
When concomitant CSME is present and PRP may exacerbate edema, perform focal photocoagulation and/or anti-VEGF therapy before or together with PRP.
Do not delay PRP for high-risk PDR; anti-VEGF therapy and PRP may instead be given together.
Consider combined anti-VEGF therapy and PRP at the first treatment session when CI-DME is concurrent.

toxicities.event: Peripheral visual-field loss and delayed dark adaptation
associated_therapies: Panretinal photocoagulation surgery (scatter) for severe NPDR or PDR
recognition: Peripheral field constriction and slower dark adaptation can follow PRP.
An ETDRS post hoc analysis found substantial field loss at 1 year after PRP and further loss over time; field loss also occurred with ranibizumab alone, requiring further research.
prevention: Before PRP, fluorescein angiography with or without formal visual-field testing can help distinguish pre-existing field loss from loss perceived after laser treatment.
Explain treatment risks and obtain informed consent before PRP.

toxicities.event: Other complications of panretinal photocoagulation
associated_therapies: Panretinal photocoagulation surgery (scatter) for severe NPDR or PDR
recognition: Vitreous hemorrhage when neovascularization is present
Reduced or impaired accommodation
Pupillary dilation (mydriasis)
prevention: Discuss potential adverse effects and the risk of visual loss before treatment and obtain informed consent.

toxicities.event: Complications of vitrectomy
recognition: Vitreous hemorrhage
Retinal tear or detachment
Vision loss
Infectious endophthalmitis
Cataract
Capsular tear
prevention: A meta-analysis suggested that preoperative anti-VEGF treatment reduces retinal breaks and intra-operative bleeding.
A Cochrane review suggested that preoperative or intra-operative bevacizumab may reduce postoperative vitreous hemorrhage.

toxicities.event: Severe medical complications of fluorescein angiography
toxicities.incidence: Death occurs in about 1/200,000 patients; nausea occurs in 3%-15% and urticaria in 0.5%.
recognition: Nausea
Urticaria
Severe medical reactions
prevention: Each angiography facility should maintain an emergency care plan and a defined protocol for risk reduction and complication management.

toxicities.event: Fetal or breastfeeding exposure to fluorescein
toxicities.incidence: Fluorescein has been detected in breastmilk for up to 72 hours.
recognition: Fluorescein crosses the placenta; detrimental fetal effects of the dye have not been documented.

toxicities.event: Early onset or worsening of DR during rapid glycemic control
toxicities.incidence: About 10% of patients with type 1 diabetes who had retinopathy at DCCT entry experienced increased retinopathy progression. In SUSTAIN 6, the composite of vitreous hemorrhage, blindness, or conditions requiring intravitreal treatment or photocoagulation was more frequent with semaglutide than placebo (HR = 1.76; 95% CI, 1.11–2.78; P = 0.02). In a meta-analysis of 23 randomized trials involving 22,096 patients with type 2 diabetes, 730 incident DR cases occurred: 463 with semaglutide and 267 in control groups. The relative risk was 1.14 overall; for semaglutide versus placebo, it was 1.24 (95% CI, 1.03–1.50). With semaglutide, relative risk was 1.27 (95% CI, 1.02–1.59) for age 60 and older and 1.28 (95% CI, 1.04–1.58) for diabetes duration 10 years or more.
recognition: DR may progress transiently during the first year of rapid improvement after long-standing poor glycemic control.
A transient increase in retinal cotton wool spots may be seen.
prevention: Monitor the eyes frequently when patients are being brought under improved metabolic control.

toxicities.event: Severe hypoglycemia and excess weight gain with intensive glycemic treatment
toxicities.incidence: The DCCT reported a threefold increase in severe hypoglycemic events and excess weight gain with intensive treatment regimens.
recognition: Irregular eating, not checking blood glucose before vigorous exercise or driving, and excess alcohol are risk factors for hypoglycemia.
The guideline reports that semaglutide can produce rapid glycemic control and severe hypoglycemia.
prevention: Diabetes nurses and dietitian educators should provide diabetes education and regular reinforcement, which may help reduce hypoglycemia risk.

toxicities.event: Increased mortality with intensive glucose-lowering strategy
associated_therapies: Intensive lowering of blood sugar levels
toxicities.incidence: In ACCORD, over an average of 3.5 years of treatment, ranging from about 2 years to about 7 years, 257 participants died in the intensive group versus 203 in the standard group: a difference of 54 deaths, or an excess of about three deaths per 1,000 participants treated for a year. The intensive group had a statistically significant 22% higher rate of death.
recognition: The ACCORD Data and Safety Monitoring Board found that harm from the intensive strategy outweighed its potential benefit.

management.actions: The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute stopped the intensive blood sugar strategy in 2008 and transitioned its participants to the standard strategy.

toxicities.event: Worsening of DME associated with diabetes medications
recognition: A medication review found evidence of DME worsening with peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARgamma) agonists.
Case reports describe idiosyncratic macular edema temporally associated with oral glitazone use.

toxicities.event: Retinal vein occlusion reported with diabetes medication
recognition: A medication review reported increased retinal vein occlusions among elderly patients and patients with advanced kidney disease treated with sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors.
A separate retrospective cohort analysis did not associate SGLT-2 inhibitor therapy with NPDR progression compared with other diabetes therapies.

toxicities.event: Vitreous hemorrhage in patients taking aspirin
recognition: The ETDRS found that aspirin did not make vitreous hemorrhage more severe, more frequent, or longer-lasting in patients with PDR.
prevention: No change to medically administered aspirin therapy is indicated solely because of diabetic retinal disease.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Use topical povidone iodine when administering an intravitreal injection.
Do not routinely administer antibiotic eye drops before or after intravitreal injections; they do not reduce endophthalmitis risk and increase antibiotic resistance in ocular flora.
Each fluorescein angiography facility should have an emergency care plan and a clear protocol for minimizing risks and managing complications.
Monitor patients frequently during improvement of metabolic control because rapid improvement after prolonged poor control may initially accelerate retinopathy.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with diabetes undergoing improved metabolic control

prophylaxis.recommendation: Provide diabetes education and regular reinforcement through diabetes nurses and dietitian educators; this may help minimize hypoglycemia during strict glucose control.
When PDR coexists with CSME and PRP may aggravate edema, perform focal photocoagulation and/or anti-VEGF therapy before or with PRP; do not postpone PRP when PDR is high-risk.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with PDR and concomitant CSME

prophylaxis.recommendation: A meta-analysis suggested that preoperative anti-VEGF treatment reduces surgical duration, retinal breaks, and intra-operative bleeding; a Cochrane review suggested that preoperative or intra-operative bevacizumab may reduce postoperative vitreous hemorrhage.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients undergoing vitrectomy for diabetic retinopathy

infection_management.prevention: Topical povidone iodine is recommended for intravitreal injections. Routine antibiotic eye drops before or afterward are not recommended because they do not lower endophthalmitis risk and increase resistance in ocular flora.

therapies_index.name: aflibercept
therapies_index.mechanism: A fusion protein that inhibits VEGF A, VEGF B, and placental growth factor (PLGF).
approved_indications: The guide describes its use for CI-DME and PDR.
therapies_index.administration: Intravitreal aflibercept 2 mg was studied every 4 or 8 weeks for DME. For CI-DME, the DRCR protocol begins with monthly injections for 4 to 6 months, followed by response-guided treatment.
key_toxicities: Intravitreal anti-VEGF treatment carries a theoretical risk of systemic arterial thromboembolic events and increased IOP; clinical-trial findings on these risks remain inconclusive.
Infectious endophthalmitis is the most serious ocular complication of intravitreal injection.
monitoring: Assess visual acuity and OCT central subfield thickness to guide treatment.
Patients receiving intravitreal anti-VEGF injections may be examined at 1 month.
Reliable follow-up is important when anti-VEGF treatment is used for PDR.

therapies_index.name: aflibercept 8 mg
therapies_index.mechanism: The guide describes aflibercept as a fusion protein that inhibits VEGF A, VEGF B, and placental growth factor (PLGF).
approved_indications: The 8 mg formulation was approved for DME in 2023.
therapies_index.administration: In PHOTON, aflibercept 8 mg was given at 12-week or 16-week intervals after 3 monthly loading doses; intervals could be shortened after week 16 according to prespecified disease-activity criteria.
key_toxicities: PHOTON found its safety profile comparable to that of aflibercept 2 mg.
Infectious endophthalmitis is the most serious ocular complication of intravitreal injection.
monitoring: Assess disease activity when determining whether to shorten the dosing interval.
Monitor visual acuity and retinal thickness.

therapies_index.name: bevacizumab
therapies_index.mechanism: An antibody directed against VEGF A.
approved_indications: The guide describes intravitreal use for DME, CI-DME, and PDR; its intravitreal use is identified as off-label.
therapies_index.administration: In BOLT, intravitreal 1.25 mg bevacizumab was administered every 6 weeks. The DRCR protocol for CI-DME begins with monthly injections for 4 to 6 months and then adjusts treatment according to response.
key_toxicities: Infectious endophthalmitis is the most serious ocular complication of intravitreal injection.
Intravitreal anti-VEGF treatment carries theoretical risks of systemic arterial thromboembolic events and increased IOP, with inconclusive clinical-trial findings.
monitoring: Follow visual acuity and OCT central macular thickness during response-guided treatment.
Patients receiving intravitreal anti-VEGF injections may be examined at 1 month.

therapies_index.name: ranibizumab
approved_indications: The guide describes treatment of DME, CI-DME, and PDR.
therapies_index.administration: RISE and RIDE studied monthly intravitreal 0.5 or 0.3 mg injections for DME. In Protocol S, patients with PDR received monthly treatment for 6 months unless neovascularization had fully regressed at 4 months, followed by treatment as needed.
key_toxicities: Infectious endophthalmitis is the most serious ocular complication of intravitreal injection.
A relationship between intravitreal VEGF inhibition and the fatal events reported in pooled RISE and RIDE analyses could not be excluded.
Intravitreal anti-VEGF treatment carries theoretical risks of systemic arterial thromboembolic events and increased IOP, with inconclusive clinical-trial findings.
monitoring: For PDR, assess the presence and activity of retinal neovascularization and the reliability of follow-up.
For DME, assess visual acuity and OCT findings.
Patients receiving intravitreal anti-VEGF injections may be examined at 1 month.

therapies_index.name: Ranibizumab implant
therapies_index.mechanism: The guide describes ranibizumab as an anti-VEGF A Fab fragment.
approved_indications: In February 2025, the FDA approved the ranibizumab implant (Susvimo®) for patients with DME who had previously responded to at least 2 anti-VEGF injections.
therapies_index.administration: Implant; no dosing interval is specified.

therapies_index.name: brolucizumab
therapies_index.mechanism: A single-chain monoclonal antibody fragment directed against VEGF A.
approved_indications: Approved in June 2022 for DME.
therapies_index.administration: In KITE and KESTREL, eyes received 5 loading doses every 6 weeks, followed by dosing every 8 or 12 weeks.
key_toxicities: Intraocular inflammation, including retinal vasculitis, occurred at higher rates in brolucizumab-treated eyes than in aflibercept-treated eyes in the reported studies.
Cases of occlusive retinal vasculitis were reported after intravitreal brolucizumab injection following approval.
Infectious endophthalmitis is the most serious ocular complication of intravitreal injection.
monitoring: Monitor for intraocular inflammation and retinal vasculitis.
Assess visual acuity and retinal fluid during DME treatment.

therapies_index.name: faricimab-svoa
therapies_index.mechanism: A bispecific monoclonal antibody directed against VEGF and angiopoietin-2.
approved_indications: Approved in 2022 for DME.
therapies_index.administration: YOSEMITE and RHINE studied faricimab 6 mg every 8 weeks after six monthly loading doses, or at a personalized treatment interval (PTI) of up to every 16 weeks after four monthly loading doses.
key_toxicities: Intraocular inflammation, excluding endophthalmitis, was reported in the faricimab groups.
Infectious endophthalmitis is the most serious ocular complication of intravitreal injection.
monitoring: Use treatment response to determine the personalized treatment interval.
Assess visual acuity, OCT central subfield thickness, and intraocular inflammation.

therapies_index.name: ranibizumab-nuna
therapies_index.mechanism: A biosimilar of ranibizumab, which the guide describes as an anti-VEGF A Fab fragment.
approved_indications: The FDA approved this retinal-disease biosimilar in 2021, but the guide states that ranibizumab-nuna 0.5 mg is not approved for DME.
therapies_index.administration: The guide identifies a 0.5 mg formulation; no treatment schedule is specified.

therapies_index.name: ranibizumab-eqrn
therapies_index.mechanism: A biosimilar of ranibizumab, which the guide describes as an anti-VEGF A Fab fragment.
approved_indications: The 0.3 mg formulation is interchangeable with ranibizumab 0.3 mg for DME and DR.
therapies_index.administration: The FDA approved 0.3mg and 0.5-mg dosages; the guide does not specify a dosing schedule for this biosimilar.
monitoring: The treating ophthalmologist and patient should choose the biologic product, since responses may differ between products.

therapies_index.name: aflibercept-jbyf
therapies_index.mechanism: An aflibercept biosimilar; the guide describes aflibercept as inhibiting VEGF A, VEGF B, and placental growth factor (PLGF).
approved_indications: Listed among the aflibercept biosimilars FDA approved for DR and DME in 2024.

therapies_index.name: Aflibercept-jbvf
therapies_index.mechanism: An aflibercept biosimilar; the guide describes aflibercept as inhibiting VEGF A, VEGF B, and placental growth factor (PLGF).
approved_indications: Listed in Table A6-1 among agents for patients with DR and DME.
therapies_index.administration: Intravitreal injection 2.0 mg.

therapies_index.name: aflibercept-yszy
therapies_index.mechanism: An aflibercept biosimilar; the guide describes aflibercept as inhibiting VEGF A, VEGF B, and placental growth factor (PLGF).
approved_indications: Listed among the aflibercept biosimilars FDA approved for DR and DME in 2024.
therapies_index.administration: Table A6-1 lists an intravitreal injection of 2.0 mg; no schedule is specified.

therapies_index.name: aflibercept-mrbb
therapies_index.mechanism: An aflibercept biosimilar; the guide describes aflibercept as inhibiting VEGF A, VEGF B, and placental growth factor (PLGF).
approved_indications: Listed among the aflibercept biosimilars FDA approved for DR and DME in 2024.
therapies_index.administration: Table A6-1 lists an intravitreal injection of 2.0 mg; no schedule is specified.

therapies_index.name: aflibercept-ayyh
therapies_index.mechanism: An aflibercept biosimilar; the guide describes aflibercept as inhibiting VEGF A, VEGF B, and placental growth factor (PLGF).
approved_indications: Listed among the aflibercept biosimilars FDA approved for DR and DME in 2024.
therapies_index.administration: Table A6-1 lists an intravitreal injection of 2.0 mg; no schedule is specified.

therapies_index.name: afliberceptjbvf
therapies_index.mechanism: The guide identifies this as an aflibercept biosimilar.
approved_indications: A phase 3 study evaluated its efficacy and safety against reference aflibercept.

therapies_index.name: triamcinolone acetonide
approved_indications: The guide describes intravitreal use for DME, including use with focal laser surgery.
therapies_index.administration: Intravitreal injection; Table A6-1 lists 4.0 mg. Studies also evaluated 1-mg and 4-mg intravitreal doses.
key_toxicities: Cataract progression and elevated IOP.
In a study of intravitreal treatment, half of phakic eyes underwent cataract surgery within 2 years and about 30% of eyes had an IOP increase above 10 mmHg from baseline.
monitoring: Monitor IOP and cataract progression.

therapies_index.name: dexamethasone implant
approved_indications: The guide describes treatment of DME and CI-DME.
therapies_index.administration: Intravitreal extended-release, biodegradable 0.7-mg implant. In MEAD, the mean number of treatments was four to five injections over 3 years.
key_toxicities: Cataract-related adverse events and IOP increases requiring treatment.
Migration into the anterior chamber can cause corneal endothelial damage and edema.
monitoring: Monitor IOP and cataract progression.
Anterior-chamber migration requires urgent assessment for removal or repositioning to prevent corneal decompensation.

therapies_index.name: fluocinolone acetonide implant
approved_indications: Approved for DME in patients previously treated with corticosteroids without an IOP rise.
therapies_index.administration: Sustained-release intravitreal 0.19-mg implant. In FAME, 75% of patients received only one implant over 3 years.
key_toxicities: Cataract requiring extraction and elevated IOP, including cases requiring incisional glaucoma surgery.
Migration into the anterior chamber can produce mechanical corneal endothelial injury, corneal edema, or IOP elevation.
monitoring: Assess IOP and cataract progression.
Anterior-chamber migration requires assessment for surgical removal.

therapies_index.name: fenofibrate
approved_indications: The guide discusses its possible role in slowing DR progression in patients with type 2 diabetes and existing DR; it also reports differing study findings.

therapies_index.name: aspirin
approved_indications: Patients with diabetes may continue aspirin for other medical indications; the guide does not recommend changing medically administered aspirin because of diabetic retinal disease.
The ETDRS found that aspirin did not slow DR progression.
therapies_index.administration: The ETDRS evaluated 650 mg per day.
key_toxicities: The guide reports that aspirin did not make vitreous hemorrhages in PDR more severe, frequent, or prolonged.

therapies_index.name: semaglutide
therapies_index.mechanism: Described as a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist.
approved_indications: The guide describes its use to treat type 2 diabetes mellitus.
key_toxicities: Rapid glycemic control and severe hypoglycemia are reported.
The guide reports higher rates of retinopathy complications with semaglutide and describes evidence of slight DR worsening.
monitoring: Frequent ophthalmologic monitoring is important when metabolic control improves rapidly.

therapies_index.name: nepafenac
approved_indications: Protocol R studied topical nepafenac for noncenter-involved DME but found no difference from placebo in OCT parameters or visual acuity at 1-year follow-up.
therapies_index.administration: Topical nepafenac 0.1% drops were studied in Protocol R.

therapies_index.name: povidone iodine
approved_indications: Recommended for intravitreal injection procedures to reduce the risk of infectious endophthalmitis.
therapies_index.administration: Applied topically for intravitreal injections.

therapies_index.name: antibiotic eye drops
approved_indications: Routine use before or after intravitreal injections is not recommended: it does not reduce endophthalmitis risk.
therapies_index.administration: The guide discusses use before or after intravitreal injection procedures.
key_toxicities: Routine use increases antibiotic resistance in ocular flora.

therapies_index.name: sulfonylureas
approved_indications: The UKPDS studied these agents as an option for intensive blood glucose control in newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes.
monitoring: Blood glucose control was assessed in the UKPDS.

therapies_index.name: insulin
approved_indications: The guide describes its use in diabetes management and its evaluation as an intensive glucose-control option in the UKPDS.
key_toxicities: The DCCT reported more severe hypoglycemic events and excess weight gain with intensive treatment regimens; it does not attribute those findings to insulin alone.
monitoring: Monitor glycemic control, including HbA1c.

therapies_index.name: sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors
approved_indications: The guide discusses these agents as diabetes therapies, not as a recommended DR treatment.
key_toxicities: A review reported increased retinal vein occlusions in elderly patients and patients with advanced kidney disease treated with these agents.
A retrospective cohort review did not associate their use with NPDR progression compared with other diabetes therapies.

therapies_index.name: peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARgamma) agonists
approved_indications: The guide discusses these as diabetes therapies, not as a recommended DME treatment.
key_toxicities: A review reported evidence of worsening DME during treatment.

therapies_index.name: glitazone
approved_indications: Described as a class of oral antihyperglycemic agents.
therapies_index.administration: Oral.
key_toxicities: Case reports described idiosyncratic macular edema temporally associated with use.

therapies_index.name: omega-3 fatty acids
approved_indications: The guide describes studies suggesting an association with less DR development or severity; it states that further research on nutrients and nutraceuticals is needed.

therapies_index.name: docosahexaenoic acid
approved_indications: One study suggested a possible association with reduced retinopathy severity; the guide does not establish it as a treatment.

therapies_index.name: eicosapentaenoic acid
approved_indications: One study suggested a possible association with reduced retinopathy severity; the guide does not establish it as a treatment.

therapies_index.name: ranibizumab with prompt or deferred laser surgery
approved_indications: Studied for CI-DME with visual impairment.
therapies_index.administration: Intravitreal ranibizumab was paired with prompt focal/grid laser surgery or laser surgery deferred for ≥24 weeks.
key_toxicities: Intravitreal injection carries a risk of infectious endophthalmitis.
Focal laser surgery can cause scotomas and other retinal injury.
monitoring: Assess visual acuity and macular edema response.

therapies_index.name: triamcinolone acetonide plus laser surgery
approved_indications: Studied for DME; the guide notes visual gains in pseudophakic eyes.
therapies_index.administration: Intravitreal triamcinolone acetonide combined with focal laser surgery.
key_toxicities: IOP elevation and cataract associated with intravitreal corticosteroid treatment.
Potential complications of focal laser surgery.
monitoring: Monitor IOP, cataract progression, visual acuity, and macular edema.

therapies_index.name: anti-VEGF + dexamethasone
approved_indications: Studied for persistent CI-DME after prior anti-VEGF injections; the guide reports reduced macular thickness but no overall visual-acuity benefit from adding the implant.
therapies_index.administration: The DRCR.net study added a dexamethasone implant after at least three anti-VEGF injections in the previous 20 weeks.
key_toxicities: Corticosteroids carry greater cataract and elevated-IOP risks than anti-VEGF treatment.
monitoring: Monitor visual acuity, macular thickness, IOP, and cataract progression.

therapies_index.name: focal laser photocoagulation surgery
therapies_index.mechanism: Targets leaking microaneurysms to reduce chronic fluid leakage in macular edema.
approved_indications: A treatment option for NCI-DME and CSME.
May be used subsequently for persistent CI-DME after anti-VEGF treatment.
therapies_index.administration: The recommended modified ETDRS approach uses less intense energy, greater spacing than a grid, direct microaneurysm targeting, and avoidance of foveal vasculature within at least 500 µm of the macular center.
key_toxicities: Possible early transient central-vision reduction.
Paracentral scotomas from burns close to the fovea and permanent central scotoma from inadvertent foveal burns.
Laser-scar expansion over many years, choroidal neovascularization, and subretinal fibrosis.
monitoring: Arrange post-treatment evaluation within 3 to 4 months.

therapies_index.name: focal/grid laser surgery
therapies_index.mechanism: Focal treatment addresses discrete leakage; grid treatment applies scattered burns to areas of diffuse macular edema and nonperfusion.
approved_indications: Recommended as a treatment option for NCI-DME.
Studied for DME alone and alongside intravitreal treatments.
therapies_index.administration: Laser treatment is directed to the macula; the guide does not specify a uniform treatment schedule.
key_toxicities: Focal laser treatment can cause central or paracentral scotomas, laser-scar enlargement, choroidal neovascularization, and subretinal fibrosis.
monitoring: A post-laser evaluation should be scheduled within 3 to 4 months.

therapies_index.name: panretinal photocoagulation surgery (PRP)
therapies_index.mechanism: Peripheral scatter laser treatment intended to produce regression of neovascularization.
approved_indications: An important treatment for PDR, including prompt treatment of most high-risk PDR.
May be considered for severe NPDR or non-high-risk PDR in selected circumstances.
therapies_index.administration: The full ETDRS PRP protocol used 1200 to 1600 moderately intense spots lasting 0.1 second, spaced one-half burn width apart and placed at least 2 disc diameters from the fovea through the equator. Partial or limited PRP is not recommended.
key_toxicities: Transient central-vision loss from macular edema.
Peripheral visual-field constriction and delayed dark adaptation.
Vitreous hemorrhage when neovascularization is present.
Reduced accommodation, mydriasis, and accelerated cataract development.
monitoring: Assess for macular edema before treatment.
Follow neovascularization for regression, enlargement, or new lesions and assess for new vitreous hemorrhage.
Consider additional PRP and/or anti-VEGF therapy when the guide's specified signs of persistent or worsening neovascularization occur.

therapies_index.name: pars plana vitrectomy
approved_indications: Consider for PDR with nonclearing vitreous hemorrhage, vision- or treatment-obscuring vitreous opacity, severe fibrovascular proliferation, macula-threatening or macula-involving tractional retinal detachment, combined rhegmatogenous and tractional detachment, or dense premacular subhyaloid hemorrhage.
May improve vision in selected patients with substantial vitreomacular traction and diffuse DME unresponsive to prior treatment.
therapies_index.administration: The DRVS compared vitrectomy within 1 to 6 months after vitreous-hemorrhage onset with later surgery at 1 year.
key_toxicities: Vitreous hemorrhage, retinal tear or detachment, vision loss, infectious endophthalmitis, cataract, and capsular tear.
monitoring: Follow vitreous hemorrhage with serial ultrasonography to assess for retinal tear or detachment.

therapies_index.name: subthreshold laser surgery
approved_indications: Evaluated for DME; a 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis concluded that it was as effective as traditional laser surgery.
monitoring: The cited review stated that increased follow-up is required to observe safety effects.

therapies_index.name: subthreshold diode micropulse laser photocoagulation surgery
approved_indications: Evaluated for DME; a cited meta-analysis found no visual-acuity difference from conventional laser photocoagulation surgery.

therapies_index.name: photobiomodulation
approved_indications: Protocol AE evaluated it for DME in eyes with good vision and did not find it effective.
key_toxicities: Protocol AE described it as safe and well tolerated.

therapies_index.name: intensive blood glucose control
approved_indications: Studied to delay DR onset or progression; the guide also cautions that rapid improvement of longstanding poor control may initially worsen retinopathy in some patients.
therapies_index.administration: The guide recommends individualizing glycemic goals and controlling blood glucose as near to normal as safely possible; it does not prescribe a single regimen.
key_toxicities: The DCCT reported a threefold increase in severe hypoglycemic events and excess weight gain with intensive treatment regimens.
ACCORD stopped its intensive glucose-lowering strategy because of an increased death rate compared with standard treatment.
monitoring: Monitor HbA1c and hypoglycemia risk.
Frequent ophthalmologic monitoring is important during improvement of metabolic control.

therapies_index.name: blood pressure control
approved_indications: Management of blood pressure is described as a modifiable factor that lowers the risk of DR developing or progressing.
monitoring: Follow blood pressure as part of coordinated systemic diabetes care.

therapies_index.name: visual rehabilitation
approved_indications: Referral is recommended for patients whose visual impairment functionally limits them.
therapies_index.administration: Provided through referral to vision-rehabilitation services.

conditions.name: Diabetic retinopathy
conditions.description: An ocular manifestation of diabetes mellitus that affects the retinal microvasculature and also involves early neurodegenerative and inflammatory changes. Vascular injury can cause capillary nonperfusion, increased permeability, macular edema and, in proliferative disease, neovascularization.
conditions.epidemiology: Among U.S. adults aged 40 and older with diabetes, a cited estimate placed retinopathy prevalence at 28.5% (4.2 million people) and vision-threatening DR at 4.4% (0.7 million people); corresponding worldwide estimates were 34.6% (93 million people) and 10.2% (28 million people). A separate analysis estimated global prevalence at 22.3% for DR and 6.2% for vision-threatening DR, with 103.12 million and 28.54 million affected adults, respectively, in 2020. A study using 2021 data reported DR prevalence of 26.43% among people with diabetes and estimated vision-threatening DR prevalence at 5.06% (1.84 million people). Estimates differ across studies and populations. DR is a leading cause of new legal blindness among working-age Americans.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Disease may remain asymptomatic despite advanced retinal changes. Visible findings range from microaneurysms and intraretinal hemorrhages to cotton wool spots, venous abnormalities, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities, edema, exudates and neovascularization. Macular nonperfusion or edema can impair central vision; proliferative disease can additionally cause vitreous hemorrhage, retinal distortion, tractional detachment and neovascular glaucoma.

subtypes.name: Very severe NPDR
subtypes.distinguishing_features: At least two features used to define severe NPDR are present.

subtypes.name: PDR

subtypes.name: High-risk PDR
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Neovascularization meets the DRS high-risk criteria, which incorporate its site and extent and the presence of vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage.

subtypes.name: Diabetic macular edema
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Fluid accumulation in the macula from vascular leakage; it can occur at any DR stage.

staging.system: Diabetic Retinopathy Disease Severity Scale and International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy Disease Severity Scale; ETDRS classification

definitions.description: Dilated ophthalmoscopy shows no retinal abnormalities.
Only microaneurysms are visible.
Findings extend beyond microaneurysms but remain below severe NPDR.

Without proliferative signs, the U.S. 4-2-1 definition requires any of: severe intraretinal hemorrhages and microaneurysms in each of 4 quadrants; definite venous beading in 2 or more quadrants; or moderate IRMA in 1 or more quadrants. The international definition specifies more than 20 intraretinal hemorrhages in each of 4 quadrants, definite venous beading in 2 or more quadrants, or prominent IRMA in 1 or more quadrants.
At least two of the severe NPDR defining characteristics are present.
Neovascularization, vitreous/preretinal hemorrhage, or both are present.

The DRS criteria are met by any three of four features: neovascularization anywhere; neovascularization at or near the optic disc; neovascularization of at least moderate extent; and vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage. Moderate extent includes disc-area vessels within 1 disc diameter of the nerve head larger than one-quarter to one-third disc area, or vessels elsewhere measuring at least one-half disc area.

staging.additional_rules: Each eye is classified separately for DR and macular edema. The ETDRS classification supplies more detailed lesion and standard-photograph criteria, and higher severity levels are associated with greater progression risk. PDR can additionally be classified as high-risk or non-high-risk.

Definite venous beading in 2 or more quadrants
Moderate IRMA in 1 or more quadrants

risk_groups.criteria: At least one component without proliferative findings.
Two or more severe NPDR characteristics.
risk_groups.expected_outcome: The guide reports a nearly 50% risk of progression to high-risk PDR within 1 year for eyes with very severe NPDR and non-high-risk PDR.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: Used to classify nonproliferative disease severity.

prognostic_tools.name: DRSS
prognostic_tools.interpretation: Higher baseline severity is associated with subsequent worsening; studies also use a two-step or greater change to evaluate treatment response.

follow_up.schedule: For type 1 diabetes without DR, begin annual dilated examinations 5 years after diagnosis. For type 2 diabetes without DR, examine at diagnosis and at least yearly thereafter. Subsequent intervals depend on retinopathy and edema severity; abnormal findings can require more frequent visits.

Peripheral retinal and vitreous examination when indicated
Review of symptoms, pregnancy, blood pressure, serum lipids, renal status, HbA1c and treatments
long_term_effects: Progression to PDR, macular edema and vision loss
Vitreous hemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment and neovascular glaucoma in advanced disease
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Ongoing retinal surveillance remains important even with good vision or no ocular symptoms. Patients with functionally limiting visual impairment should be offered vision rehabilitation and appropriate support.

conditions.name: Mild NPDR
conditions.description: An early nonproliferative stage defined by microaneurysms without findings that meet a more advanced stage.
conditions.epidemiology: In WESDR, approximately 16% of patients with type 1 diabetes and mild retinopathy progressed to proliferative stages within 4 years. The guide reports an approximately 12% 4-year incidence of either CSME or macular edema that is not clinically significant in mild NPDR.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Microaneurysms may be the only visible abnormality. Patients can lack visual symptoms.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm microaneurysms and exclude findings of more advanced DR.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnosis and surveillance visits.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Microaneurysms alone satisfy the disease severity scale definition.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate possible macular edema.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When edema is suspected or the macular examination is uncertain.

staging.system: Diabetic Retinopathy Disease Severity Scale and International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy Disease Severity Scale; ETDRS classification

definitions.description: Microaneurysms alone under the disease severity scale; the ETDRS definition requires at least 1 microaneurysm without meeting criteria for a higher stage.

follow_up.schedule: The initial-management table gives 12 months without macular edema, 3–6 months with NCI-DME and 1 month with CI-DME. Elsewhere, patients with mild to moderate NPDR without edema are advised to return within 6 to 12 months.
long_term_effects: Possible progression to more severe DR or macular edema
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Closer surveillance may be necessary after anti-VEGF treatment for edema is stopped, particularly when the underlying retinopathy is more advanced.

conditions.name: Moderate NPDR
conditions.description: A nonproliferative stage with abnormalities beyond isolated microaneurysms that do not meet severe NPDR criteria.
conditions.epidemiology: The guide reports a 23% 4-year risk of either CSME or macular edema that is not clinically significant in moderate NPDR among patients with type 1 or 2 diabetes.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Findings can include intraretinal hemorrhages and microaneurysms; the ETDRS definition also allows definite soft exudates, venous beading or IRMA without criteria for more advanced disease.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess lesions and distinguish moderate from severe NPDR.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnosis and follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Abnormalities exceed microaneurysms alone but remain below severe NPDR.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect and monitor coexisting DME.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When edema is present or suspected.

staging.system: Diabetic Retinopathy Disease Severity Scale and International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy Disease Severity Scale; ETDRS classification

definitions.description: More than microaneurysms alone, but less than severe NPDR. The ETDRS definition includes hemorrhages and/or microaneurysms ≥ standard photograph 2A and/or definite soft exudates, venous beading or IRMA, without meeting a more severe stage.

follow_up.schedule: The initial-management table gives 6–12 months without edema, with shorter intervals if findings approach severe NPDR; 3–6 months with NCI-DME; and 1 month with CI-DME.
long_term_effects: Progression to severe or proliferative DR and development of macular edema

conditions.name: Severe NPDR
conditions.description: Advanced nonproliferative disease meeting at least one 4-2-1 criterion without evidence of proliferative retinopathy.
conditions.epidemiology: In ETDRS data described by the guide, 15% of patients with severe NPDR developed PDR within 1 year.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Extensive intraretinal hemorrhages and microaneurysms, venous beading or IRMA indicate increasing retinal ischemia; macular edema may coexist.

subtypes.name: Very severe NPDR
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Two or more defining features of severe NPDR are present.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess hemorrhages, microaneurysms, venous beading, IRMA and any proliferative signs.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnosis and close follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: At least one 4-2-1 feature without proliferative findings establishes severe NPDR.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess concurrent DME.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When macular edema is suspected or present.

staging.system: 4-2-1 rule; International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy Disease Severity Scale; ETDRS classification

definitions.description: The U.S. definition requires any of: severe intraretinal hemorrhages and microaneurysms in each of 4 quadrants, definite venous beading in 2 or more quadrants, or moderate IRMA in 1 or more quadrants, with no proliferative signs. The international definition specifies more than 20 intraretinal hemorrhages in each of 4 quadrants, definite venous beading in 2 or more quadrants, or prominent IRMA in 1 or more quadrants, again without proliferative signs.

staging.additional_rules: The ETDRS classification provides additional lesion combinations and standard-photograph thresholds.

prognostic_tools.name: 4-2-1 rule
components: Venous beading in 2 or more quadrants

risk_groups.criteria: One defining feature without proliferative signs.
risk_groups.expected_outcome: The guide cites 15% progression from severe NPDR to PDR within 1 year in ETDRS.
The guide reports a nearly 50% risk of progression to high-risk PDR within 1 year for very severe NPDR and non-high-risk PDR.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: Distinguishes severe from very severe nonproliferative disease.

follow_up.schedule: The initial-management table gives 3–4 months without edema, 2–4 months with NCI-DME and 1 month with CI-DME. The narrative advises re-examination within 2 to 4 months for severe NPDR and non-high-risk PDR.
recommended_tests: Dilated examination for neovascularization and other progression signs
long_term_effects: Progression to PDR and vision-threatening complications

conditions.description: A particularly advanced nonproliferative stage with at least two characteristics that individually qualify as severe NPDR.
conditions.epidemiology: The guide reports a nearly 50% risk of progression to high-risk PDR within 1 year for eyes with very severe NPDR and non-high-risk PDR.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Multiple severe retinal hemorrhage, venous-beading or IRMA features are present without proliferative signs.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Count severe NPDR features and detect any transition to PDR.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnosis and close follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Two or more severe NPDR characteristics define very severe NPDR.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Check for coexisting DME.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When macular edema is suspected or present.

definitions.description: At least two of the severe NPDR defining characteristics are present without proliferative findings.

prognostic_tools.name: 4-2-1 rule
components: Severe hemorrhages and microaneurysms in 4 quadrants
Definite venous beading in 2 or more quadrants
Moderate IRMA in 1 or more quadrants

risk_groups.expected_outcome: The guide reports a nearly 50% risk of reaching high-risk PDR within 1 year for eyes with very severe NPDR and non-high-risk PDR.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: Identifies eyes approaching high-risk proliferative disease.

follow_up.schedule: Re-examination within 2 to 4 months is advised in the narrative discussing severe NPDR and non-high-risk PDR; concurrent edema can require a shorter interval under the initial-management table.

conditions.name: PDR
conditions.description: Proliferative DR develops when retinal ischemia is accompanied by new vessels on the retina, optic disc, iris or filtration angle.
conditions.epidemiology: In WESDR, PDR was present in approximately 50% of patients with type 1 diabetes who were 30 and younger and had diabetes for 20 years. In another cited population, 18% of participants with diabetes lasting more than 15 years had PDR. Among patients with type 2 diabetes, the guide cites development of PDR in 2% with diabetes for less than 5 years and 25% with diabetes for 25 years or more.
conditions.clinical_presentation: New vessels can bleed into the vitreous or preretinal space. Fibrosis and contraction can produce vitreoretinal traction, retinal tears or detachment; anterior-segment neovascularization can cause neovascular glaucoma.

subtypes.name: Non-high-risk PDR
subtypes.distinguishing_features: New vessels are present without high-risk characteristics.

subtypes.name: High-risk PDR
subtypes.distinguishing_features: New vessels meet specified site-and-size criteria or are accompanied by vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage.

diagnostic_workup.test: Dilated fundoscopy and peripheral retinal examination
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify NVD, NVE, hemorrhage, fibrosis and traction; classify high-risk status.

diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Neovascularization and/or vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage satisfies the PDR disease severity scale.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For selected diagnostic questions; it is not usually necessary to perform PRP effectively.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess coexisting DME and vitreomacular traction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When clinically appropriate.

staging.system: Diabetic Retinopathy Disease Severity Scale and International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy Disease Severity Scale; DRS high-risk criteria

Proliferative neovascularization does not meet the high-risk definition.
The DRS high-risk definition is met by any three of four features involving neovascularization, its disc location, at least moderate extent and vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage.

prognostic_tools.name: DRS high-risk characteristics
components: Neovascularization at or near the optic disc

The guide reports a nearly 50% risk of progression to high-risk PDR within 1 year for eyes with very severe NPDR and non-high-risk PDR.

conditions.description: Proliferative disease with new vessels that do not satisfy high-risk PDR criteria.
conditions.epidemiology: The guide reports a nearly 50% risk of progression to high-risk PDR within 1 year for eyes with very severe NPDR and non-high-risk PDR.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Retinal or disc neovascularization is present without the defining high-risk constellation.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnosis and follow-up.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When edema is suspected or present.

prognostic_tools.name: DRS high-risk characteristics

risk_groups.criteria: Proliferative disease without the high-risk combination.
risk_groups.expected_outcome: The guide reports a nearly 50% risk of progression to high-risk PDR within 1 year for eyes with very severe NPDR and non-high-risk PDR.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: Identifies proliferative disease before high-risk characteristics appear.

follow_up.schedule: The narrative advises re-examination within 2 to 4 months. The initial-management table lists 3–4 months without edema, 2–4 months with NCI-DME and 1 month with CI-DME.
recommended_tests: Dilated examination for neovascularization and hemorrhage
long_term_effects: Progression to high-risk PDR and severe vision loss

conditions.name: High-risk PDR
conditions.description: Proliferative retinopathy meeting DRS high-risk characteristics on the basis of neovascularization location and extent and associated hemorrhage.
conditions.epidemiology: In the DRS visual-outcome table, severe visual loss in the high-risk proliferative group occurred at 2 years in 26% of control patients and 11% of treated patients, and at 4 years in 44% and 20%, respectively.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Disc or other retinal neovascularization may be extensive or accompanied by vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage. Neovascular glaucoma can coexist.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure and locate neovascularization and identify vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Promptly when high-risk PDR is suspected and during treatment follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Any three DRS high-risk features establish the high-risk category.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess for neovascular glaucoma and angle neovascularization.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Especially when iris new vessels are suspected or IOP is elevated.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Check for retinal tears or detachment when vitreous hemorrhage obstructs examination.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: With an obscured retinal view.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify concurrent macular edema.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When appropriate.

definitions.description: Any three of: neovascularization anywhere, neovascularization at or near the disc, at least moderate neovascularization, and vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage. The ETDRS definition includes disc neovascularization on or within 1 disc diameter of the optic disc ≥ standard photograph 10A, about one-quarter to one-third disc area, with or without hemorrhage; it also includes hemorrhage accompanied by smaller disc vessels or new vessels elsewhere ≥ one-quarter disc area.

staging.additional_rules: For the DRS moderate-neovascularization feature, vessels within 1 disc diameter of the nerve head must exceed one-quarter to one-third disc area, or vessels elsewhere must measure at least one-half disc area.

prognostic_tools.name: DRS high-risk characteristics
components: Neovascularization at or near the optic disc

risk_groups.expected_outcome: The DRS found substantial severe-vision-loss risk and a marked reduction with PRP.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: Determines which proliferative eyes require especially prompt attention.

follow_up.schedule: Prompt treatment is advised. Subsequent assessment evaluates neovascular regression, new hemorrhage and treatment response; the initial-management table lists 2–4 months with NCI-DME and 1 month with CI-DME.
recommended_tests: Ultrasonography when hemorrhage obscures the retina
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Sustained attendance is particularly important when management relies on repeated anti-VEGF injections.

conditions.name: Diabetic macular edema
conditions.description: Macular fluid accumulation caused by leakage from retinal vessels. It can accompany any severity level of DR.
conditions.epidemiology: A global review estimated clinically significant macular edema prevalence at 4.1%, corresponding to 18.83 million adults in 2020; it projected 28.61 million affected adults by 2045. In ETDRS, an estimated 40% of eyes with DME had visual acuity of 20/20 or better.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Retinal thickening and sometimes hard exudates may impair central visual acuity, although good visual acuity can persist despite center-involved edema.

subtypes.name: CI-DME
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Edema involves the center of the macula.

subtypes.name: NCI-DME
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Edema does not involve the center of the macula.

subtypes.name: CSME
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The ETDRS definition uses specified proximity and extent criteria for retinal thickening or associated hard exudates.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess retinal thickening, hard exudates and center involvement.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When DME is suspected and during follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Macular edema should be categorized as center-involved or non-center-involved.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect and quantify edema, measure central macular thickness and monitor anatomical response.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For evaluation and follow-up of DME.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guide describes OCT as the best method for detecting and quantifying CI-DME; retinal thickness alone does not always correlate with visual acuity.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Differentiate DME from another macular disorder, assess otherwise unexplained visual loss or identify leaking microaneurysms and capillary dropout for selected treatment planning.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When the diagnosis or examination is uncertain or focal laser surgery is being planned; not routinely for every patient with diabetes.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate macular nonperfusion and foveal avascular zone enlargement.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When vascular or ischemic assessment would be useful.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: It depicts nonperfusion but not vascular leakage.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess functional impairment and response alongside retinal imaging.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial and follow-up examinations.

pathology_markers.expected_result: An increase can reflect central retinal thickening.
pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Changes are used with visual acuity to assess response; a DRCR.net study proposed a CI-DME clinical threshold two standard deviations above the normative study population of diabetics without macular edema.

staging.system: ETDRS definition of CSME; center-involved and non-center-involved DME classification

definitions.description: Macular edema affects the center of the macula.
Macular edema does not affect the center of the macula.

Retinal thickening lies at or within 500 µm of the macular center; or hard exudates lie at or within 500 µm of the center with adjacent thickening; or a thickened zone measures at least 1 disc area and extends to within 1 disc diameter of the center.

staging.additional_rules: Residual hard exudates after successfully treated thickening do not, by themselves, satisfy the hard-exudate criterion.

follow_up.schedule: Frequency depends on center involvement, visual acuity and concurrent DR severity. OCT thickness and visual acuity are assessed together during treatment follow-up.

conditions.name: CI-DME
conditions.description: Diabetic macular edema affecting the macular center; visual acuity may either remain good or decline.
conditions.epidemiology: The guide estimates that 40% of eyes with DME in ETDRS had visual acuity of 20/20 or better; this estimate applies to DME generally, not specifically to CI-DME.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Central retinal thickening may accompany impaired visual acuity, but center involvement does not invariably cause immediate visual symptoms.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm central involvement and quantify central retinal thickness for subsequent comparisons.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At evaluation and throughout follow-up.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A DRCR.net study proposed a reasonable clinical threshold at central macular thickness two standard deviations above the normative study population of diabetics without macular edema.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine whether center-involved edema is associated with vision loss and detect later decline.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At every clinical assessment of treatment need or response.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guide discusses deferring treatment in eyes with good acuity until vision reaches 20/30 or worse; Protocol V studied eyes starting at 20/25 or better.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess retinal thickening and concurrent DR.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At initial and follow-up visits.

pathology_markers.clinical_significance: Baseline thickness and its change help assess anatomical disease and treatment response, but do not consistently predict visual acuity.

definitions.description: Diabetic edema includes the macular center.

follow_up.schedule: For eyes with good visual acuity and deferred treatment, the guide specifies examination every 2 to 4 months. The initial-management table lists 1 month for CI-DME across DR severity categories; patients receiving anti-VEGF injections may be re-examined as early as 1 month after injection.
recommended_tests: IOP measurement when monitoring treatment effects
long_term_effects: Potential visual acuity loss and persistent or recurrent edema

conditions.name: NCI-DME
conditions.description: Diabetic macular edema that does not involve the macular center.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Macular retinal thickening is present outside the center; central visual acuity may remain excellent.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess thickening and its distance from the macular center.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At diagnosis and surveillance.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Edema is categorized as non-center-involved when the macular center is spared.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the location and extent of edema and detect subsequent center involvement.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When evaluating or monitoring DME.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect functional change.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At assessment and follow-up.

definitions.description: Macular edema spares the center.

follow_up.schedule: The initial-management table lists 3–6 months with mild or moderate NPDR, 2–4 months with severe NPDR or non-high-risk PDR, and 2–4 months with high-risk PDR. Deferring treatment is an option when acuity is better than 20/32, close follow-up is feasible and the patient understands the risks.

conditions.name: CSME
conditions.description: An ETDRS-defined pattern of retinal thickening or associated hard exudates that involves or threatens the central macula.
conditions.epidemiology: A cited global review estimated CSME prevalence at 4.1%, or 18.83 million adults in 2020, and projected 28.61 million affected adults by 2045.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Retinal thickening and sometimes nearby hard exudates can be present at or near the macular center, with possible central vision loss.

subtypes.name: NCI-DME
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Edema does not involve the center.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify thickening, hard exudates and their relationship to the center.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When CSME is suspected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Apply the ETDRS distance, extent and adjacent-thickening criteria.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify and measure macular thickening and determine center involvement.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For diagnosis and follow-up.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Find leaking microaneurysms or capillary dropout when planning focal laser treatment; assess another explanation for visual loss.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When it would assist selected diagnostic or laser-planning decisions.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess existing or developing functional impairment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: At evaluation and follow-up.

definitions.description: Any of: retinal thickening at or within 500 µm of the macular center; hard exudates at or within 500 µm of the center with adjacent thickening; or retinal thickening covering 1 disc area or larger, with part of it within 1 disc diameter of the center.

staging.additional_rules: Hard exudates persisting after successful treatment of earlier thickening do not satisfy the hard-exudate criterion on their own. CSME can be divided into center-involved and non-center-involved edema.

follow_up.schedule: Follow-up and treatment timing depend on center involvement, proximity of thickening or exudates to the center, visual loss or its potential, and concurrent DR severity.

recommendations.statement: Screen people with type 1 diabetes for diabetic retinopathy annually, beginning 5 years after diabetes onset.
recommendations.context: The recommended examination is a dilated eye examination.
recommendations.rationale: This schedule detects the great majority of people with type 1 diabetes who need treatment.
recommendations.source_heading: HIGHLIGHTED FINDINGS AND RECOMMENDATIONS FOR CARE

recommendations.statement: Arrange an eye examination when type 2 diabetes is diagnosed, followed by examinations at least annually.
recommendations.context: Refer for a comprehensive diabetic eye examination at diagnosis.
recommendations.rationale: Retinopathy may already be present when type 2 diabetes is diagnosed.

recommendations.statement: Explain to patients that maintaining appropriate HbA1c and blood pressure levels reduces the likelihood of diabetic retinopathy developing or progressing.
recommendations.rationale: Near-normal glucose and blood pressure levels lower these risks.

recommendations.statement: Examine women who already have diabetes early in pregnancy and monitor them closely throughout pregnancy.
recommendations.context: Arrange an examination soon after conception and early in the first trimester; follow up every 3–12 months with no retinopathy through mild or moderate NPDR, or every 1–3 months with severe NPDR or worse.
recommendations.rationale: Diabetic retinopathy can progress rapidly during pregnancy.
recommendations.source_heading: HIGHLIGHTED FINDINGS AND RECOMMENDATIONS FOR CARE

recommendations.statement: Increase vigilance for progression of diabetic retinopathy during puberty.
recommendations.context: Patients with diabetes who are pubertal require closer monitoring.
recommendations.rationale: Progression accelerates during puberty.
recommendations.source_heading: HIGHLIGHTED FINDINGS AND RECOMMENDATIONS FOR CARE

recommendations.statement: Leave the choice among reference, biosimilar, and interchangeable biologic products to the treating ophthalmologist and patient.
recommendations.context: Choice of a biologic product for treatment.
recommendations.rationale: An individual patient may respond better to one biologic product than another.

recommendations.statement: Use topical povidone iodine when performing intravitreal injections.
recommendations.context: Intravitreal injection procedures.
recommendations.rationale: Omission has been associated with an unacceptably high risk of infectious endophthalmitis.

recommendations.statement: Do not routinely prescribe antibiotic eye drops before or after an intravitreal injection.
recommendations.context: Intravitreal injection procedures.
recommendations.rationale: Routine drops do not reduce endophthalmitis risk and increase antibiotic resistance in ocular flora.

recommendations.statement: Consider an HbA1c target of 7% or lower for most patients; a target of 6.5% may benefit selected patients.
recommendations.context: Glycemic control in patients with diabetes.
recommendations.rationale: Hyperglycemia is a major modifiable risk factor for diabetic retinopathy.

recommendations.statement: Encourage patients with diabetes to follow treatment for all medical aspects of their disease as closely as possible.
recommendations.context: Systemic risk-factor management.
recommendations.rationale: Several associated risk factors also contribute to cardiovascular morbidity, mortality, and other diabetes complications.

recommendations.statement: Consider timely treatment for CSME involving the macular center, or when retinal thickening or hard exudates lie near the center and vision loss is present or may occur.
recommendations.context: Assessment of clinically significant macular edema.
recommendations.rationale: The risk of visual loss is greatest when edema affects the macular center.

recommendations.statement: Consider PRP or anti-VEGF agents for patients with severe NPDR.
recommendations.context: Disease has reached the defined severe NPDR thresholds.
recommendations.rationale: These findings indicate increasing retinal ischemia and risk of progression.

recommendations.statement: Treat neovascular glaucoma or high-risk PDR promptly with anti-VEGF agents and PRP.
recommendations.rationale: Advanced neovascular disease threatens vision.

recommendations.statement: Explain that substantial diabetic eye disease may be present despite good vision and no ocular symptoms, and that retinal examinations are needed at least annually to detect it early.
recommendations.context: Patient education about screening and early treatment.
recommendations.rationale: Patients may be unaware of retinopathy, including vision-threatening disease.

recommendations.statement: Before pregnancy, examine patients with diabetes who intend to become pregnant and counsel them about the possibility that retinopathy will develop or progress.
recommendations.context: Pregnancy planning.
recommendations.rationale: Pregnancy-related physiological and metabolic changes may worsen diabetic retinopathy.

recommendations.statement: Classify each eye by diabetic retinopathy and macular edema category, and use that category together with diabetes control to determine intervention and follow-up timing.
recommendations.context: Discuss examination findings and their implications with the patient.
recommendations.rationale: Progression risk varies by diagnostic category and adherence to diabetes control.

recommendations.statement: Perform the initial retinal examination through a dilated pupil when possible.
recommendations.context: Assessment of diabetic retinopathy presence and severity.
recommendations.rationale: Only 50% of eyes are correctly classified through undilated pupils.

recommendations.statement: Use slit-lamp biomicroscopy with a 90 diopter (D) or 78 D lens to evaluate retinopathy in the posterior pole and midperipheral retina.
recommendations.context: Initial ophthalmic examination.

recommendations.statement: Obtain gonioscopy before dilation when iris neovascularization is present or suspected, or when IOP is elevated.
recommendations.context: Assessment for neovascularization of the anterior chamber angle.
recommendations.rationale: Iris neovascularization is most readily recognized before dilation.

recommendations.statement: Do not include FA routinely in the regular examination of patients with diabetes.
recommendations.context: Reserve FA for pertinent diagnostic or treatment-planning questions.
recommendations.rationale: The need to localize leakage for focal laser treatment has declined.

recommendations.statement: Ensure that facilities performing FA have an emergency care plan and a clear protocol for reducing and managing complications.
recommendations.context: Safety arrangements for fluorescein angiography.
recommendations.rationale: Severe medical complications, including death in about 1/200,000 patients, can occur.

recommendations.statement: Individualize the choice of laser surgery, an anti-VEGF agent, or an approved intravitreal corticosteroid through discussion between the patient and physician.
recommendations.context: Selection of diabetic retinopathy treatment.
recommendations.rationale: Patient needs vary.

recommendations.statement: Use established guidelines when operating a diabetic retinopathy screening program.
recommendations.context: Programs based on retinal imaging.
recommendations.rationale: Screening can facilitate early identification and appropriate referral where access to ophthalmic care is limited.

recommendations.statement: OCT appears to be an effective and sensitive imaging tool for detecting DME when there is no other cause of cystoid macular edema.
recommendations.context: Early detection of diabetic macular edema.
recommendations.rationale: OCT appears sensitive and effective for detecting DME under this condition.

recommendations.statement: Consider deferring treatment of CI-DME when visual acuity is 20/25 or better until visual acuity becomes worse than 20/25.
recommendations.context: Observation or focal laser surgery may be paired with aflibercept if visual acuity subsequently decreases.
recommendations.rationale: The compared initial strategies did not differ in visual acuity loss for eyes with good baseline acuity.

recommendations.statement: Consider deferring treatment of NCI-DME if visual acuity is better than 20/32, close follow-up is feasible, and the patient understands the risks.
For eyes with CI-DME and good visual acuity, it is reasonable to delay treatment until acuity is affected at 20/30 or worse, while examining the patient every 2 to 4 months.
recommendations.context: Decision to defer initial treatment.
recommendations.rationale: DRCR Protocol V found no difference in visual acuity loss among its initial aflibercept, laser-with-rescue, and observation-with-rescue strategies for eyes starting at 20/25 or better.

recommendations.statement: Use anti-VEGF therapy as the initial treatment for CI-DME with vision loss rather than focal laser surgery alone.
recommendations.context: Anti-VEGF treatment may be followed by focal laser surgery for persistent edema.
recommendations.rationale: Clinical trials and systematic reviews found better vision improvement with anti-VEGF therapy than with focal laser monotherapy.

recommendations.statement: Consider ranibizumab or aflibercept rather than conventional laser surgery for DME when selecting treatment to improve efficacy.
recommendations.context: The cited evidence compares these agents with conventional laser surgery.
recommendations.rationale: Numerous cited studies found both agents more effective than conventional laser surgery for DME.

recommendations.statement: Consider focal/grid laser surgery for NCI-DME.
recommendations.context: The role of anti-VEGF therapy in NCI-DME has not been studied.
recommendations.rationale: Focal/grid laser surgery remains the recommended treatment option in this setting.

recommendations.statement: When using focal/grid laser surgery, apply the modified ETDRS approach: use less intense energy, space treatments more widely than a grid pattern, target microaneurysms directly, and avoid foveal vessels within at least 500 µm of the macular center.
recommendations.context: Laser treatment for diabetic macular edema.

recommendations.statement: Consider laser photocoagulation surgery for DME rather than no intervention when the objective is to reduce visual loss or promote edema resolution.
recommendations.context: The cited Cochrane review assessed outcomes at 1 to 3 years.
recommendations.rationale: The review found reduced chances of visual loss and increased chances of partial or complete DME resolution compared with no intervention.

recommendations.statement: Discuss the potential adverse effects and risks of laser treatment with the patient before the procedure.
recommendations.context: Preoperative counseling for macular laser surgery.

recommendations.statement: Arrange an evaluation within 3 to 4 months after macular laser surgery.
recommendations.context: Post-treatment assessment.

recommendations.statement: Generally reserve intravitreal corticosteroids for second-line treatment of DME, particularly in phakic patients.
recommendations.context: Their use may be considered when response to anti-VEGF therapy is suboptimal or absent.
recommendations.rationale: Intravitreal corticosteroids can accelerate cataract and elevate IOP.

recommendations.statement: Do not expect additional overall benefit from routinely combining a corticosteroid with anti-VEGF therapy instead of using anti-VEGF therapy alone for DME.
