recommendations.context: The cited review judged the evidence base for its conclusion to be low-certainty because relatively few studies had long-term follow-up.
recommendations.rationale: A cited Cochrane review concluded that the combination provided no additional benefit over anti-VEGF monotherapy.

recommendations.statement: Consider pars plana vitrectomy for selected patients with diffuse DME, substantial vitreomacular traction, and inadequate response to prior macular laser surgery and/or anti-VEGF therapy.
recommendations.rationale: Visual acuity may improve in selected eyes, although outcomes vary.

recommendations.statement: Re-examine patients with a normal retinal examination or only rare microaneurysms annually.
recommendations.context: Normal retina or minimal NPDR.
recommendations.rationale: Within 1 year, 5% to 10% of patients without retinopathy develop diabetic retinopathy.

recommendations.statement: Re-examine patients with mild to moderate NPDR without macular edema within 6 to 12 months.
recommendations.context: Findings may include microaneurysms and occasional blot hemorrhages or hard exudates.
recommendations.rationale: Progression is common.
recommendations.source_heading: Mild to Moderate NPDR without Macular Edema

recommendations.statement: Consider closer follow-up after stopping anti-VEGF treatment for well-controlled edema, particularly when the patient has more advanced retinopathy.
recommendations.context: Mild to moderate retinopathy treated with anti-VEGF therapy.
recommendations.rationale: Diabetic retinopathy may be more likely to progress after treatment stops.
recommendations.source_heading: Mild to Moderate NPDR without Macular Edema

recommendations.statement: Consider early PRP for very severe NPDR or non-high-risk PDR, while recognizing that postponement until high-risk features appear can be reasonable.
recommendations.context: The decision is particularly pertinent as retinopathy approaches the high-risk stage.
recommendations.rationale: These eyes have a nearly 50% risk of reaching high-risk PDR within 1 year.

recommendations.statement: Re-examine patients with severe NPDR or non-high-risk PDR within 2 to 4 months.
recommendations.rationale: Their risk of progression to more advanced proliferative disease is high.

recommendations.statement: Provide PRP promptly to most patients with high-risk PDR.
recommendations.rationale: PRP substantially reduces severe visual loss risk and usually causes retinal neovascularization to regress.

recommendations.statement: Choose anti-VEGF treatment instead of PRP for PDR cautiously, taking patient-related factors and the reliability of follow-up into account; anti-VEGF treatment alone may be considered when follow-up is reliable.
recommendations.context: Selection between repeated injections and PRP.
recommendations.rationale: Outcomes after loss to follow-up are worse in patients receiving injections than in those who received PRP.

recommendations.statement: Consider additional PRP and/or anti-VEGF therapy if neovascularization fails to regress, retinal or iris neovascularization increases, a new vitreous hemorrhage occurs, or new neovascular areas appear.
recommendations.context: Monitoring response to treatment of PDR.

recommendations.statement: Consider pars plana vitrectomy for PDR with vitreous opacity that obstructs vision or treatment, severe fibrovascular proliferation, or tractional retinal detachment threatening or involving the macula.
recommendations.rationale: The value of early surgery rises as neovascularization becomes more severe.

recommendations.statement: If laser treatment is chosen for PDR or severe NPDR, use full PRP rather than partial or limited PRP.
recommendations.rationale: Full PRP is the established treatment approach.

recommendations.statement: Before PRP, assess for macular edema, discuss treatment adverse effects and visual-loss risks with the patient, and obtain informed consent.
recommendations.context: Preoperative assessment and counseling.
recommendations.rationale: PRP may worsen coexisting macular edema.

recommendations.statement: When PDR coexists with CSME and PRP may aggravate macular edema, perform focal photocoagulation and/or anti-VEGF therapy before or alongside PRP.
recommendations.context: Concurrent proliferative disease and macular edema.
recommendations.rationale: PRP can exacerbate edema and increase moderate visual-loss risk.

recommendations.statement: Do not postpone PRP for high-risk PDR because of concurrent macular edema; anti-VEGF therapy and PRP may be given together.
recommendations.context: Especially when NVD is extensive or vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage has occurred recently.
recommendations.rationale: High-risk proliferative disease requires timely treatment.

recommendations.statement: Consider combined anti-VEGF therapy and PRP at the first treatment session when CI-DME accompanies PDR.
Consider anti-VEGF therapy as an alternative to PRP for PDR when treatment adherence and follow-up are sufficiently reliable.
recommendations.context: Comparison of anti-VEGF treatment with PRP.
recommendations.rationale: A cited systematic review and meta-analysis favored anti-VEGF therapy because it was associated with fewer adverse events, including severe or moderate visual loss.

recommendations.statement: Consider anti-VEGF treatment for PDR when seeking better visual outcomes than PRP alone or combined anti-VEGF and PRP.
recommendations.context: Conclusion of a cited systematic review.
recommendations.rationale: The cited review associated anti-VEGF therapy with better visual outcomes than either comparator.

recommendations.statement: Consider vitrectomy when proliferative disease remains active despite anti-VEGF therapy or PRP, or cannot be managed medically; typical indications include nonclearing vitreous hemorrhage, tractional detachment involving or threatening the macula, combined rhegmatogenous and tractional detachment, and dense premacular subhyaloid hemorrhage.
Use serial ultrasound examinations to monitor vitreous hemorrhage for a retinal tear or a threatening tractional or rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
recommendations.context: Follow-up of diabetic vitreous hemorrhage.
recommendations.rationale: Hemorrhage may obstruct direct assessment of the retina.

recommendations.statement: Consider anti-VEGF treatment before vitrectomy for proliferative diabetic disease.
recommendations.context: Preoperative preparation.
recommendations.rationale: A cited meta-analysis suggested shorter operations, fewer retinal breaks, and less intraoperative bleeding.

recommendations.statement: Consider bevacizumab before or during vitrectomy to reduce postoperative vitreous hemorrhage.
recommendations.context: Perioperative treatment.
recommendations.rationale: A cited Cochrane review suggested that bevacizumab may lower postoperative hemorrhage incidence.

recommendations.statement: Consider either anti-VEGF therapy or vitrectomy as initial treatment when persistent vitreous hemorrhage is the only presenting problem.
recommendations.rationale: Visual and anatomical outcomes can be similar, although visual recovery takes substantially longer with anti-VEGF therapy.

recommendations.statement: Refer patients with diabetes to a primary care physician or endocrinologist for systemic management, and communicate the ophthalmic examination findings to the clinician overseeing diabetes care.
recommendations.context: Coordination of ophthalmic and systemic care.

recommendations.statement: Offer appropriate professional support and referral for counseling, vision rehabilitation, or social services when vision loss persists despite treatment or no further treatment is available.
recommendations.context: Patients with substantial visual impairment.

recommendations.statement: Refer patients whose visual impairment limits daily functioning for vision rehabilitation and social services.
recommendations.rationale: Vision rehabilitation improves functional ability.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with type 1 diabetes and no DR
decision_rules: Begin dilated ophthalmic examinations 5 years after the diagnosis of type 1 diabetes and repeat them yearly.
Increase vigilance during puberty because DR can progress more rapidly.
Educate patients about the visual importance of glucose control from the onset of diabetes.

recommended_regimens.name: Dilated fundus examination
recommended_regimens.summary: Use regular examinations to detect retinopathy before visual symptoms appear.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Yearly, beginning 5 years after diagnosis

response_assessment.method: Classify DR and macular edema separately in each eye and review the level of diabetes control.
response_assessment.interpretation: The ocular findings and diabetes control determine subsequent examination and intervention timing.

supportive_care: Encourage control of blood glucose, blood pressure, serum lipids, body weight, and other systemic risk factors in coordination with the clinicians managing diabetes.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Abnormal ocular findings may warrant shorter examination intervals.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with type 2 diabetes and no DR
decision_rules: Arrange a comprehensive diabetic eye examination when type 2 diabetes is diagnosed, then continue examinations at least yearly.

recommended_regimens.name: Dilated fundus examination
recommended_regimens.summary: Examine the retina at diagnosis and continue surveillance to identify new DR.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: At diagnosis and at least yearly thereafter

response_assessment.method: Assess both eyes for DR and macular edema and classify any detected disease.
response_assessment.interpretation: The findings guide the need for closer follow-up or treatment.

supportive_care: Promote management of blood glucose, blood pressure, serum lipids, and other systemic risks with the patient's diabetes-care clinicians.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Type 2 diabetes may have been present for years before its diagnosis.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with diabetes who need retinal screening, particularly where access to ophthalmic care is limited
decision_rules: A dilated fundus examination is the screening reference standard; validated digital retinal imaging may also detect DR.
Use screening to identify patients who need ophthalmologist assessment and possible treatment, rather than annual screening alone.
Photographic screening programs should follow established guidelines.

recommended_regimens.name: Dilated fundus examination
recommended_regimens.summary: Provide regular retinal assessment even when vision is good and ocular symptoms are absent.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: At least yearly, subject to diabetes type and ocular findings

alternative_regimens.name: Digital retinal imaging
alternative_regimens.summary: Validated photographic screening may detect DR and support timely referral for a more detailed examination.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Screening programs may be particularly relevant where direct ophthalmic care is difficult to access.

alternative_regimens.name: OCT
alternative_regimens.summary: May sensitively detect DME when another cause of cystoid macular edema is absent.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Use when evaluating possible DME; it does not replace classification of the complete retinal examination.

not_recommended.name: Routine FA
not_recommended.reason: FA is not indicated as a routine part of the regular examination of patients with diabetes.

response_assessment.method: Determine whether retinal findings warrant ophthalmologist follow-up, retinal treatment assessment, or continued annual screening.
response_assessment.interpretation: Patients requiring closer assessment should be referred promptly.

supportive_care: Explain that substantial retinal disease may be present despite good vision and no ocular symptoms.
Coordinate examination results and systemic risk-factor management with the clinician overseeing diabetes care.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The effects of autonomous screening systems on visual outcomes have not yet been established.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with diabetes who are planning pregnancy or are pregnant
decision_rules: For pre-existing diabetes, perform an ophthalmic examination before a planned pregnancy and counsel about the possibility of DR developing or progressing.
Examine patients early in pregnancy, then set follow-up frequency according to DR severity.
An eye examination during pregnancy is not required solely because gestational diabetes develops.

recommended_regimens.name: Ophthalmologic examination
recommended_regimens.summary: Monitor patients with pre-existing diabetes because retinopathy can worsen during pregnancy.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Before a planned pregnancy; soon after conception and early in the first trimester; every 3–12 months for no retinopathy to mild or moderate NPDR, or every 1–3 months for severe NPDR or worse

response_assessment.method: Reassess DR severity at follow-up eye examinations.
response_assessment.interpretation: Greater severity calls for more frequent surveillance.

supportive_care: Coordinate blood glucose and blood pressure management and other pregnancy-related care with the obstetrician or primary care physician.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Patients who develop gestational diabetes do not appear to have increased DR risk during pregnancy. Pregnancy can also affect decisions about PRP and the timing of treatment for macular edema.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with diabetes receiving systemic risk-factor management
decision_rules: Encourage near-normal glucose and blood pressure control to lower the risk of DR developing or progressing, while individualizing systemic treatment.
The stated HbA1c target for most patients is 7% or lower; selected patients may benefit from a target of 6.5%.
Monitor the eyes more frequently when long-standing poor metabolic control is improved rapidly, because retinopathy may initially worsen.
Do not change aspirin prescribed for another medical indication solely because of diabetic retinal disease.

recommended_regimens.name: Blood glucose and blood pressure control
recommended_regimens.summary: Work with the clinicians managing diabetes to optimize glycemia and blood pressure while considering the safety of intensified treatment.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In the DCCT, each 10% decrease in HbA1c was associated with a 39% decrease in the risk of retinopathy progression across the HbA1c range studied.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Ongoing

not_recommended.name: Aspirin for DR progression
not_recommended.reason: The ETDRS found that aspirin therapy at 650 mg per day did not slow DR progression.

response_assessment.method: Monitor retinal findings, including possible transient cotton wool spots or other evidence of progression.
response_assessment.interpretation: Rapid improvement after prolonged poor control may be followed by worsening during the first year in some patients.

supportive_care: Communicate retinal findings and the need for systemic risk-factor control to the patient's primary care physician or endocrinologist.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Intensive glucose control can increase hypoglycemia risk. The guide also reports possible early DR worsening with rapid glycemic control, including in patients receiving semaglutide.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with mild NPDR without macular edema
decision_rules: Continue retinal surveillance rather than initiating ocular treatment solely for mild NPDR without macular edema.
Assess for new edema, increasing hemorrhages, or progression to a more severe DR category.

recommended_regimens.name: Ophthalmologic examination
recommended_regimens.summary: Observe retinal disease and reassess the need for treatment if severity or macular findings change.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: The initial-management table gives follow-up at 12 months; the accompanying discussion advises re-examination within 6 to 12 months for mild to moderate NPDR without macular edema.

response_assessment.method: Assess retinal severity, visual acuity, and the presence of DME.
response_assessment.interpretation: Progression or edema may require a different follow-up interval or treatment pathway.

supportive_care: Encourage control of systemic diabetes risk factors.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: If anti-VEGF therapy given for DME is stopped after edema control, closer surveillance may be needed because clinically observed DR severity may increase again.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with moderate NPDR without macular edema
decision_rules: Continue observation and shorten the examination interval if findings begin to approach severe NPDR.

recommended_regimens.name: Ophthalmologic examination
recommended_regimens.summary: Monitor for worsening retinopathy and newly developing macular edema.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Every 6–12 months, or sooner if signs approach severe NPDR

response_assessment.method: Reclassify DR severity and assess the macula.
response_assessment.interpretation: Findings approaching severe NPDR warrant closer follow-up.

supportive_care: Encourage systemic glycemic and blood pressure control.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The clinical indications for anti-VEGF treatment of moderate NPDR without another treatment indication remain unknown; blood glucose control and ability to attend follow-up also affect clinical judgment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with severe NPDR without high-risk PDR
decision_rules: Consider PRP or anti-VEGF treatment according to retinal severity and patient circumstances.

Deferring PRP until high-risk features appear can be reasonable, but consider earlier PRP especially for very severe NPDR, for patients with type 2 diabetes, or when progression risk affects the treatment decision.
Very severe NPDR denotes at least two of the severe NPDR features in the 4-2-1 rule.

recommended_regimens.name: Close ophthalmologic follow-up
recommended_regimens.summary: Re-examine patients closely when immediate treatment is deferred.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Within 2 to 4 months in the discussion of severe NPDR and non-high-risk PDR

alternative_regimens.name: PRP
alternative_regimens.summary: Early treatment can be considered before high-risk PDR develops, particularly in very severe NPDR and in patients with type 2 diabetes.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider disease severity, reliability of follow-up, fellow-eye status and response, impending or recent cataract surgery, and pregnancy.

alternative_regimens.name: Anti-VEGF
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered as treatment for severe NPDR; proactive aflibercept reduced progression to vision-threatening complications in cited studies, without a demonstrated visual acuity advantage in DRCR Protocol W.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Weigh the need for repeated treatment and dependable follow-up against the patient's circumstances.

response_assessment.method: Check for neovascularization, worsening DR, and CI-DME.
response_assessment.interpretation: New high-risk PDR or visually significant edema changes the treatment decision.

supportive_care: Continue systemic risk-factor management.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: In ETDRS analyses of patients with type 2 diabetes and severe NPDR to non-high-risk PDR, early PRP reduced severe vision loss or vitrectomy by 50% (2.5% vs. 5%; P = 0.0001) compared with deferring PRP until high-risk PDR.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Eyes with moderate to severe NPDR being considered for proactive treatment before PDR or CI-DME with vision loss develops
decision_rules: Discuss the lower observed risk of PDR or CI-DME with vision loss under proactive aflibercept treatment alongside the absence of a visual acuity benefit in DRCR Protocol W.
Take account of repeated injections and the patient's ability to continue follow-up.

alternative_regimens.name: aflibercept 2 mg
alternative_regimens.summary: PANORAMA and DRCR Protocol W evaluated proactive injections for NPDR; both reported fewer vision-threatening complications than their control groups.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An individualized option for selected patients with moderate to severe NPDR after consideration of treatment burden and uncertain visual acuity benefit.

response_assessment.method: Assess DRSS level, development of PDR, CI-DME with vision loss, and visual acuity.
response_assessment.interpretation: In DRCR Protocol W, aflibercept lowered the probability of PDR or CI-DME with vision loss but did not improve visual acuity relative to treatment after a complication developed.

supportive_care: Maintain reliable retinal follow-up and systemic diabetes management.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: In DRCR Protocol W, CI-DME with vision loss or PDR occurred by 2 years in 16.3% of aflibercept-treated eyes versus 43.5% of sham-treated eyes (HR = 0.32; P < 0.001). The mean (SD) change in visual acuity from baseline to 2 years was -0.9 (5.8) letters with aflibercept versus -2.0 (6.1) letters with sham (adjusted mean difference, 0.5 letters; P = 0.47).

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with non-center-involved diabetic macular edema
decision_rules: Consider focal/grid laser surgery when treatment of NCI-DME is indicated.
Deferring treatment is an option if visual acuity is better than 20/32, close follow-up is feasible, and the patient understands the risks.
The role of anti-VEGF treatment for NCI-DME has not been studied.

recommended_regimens.name: Focal/grid laser surgery
recommended_regimens.summary: The guide recommends focal/grid laser surgery as the treatment option for NCI-DME when ocular treatment is needed.

alternative_regimens.name: Observation
alternative_regimens.summary: Treatment can be deferred while monitoring vision and retinal findings.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Visual acuity better than 20/32, ability to attend close follow-up, and understanding of the risks.

response_assessment.timepoint: Within 3 to 4 months after laser surgery
response_assessment.method: Reassess visual acuity and macular edema.
response_assessment.interpretation: Persistent or changing edema informs subsequent care.

supportive_care: Discuss the adverse effects and risks of laser treatment before the procedure.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Modified ETDRS laser treatment uses less intense energy and wider spacing than grid treatment, targets microaneurysms, and avoids foveal vasculature within at least 500 µm of the macular center.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Eyes with center-involved diabetic macular edema and visual acuity of 20/25 or better
decision_rules: Treatment may reasonably be deferred while vision remains good; the guide describes deferral until visual acuity reaches 20/30 or worse.
DRCR Protocol V found no difference in visual acuity loss among initial aflibercept, focal laser surgery with aflibercept if vision declined, and observation with aflibercept if vision declined.

In the laser or observation strategies of DRCR Protocol V, add aflibercept when visual acuity declines from baseline by at least 10 letters at one visit or by 5 to 9 letters at two consecutive visits.

recommended_regimens.name: Observation
recommended_regimens.summary: Monitor good-vision CI-DME and begin treatment if visual acuity deteriorates.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In DRCR Protocol V, after 2 years all three studied strategies produced mean visual acuity of 20/20, without a significant change in OCT CST from baseline.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Examine every 2 to 4 months

alternative_regimens.name: Focal laser photocoagulation surgery with aflibercept if visual acuity decreases
alternative_regimens.summary: An initial laser strategy studied in DRCR Protocol V had visual outcomes comparable to initial observation or aflibercept.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Add aflibercept if the study's visual acuity decline criteria are met.

alternative_regimens.name: aflibercept 2 mg
alternative_regimens.summary: Initial intravitreal treatment was another strategy with comparable visual acuity outcomes in DRCR Protocol V.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An individualized alternative to initial observation or laser surgery.

response_assessment.method: Measure visual acuity and assess macular edema, including OCT findings.
response_assessment.interpretation: Worsening visual acuity can prompt initiation of anti-VEGF treatment.

supportive_care: Explain the need for dependable follow-up if immediate treatment is deferred.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guide identifies hypertension or fluid retention related to heart failure, renal failure, pregnancy, or another cause that may aggravate edema as exceptions requiring individualized management.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Eyes with center-involved diabetic macular edema and associated visual acuity loss
decision_rules: Select intravitreal anti-VEGF treatment as initial ocular therapy; clinical trials and systematic reviews found better visual improvement than with focal laser surgery alone.

Consider baseline visual acuity when selecting an agent: DRCR.net Protocol T found similar gains among bevacizumab, ranibizumab, and aflibercept 2 mg with visual acuity of 20/40 or better, but found an advantage for aflibercept over bevacizumab at 2 years when baseline visual acuity was 20/50 or worse.
Tailor the individual agent and dosing approach through discussion between the patient and ophthalmologist.
For persistent edema, subsequent focal laser surgery may be considered.

recommended_regimens.name: aflibercept 2 mg
recommended_regimens.summary: An intravitreal anti-VEGF initial-treatment option for CI-DME with vision loss.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In DRCR.net Protocol T eyes with baseline visual acuity of 20/50 or worse, mean visual acuity gain at 2 years was 18.3 letters with aflibercept, 13.3 letters with bevacizumab, and 16.1 letters with ranibizumab; a statistically significant difference was found only between aflibercept and bevacizumab.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: The described DRCR protocol begins with monthly injections for 4 to 6 months, followed by response-guided treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: bevacizumab
recommended_regimens.summary: An intravitreal anti-VEGF initial-treatment option; DRCR Protocol AC also studied starting with bevacizumab and switching to aflibercept 2 mg if needed.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In DRCR Protocol AC, visual outcomes at 2 years were similar for bevacizumab first with aflibercept 2 mg rescue and initial aflibercept, although 70% of patients in the bevacizumab arm eventually switched to aflibercept.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: The described DRCR protocol begins with monthly injections for 4 to 6 months, followed by response-guided treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: ranibizumab
recommended_regimens.summary: An intravitreal anti-VEGF initial-treatment option for CI-DME with vision loss.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: DRCR.net Protocol T found that all three compared anti-VEGF agents substantially improved visual acuity at 2 years.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: The described DRCR protocol begins with monthly injections for 4 to 6 months, followed by response-guided treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: faricimab-svoa
recommended_regimens.summary: An intravitreal treatment evaluated for DME in YOSEMITE and RHINE, with visual acuity gains noninferior to aflibercept 2 mg.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In the personalized treatment interval groups, 73.8% and 71.1% achieved intervals of every 12 weeks or greater at 1 year, and 52.8% and 51.0% achieved every 16 weeks.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: faricimab 6 mg every 8 weeks after six monthly loading doses, or a personalized treatment interval up to every 16 weeks after four monthly loading doses

recommended_regimens.name: aflibercept 8 mg
recommended_regimens.summary: A higher-dose aflibercept option for DME; PHOTON found noninferior visual acuity improvement relative to aflibercept 2 mg at week 48.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: At week 48, mean change in central retinal thickness was -171.7 µm with aflibercept 8 mg every 12 weeks, -148.3 µm with aflibercept 8 mg every 16 weeks, and -165.3 µm with aflibercept 2-mg.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: After 3 monthly loading doses, aflibercept 8 mg was given every 12 weeks or every 16 weeks in PHOTON; intervals could be shortened after week 16 according to prespecified disease activity criteria.

recommended_regimens.name: brolucizumab
recommended_regimens.summary: An anti-VEGF option studied in KITE and KESTREL with visual acuity noninferior to aflibercept at year 1; its intraocular inflammation and retinal vasculitis findings require consideration.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In KESTREL, intraocular inflammation occurred in 3.7% of brolucizumab 6 mg eyes, including 0.5% retinal vasculitis, versus 0.5% of aflibercept 2 mg eyes.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: 5 loading doses every 6 weeks, followed by dosing every 8 or 12 weeks in KITE and KESTREL

alternative_regimens.name: Focal laser photocoagulation surgery
alternative_regimens.summary: May be used subsequently for edema that persists despite anti-VEGF treatment.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Persistent macular edema after initial anti-VEGF therapy.

alternative_regimens.name: ranibizumab-eqrn
alternative_regimens.summary: A biosimilar interchangeable with ranibizumab 0.3 mg for DME and DR.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The treating ophthalmologist and patient choose the biologic product.

alternative_regimens.name: aflibercept-jbyf
alternative_regimens.summary: Listed among the FDA-approved aflibercept biosimilars for DR and DME.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The treating ophthalmologist and patient choose the biologic product.

alternative_regimens.name: aflibercept-yszy
alternative_regimens.summary: Listed among the FDA-approved aflibercept biosimilars for DR and DME.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The treating ophthalmologist and patient choose the biologic product.

alternative_regimens.name: aflibercept-mrbb
alternative_regimens.summary: Listed among the FDA-approved aflibercept biosimilars for DR and DME.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The treating ophthalmologist and patient choose the biologic product.

alternative_regimens.name: aflibercept-ayyh
alternative_regimens.summary: Listed among the FDA-approved aflibercept biosimilars for DR and DME.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The treating ophthalmologist and patient choose the biologic product.

not_recommended.name: ranibizumab-nuna 0.5 mg
not_recommended.reason: The guide states that it is not approved for DME, for which ranibizumab 0.3 mg is required.

response_assessment.timepoint: During the initial monthly injections and subsequent visits
response_assessment.method: Assess visual acuity and OCT central macular thickness or CST.
response_assessment.interpretation: Under the described DRCR protocol, injections may be held when vision or thickness no longer improves, or when 20/20 vision and/or edema resolution is achieved; resume injections if vision or thickness subsequently worsens.

response_assessment.timepoint: After consecutive visits without a need for treatment
response_assessment.method: Reassess visual acuity and OCT findings.
response_assessment.interpretation: The described DRCR protocol doubles the follow-up interval, up to 4 months.

supportive_care: Use topical povidone iodine for intravitreal injections.
Discuss the need for repeated visits and continued follow-up.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Anti-VEGF therapy is preferred over focal laser surgery alone for visual improvement in CI-DME with vision loss. Individual biologic selection belongs to the treating ophthalmologist and patient. The guide notes an absence of prospective long-term data beyond 1 year comparing ranibizumab biosimilars with ranibizumab.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Eyes responding to intravitreal anti-VEGF treatment for CI-DME
decision_rules: Adjust injections and visit intervals according to vision and OCT response rather than continuing initial monthly treatment unchanged.
Treat-and-extend is another approach to reducing injection burden.

recommended_regimens.name: Response-guided anti-VEGF
recommended_regimens.summary: The described DRCR approach pauses and restarts injections according to visual acuity and central macular thickness.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Monthly injections for 4 to 6 months initially; follow-up may then be doubled after consecutive visits without treatment, up to 4 months

alternative_regimens.name: Treat-and-extend
alternative_regimens.summary: Adjust the interval between visits according to treatment response; a prospective trial reported comparable visual and anatomic results to monthly dosing at 2 years with fewer injections.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An alternative approach when seeking to reduce the number of injections.

response_assessment.method: Measure visual acuity and OCT central macular thickness.
response_assessment.interpretation: Hold treatment for no further improvement or for 20/20 vision and/or edema resolution; restart if either vision or thickness worsens.

supportive_care: Maintain reliable follow-up throughout interval adjustment.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guide notes that OCT retinal thickness does not always correlate consistently with visual acuity.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with persistent or inadequately responsive DME after anti-VEGF treatment, especially patients with chronic edema
decision_rules: Consider intravitreal corticosteroid therapy when response to anti-VEGF injections is suboptimal or absent.
Weigh possible visual and anatomic improvement against cataract progression and elevated IOP, particularly in phakic eyes.
The fluocinolone acetonide implant is approved for patients previously treated with corticosteroids without an IOP rise.

recommended_regimens.name: Intravitreal corticosteroids
recommended_regimens.summary: Generally used as second-line DME treatment because of the adverse-effect profile; a response may be more likely with chronic edema.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A systematic review found no significant difference in visual acuity outcomes versus anti-VEGF treatment, lower retinal thickness, and more IOP adverse events.

alternative_regimens.name: dexamethasone implant
alternative_regimens.summary: An intravitreal implant that improved visual acuity over sham in the MEAD trial.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider the risks of cataract and IOP elevation when selecting corticosteroid treatment.

alternative_regimens.name: fluocinolone acetonide implant
alternative_regimens.summary: A sustained-release intravitreal implant that improved vision over sham in FAME.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Prior corticosteroid treatment without an increase in IOP.

alternative_regimens.name: triamcinolone acetonide
alternative_regimens.summary: Intravitreal use has been studied for DME; a study found visual gains with triamcinolone acetonide plus focal laser surgery in pseudophakic eyes similar to those in anti-VEGF-treated eyes.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Individualize use in light of cataract and IOP risks and the patient's lens status.

not_recommended.name: Topical corticosteroids and periocular corticosteroid injection
not_recommended.reason: The studies cited by the guide demonstrated no significant benefit for DME.

response_assessment.method: Monitor visual acuity, OCT retinal thickness, IOP, and lens status.
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess benefit alongside IOP elevation and cataract progression.

supportive_care: Counsel about cataract and elevated IOP.
Remain alert for anterior migration of a sustained-release implant, which may require urgent removal or repositioning.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: No large randomized clinical trial has evaluated intravitreal corticosteroid injection specifically as rescue treatment after anti-VEGF therapy for persistent DME.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Eyes with persistent center-involved DME after anti-VEGF injections
decision_rules: Consider subsequent focal laser surgery for persistent edema.
Do not infer an overall visual acuity benefit from adding a corticosteroid implant to anti-VEGF therapy solely because OCT thickness improves.

alternative_regimens.name: Focal laser photocoagulation surgery
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered after anti-VEGF therapy when edema persists; the guide notes that it might reduce the injection burden.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Persistent edema despite anti-VEGF treatment.

not_recommended.name: Routine corticosteroid plus anti-VEGF combination for additional visual benefit
not_recommended.reason: A Cochrane review concluded that the combination provided no additional benefit over anti-VEGF monotherapy, although the guide notes that the evidence base for this conclusion had low certainty because long-term studies were scarce.

response_assessment.timepoint: During follow-up after a treatment change
response_assessment.method: Compare visual acuity with OCT-assessed macular thickness.
response_assessment.interpretation: An anatomic improvement need not represent an additional visual acuity benefit.

supportive_care: Discuss the higher cataract and elevated IOP risks associated with corticosteroids.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: In the cited DRCR.net phase 2 trial, adding a dexamethasone implant after at least three anti-VEGF injections in the previous 20 weeks reduced central macular thickness without improving overall visual acuity. A preplanned subgroup analysis found 15-letter or greater improvement in 11% with combination treatment versus 2% with anti-VEGF alone (P = 0.03).

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Selected eyes with diffuse DME, substantial vitreomacular traction, and an inadequate response to previous macular laser surgery and/or anti-VEGF therapy
decision_rules: Consider pars plana vitrectomy when substantial traction accompanies persistent diffuse DME.
Discuss the possibility of either visual improvement or deterioration.

alternative_regimens.name: Pars plana vitrectomy
alternative_regimens.summary: May improve visual acuity in selected patients with tractional, treatment-unresponsive DME.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Substantial vitreomacular traction and diffuse DME unresponsive to prior macular laser surgery and/or anti-VEGF treatment.

response_assessment.method: Assess visual acuity and retinal thickening.
response_assessment.interpretation: In DRCR.net Protocol D, 38% of eyes with DME and vitreomacular traction improved in visual acuity, whereas 22% experienced visual acuity loss.

supportive_care: Counsel about the potential complications of vitrectomy.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guide states that the role of vitrectomy alongside anti-VEGF therapy is difficult to determine because most studies of vitrectomy for DME preceded anti-VEGF treatment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with proliferative retinopathy that has not developed high-risk characteristics
decision_rules: PRP may be deferred until high-risk findings appear when close follow-up is feasible.
Consider earlier PRP, particularly when the retinopathy approaches the high-risk stage or the patient has type 2 diabetes.
Choose between laser and an anti-VEGF approach with careful attention to the reliability of follow-up.

recommended_regimens.name: Close ophthalmologic follow-up
recommended_regimens.summary: Monitor for progression when PRP is deferred.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Within 2 to 4 months

alternative_regimens.name: PRP
alternative_regimens.summary: Early PRP may be considered before high-risk PDR develops.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Particularly relevant when findings approach high-risk PDR or patient circumstances favor treatment before progression.

alternative_regimens.name: Anti-VEGF
alternative_regimens.summary: An ocular treatment option for proliferative disease that requires sustained follow-up.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider only with attention to repeated-treatment requirements and the patient's ability to attend follow-up.

response_assessment.method: Assess neovascularization, hemorrhage, visual acuity, and macular edema.
response_assessment.interpretation: The appearance of high-risk features warrants prompt treatment.

supportive_care: Continue management of systemic diabetes risk factors.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: ETDRS reported that eyes with very severe NPDR or non-high-risk PDR approaching the high-risk stage had a 50% risk of reaching it within 12 to 18 months.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with high-risk proliferative diabetic retinopathy or neovascular glaucoma
decision_rules: Treat high-risk PDR promptly; most patients should receive PRP expeditiously.
Do not postpone PRP because of concomitant edema when high-risk features include extensive NVD or recent vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage.
Anti-VEGF treatment may be used for PDR, but choosing it instead of PRP requires careful consideration of follow-up reliability.

recommended_regimens.name: PRP
recommended_regimens.summary: Prompt scatter laser treatment usually leads to regression of neovascularization and substantially reduces severe visual loss in high-risk PDR.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In the DRS table, severe visual loss in high-risk proliferative disease at 2 years occurred in 26% of control patients versus 11% of treated patients, and at 4 years in 44% versus 20%, respectively.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: The ETDRS full-PRP protocol used 1200 to 1600 spots with burns of 0.1 second duration.

alternative_regimens.name: Anti-VEGF
alternative_regimens.summary: Can be considered instead of PRP for PDR when ongoing injections and dependable follow-up are feasible; cited reviews report favorable outcomes compared with PRP.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Patients with reliable follow-up after a careful assessment of patient-related factors.

alternative_regimens.name: Anti-VEGF and PRP
alternative_regimens.summary: Can be administered together when urgent PDR treatment is needed; combined treatment should be considered at the first session when CI-DME is also present.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: High-risk PDR that should not wait for prior edema treatment, particularly with concurrent CI-DME.

not_recommended.name: Partial or limited PRP
not_recommended.reason: The guide advises against partial or limited treatment when laser surgery is selected and identifies full PRP as the proven approach.

response_assessment.method: Evaluate regression or increase of retinal or iris neovascularization and check for new vitreous hemorrhage or new neovascular areas.
response_assessment.interpretation: Failure to regress, increasing neovascularization, new hemorrhage, or new neovascularization calls for consideration of additional PRP and/or anti-VEGF.

supportive_care: Before PRP, assess macular edema, discuss the risks of visual loss and other adverse effects, and obtain informed consent.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Patients lost to follow-up after anti-VEGF treatment for PDR had worse visual and anatomic outcomes than those who received PRP. PRP may itself worsen macular edema.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with PDR selected for intravitreal treatment who can attend repeated visits
decision_rules: Anti-VEGF is an alternative to PRP when follow-up is reliable.
Base subsequent injections on whether retinal neovascularization persists or remains active.
Consider the consequences of lapses in follow-up before choosing injections alone.

recommended_regimens.name: ranibizumab
recommended_regimens.summary: DRCR.net Protocol S found intravitreal ranibizumab noninferior to PRP for visual acuity at 2 years in patients primarily with PDR.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In Protocol S, mean visual acuity improvement at 2 years was +2.8 letters with ranibizumab versus +0.2 letters with PRP (P < 0.001).
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: In Protocol S, monthly treatment for 6 months unless neovascularization had completely regressed at 4 months, followed by treatment as needed according to neovascular activity.

alternative_regimens.name: aflibercept 2 mg
alternative_regimens.summary: A cited study found outcomes similar to PRP for PDR and suggested a possible visual acuity advantage at 1 year in eyes without CI-DME.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An anti-VEGF option when repeated treatment and follow-up are feasible.

alternative_regimens.name: PRP
alternative_regimens.summary: A proven treatment for PDR that is important when injection follow-up cannot be relied upon.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider patient-related factors, particularly the risk of missing repeated injection visits.

response_assessment.method: Examine retinal neovascularization and assess visual acuity, visual field findings, hemorrhage, and DME.
response_assessment.interpretation: Active or recurrent neovascularization informs retreatment.

supportive_care: Use topical povidone iodine for each intravitreal injection.
Explain the number of visits and the importance of avoiding prolonged follow-up lapses.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Protocol S reported more treatments and visits with ranibizumab than with PRP. At 5 years, the guide reports no difference in visual field changes between the two groups.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with PDR and concomitant clinically significant macular edema or CI-DME
decision_rules: Consider focal photocoagulation and/or anti-VEGF before or alongside PRP when PRP could aggravate macular edema.
Do not delay PRP for high-risk PDR; anti-VEGF and PRP may instead be given together.
Consider combined anti-VEGF treatment and PRP at the first treatment session when CI-DME is present.

recommended_regimens.name: Anti-VEGF and PRP
recommended_regimens.summary: Address proliferative disease without delaying urgent PRP and treat concurrent center-involved edema.

alternative_regimens.name: Focal photocoagulation surgery and PRP
alternative_regimens.summary: Focal treatment may precede or accompany PRP when worsening of macular edema is a concern.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Concomitant clinically significant edema for which PRP may aggravate macular findings.

response_assessment.method: Monitor visual acuity, macular edema, and neovascularization.
response_assessment.interpretation: Persistent edema or active neovascularization may call for additional treatment.

supportive_care: Discuss the risk that PRP can exacerbate macular edema.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: A cited 2023 Cochrane review found that anti-VEGF with or without PRP regressed new vessels, reduced vitreous hemorrhage, and improved visual acuity, but the visual acuity improvement compared with PRP alone did not appear clinically meaningful.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with persistent visually significant vitreous hemorrhage without another stated indication requiring immediate vitrectomy
decision_rules: Either anti-VEGF treatment or vitrectomy with PRP is a reasonable initial approach for persistent vitreous hemorrhage alone.
Explain that vitrectomy cleared hemorrhage faster in DRCR Protocol AB despite no difference in its primary visual acuity outcome at 24 weeks.
Use serial ultrasonography to assess for a retinal tear or detachment when hemorrhage obscures the retinal view.

recommended_regimens.name: aflibercept 2 mg
recommended_regimens.summary: An injection strategy compared with vitrectomy plus PRP in DRCR Protocol AB.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Protocol AB found no difference in its primary visual acuity outcome at 24 weeks; vitreous hemorrhage cleared in 36 weeks in the aflibercept group versus 4 weeks in the vitrectomy group (P < 0.001).
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Monthly injections in DRCR Protocol AB

recommended_regimens.name: Vitrectomy with PRP
recommended_regimens.summary: A reasonable initial option that provided more rapid hemorrhage clearance than aflibercept in Protocol AB.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Protocol AB reported hemorrhage clearance in 4 weeks with vitrectomy versus 36 weeks with aflibercept (P < 0.001), without a difference in the primary visual acuity outcome at 24 weeks.

response_assessment.method: Perform serial ultrasonography to look for retinal tear, macula-threatening tractional retinal detachment, or rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.
response_assessment.interpretation: A detected complication may alter the need for surgery.

supportive_care: Explain the difference in time to hemorrhage clearance between the studied approaches.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: In Protocol AB, approximately one third of eyes in each group received the alternative treatment during follow-up under protocol-specific criteria.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with nonclearing vitreous hemorrhage, severe fibrovascular proliferation, dense premacular subhyaloid hemorrhage, or tractional or combined retinal detachment
decision_rules: Consider pars plana vitrectomy when vitreous opacity prevents vision or retinal treatment, or when traction threatens or involves the macula.
Additional indications include combined rhegmatogenous and tractional retinal detachment and dense premacular subhyaloid hemorrhage.
Greater neovascularization severity increases the potential value of early surgery.

recommended_regimens.name: Pars plana vitrectomy
recommended_regimens.summary: A surgical option for hemorrhage, fibrovascular proliferation, or detachment that cannot adequately be managed with medical treatment or PRP alone.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In the DRVS, visual acuity of 20/40 or better at 2 years occurred in 25% of the early-vitrectomy group and 15% of the deferral group; the advantage was greatest in patients with type 1 diabetes (36% vs. 12% for early surgery versus deferral).
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: The DRVS compared vitrectomy within 1 to 6 months of vitreous hemorrhage onset with later vitrectomy at 1 year.

alternative_regimens.name: Preoperative anti-VEGF
alternative_regimens.summary: A cited meta-analysis suggested reductions in surgical duration, retinal breaks, and intra-operative bleeding.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider when preparing selected patients for vitrectomy.

alternative_regimens.name: Preoperative or intra-operative bevacizumab
alternative_regimens.summary: A cited Cochrane review suggested a possible reduction in postoperative vitreous hemorrhage.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider in conjunction with vitrectomy.

response_assessment.timepoint: Before surgery and during follow-up of obscuring hemorrhage
response_assessment.method: Use serial ultrasonography to assess the retina for tears and tractional or rhegmatogenous detachment.
response_assessment.interpretation: Macula-threatening traction or detachment strengthens the indication for surgical management.

response_assessment.method: Assess visual acuity, recurrent vitreous hemorrhage, and retinal status.

supportive_care: Discuss the ocular risks of vitrectomy before surgery.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: DRVS found the early-vitrectomy advantage for severe vitreous hemorrhage in type 1 diabetes but not in type 2 diabetes. The guide nevertheless advises considering early surgery in selected patients with type 2 diabetes when severe hemorrhage prevents laser treatment of active neovascularization.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients previously treated with PRP or anti-VEGF for PDR
decision_rules: Consider additional PRP and/or anti-VEGF if neovascularization fails to regress, retinal or iris neovascularization increases, vitreous hemorrhage is new, or new neovascular areas appear.
A vitreous hemorrhage caused by traction on involuted neovascularization does not necessarily require more PRP, particularly without venous dilation.

recommended_regimens.name: Additional PRP and/or anti-VEGF
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider retreatment when proliferative activity persists or recurs.

alternative_regimens.name: Observation
alternative_regimens.summary: Additional PRP may be unnecessary for hemorrhage related to traction on involuted neovascular tissue.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Involutional PDR, especially when venous dilation is absent and other retreatment indications are not present.

response_assessment.method: Assess neovascular regression, new retinal or iris vessels, and new vitreous hemorrhage.
response_assessment.interpretation: Persistent or increasing proliferative activity prompts consideration of further treatment.

supportive_care: Maintain follow-up, particularly when continuing anti-VEGF treatment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with functionally limiting vision loss or disease that has not responded to surgery and has no further available treatment
decision_rules: Offer professional support and referral when additional ocular treatment is unavailable.
Refer patients whose visual impairment limits function for vision rehabilitation and social services.
Consider counseling, vocational rehabilitation, or peer support for depression, anxiety, or loss of independence or employment.

recommended_regimens.name: Vision rehabilitation
recommended_regimens.summary: Provide or arrange services to improve functional ability in patients with limiting visual impairment.

supportive_care: Use empathetic communication to identify the patient's concerns.
Offer counseling and social-service referrals when appropriate.

special_populations.considerations: Annual dilated eye examinations should begin 5 years after diagnosis. Patient education about the visual importance of early glucose control should begin when diabetes develops.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: The DRVS found a benefit from early vitrectomy for severe vitreous hemorrhage in patients with type 1 diabetes. For severe NPDR or non-high-risk PDR, the timing of PRP depends on follow-up adherence and the status and treatment response of the fellow eye.

special_populations.considerations: Because diabetes may precede its diagnosis, a comprehensive diabetic eye examination should occur at diagnosis, followed by examinations at least annually.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: For severe NPDR or non-high-risk PDR, considering PRP before high-risk PDR develops is particularly appropriate: an ETDRS analysis found that early treatment reduced severe vision loss or vitrectomy risk by 50% (2.5% vs. 5%; P = 0.0001) compared with deferring PRP. The DRVS did not find an early-vitrectomy advantage for patients with type 2 diabetes overall, although early vitrectomy should be considered for selected patients when severe vitreous hemorrhage prevents laser treatment of active neovascularization.

special_populations.population: Women with pre-existing type 1 or type 2 diabetes who plan pregnancy or are pregnant
special_populations.considerations: DR may progress rapidly during pregnancy. An eye examination and counseling about this risk should occur before a planned pregnancy. During pregnancy, examination is recommended soon after conception and early in the first trimester. Follow-up is every 3–12 months for no retinopathy through mild or moderate NPDR, and every 1–3 months for severe NPDR or worse.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Pregnancy may influence the decision to perform PRP in severe NPDR or non-high-risk PDR. If pregnancy may aggravate macular edema, a brief postponement of photocoagulation during medical treatment may be considered.

special_populations.population: Women who develop gestational diabetes during pregnancy
special_populations.considerations: They do not appear to have an increased risk of DR during pregnancy and do not require an eye examination during pregnancy on account of gestational diabetes.
DR can progress faster during puberty; the reported relative risk was 4.8 compared with prepubescent patients despite similar durations of diabetes. Follow-up requires greater vigilance.

Vision-threatening retinopathy is uncommon before puberty. One study of youths reported DR development in 20.1% of those with type 1 diabetes and 7.2% of those with type 2 diabetes over median follow-up periods of 3.2 and 3.1 years, respectively (P < 0.0001). A separate retrospective review reported higher DR rates in youths with type 2 diabetes and suggested ophthalmoscopic assessment at least as often as, or more often than, in children with type 1 diabetes.

special_populations.population: Patients on dialysis or with advanced kidney disease
special_populations.considerations: Patients on dialysis have a higher prevalence of DR than patients not receiving dialysis. A review reported increased retinal vein occlusions among patients with advanced kidney disease treated with SGLT-2 inhibitors.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: When renal failure may aggravate macular edema, postponing photocoagulation briefly during medical treatment may be considered.

special_populations.population: Patients with hypertension or fluid retention associated with heart failure
special_populations.considerations: Hypertension and fluid retention associated with heart failure may aggravate macular edema.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: A brief deferral of photocoagulation while the contributing medical condition is treated may be considered.

special_populations.population: Eyes with CI-DME and good visual acuity
special_populations.considerations: In DRCR Protocol V, eyes with visual acuity of 20/25 or better had no difference in visual acuity loss between initial aflibercept, focal laser surgery with aflibercept if acuity declined, and observation with aflibercept if acuity declined.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Treatment can reasonably be deferred until visual acuity reaches 20/30 or worse, with examination every 2 to 4 months. In DRCR Protocol V, aflibercept was added after a decrease from baseline of at least 10 letters (> 2 lines on an eye chart) at one visit or 5 to 9 letters (1 to 2 lines) at two consecutive visits.

special_populations.population: Eyes with NCI-DME and excellent visual acuity
special_populations.considerations: Deferring treatment is an option when visual acuity is better than 20/32, close follow-up is feasible, and the patient understands the risks.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Focal/grid laser surgery is a recommended treatment option for NCI-DME; the role of anti-VEGF treatment in this setting has not been studied.

special_populations.population: Eyes with CI-DME and baseline visual acuity of 20/50 or worse
special_populations.considerations: DRCR.net Protocol T found superior mean visual acuity with aflibercept versus ranibizumab and bevacizumab at year 1. At year 2, superiority remained only versus bevacizumab.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: DRCR Protocol AC found similar visual outcomes at 2 years for starting with bevacizumab and switching to aflibercept 2 mg when needed versus starting with aflibercept; 70% of patients initially receiving bevacizumab eventually switched.

special_populations.population: Phakic and pseudophakic eyes receiving intravitreal corticosteroids
special_populations.considerations: Cataract progression and elevated IOP affect corticosteroid treatment decisions, particularly in phakic eyes. In a study, pseudophakic eyes receiving intravitreal triamcinolone acetonide with focal laser surgery had visual gains similar to eyes receiving anti-VEGF agents.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Intravitreal corticosteroids are generally used as second-line agents for DME, especially in phakic patients. The fluocinolone acetonide implant is approved for DME in patients previously treated with corticosteroids without an increase in IOP.

special_populations.population: Aphakic eyes and pseudophakic eyes with an open posterior capsule or disrupted lens zonules
special_populations.considerations: Migration of dexamethasone and fluocinolone sustained-release implants into the anterior chamber has occurred mainly in these eyes. Corneal edema or endothelial damage can result.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: A migrated dexamethasone implant requires urgent removal or repositioning to avoid corneal decompensation and keratoplasty. An anterior-chamber fluocinolone implant causing mechanical endothelial trauma or elevated IOP requires surgical removal.

special_populations.population: Patients with PDR whose follow-up may be unreliable
special_populations.considerations: Outcomes after loss to follow-up were worse for patients receiving anti-VEGF injections than for those receiving PRP. In a DRCR analysis, patients with 1 or more long follow-up lapses had a median visual acuity change of a loss of 2 letters, compared with a gain of 5 letters among those without a long lapse (P = 0.02).
special_populations.treatment_modifications: The choice of anti-VEGF treatment instead of PRP requires careful consideration of follow-up reliability; anti-VEGF treatment alone could be considered when follow-up is reliable.

special_populations.population: Patients with functionally limiting visual impairment or loss of independence
special_populations.considerations: Some patients lose substantial vision despite treatment. Depression, anxiety, or loss of independence or employment may warrant additional support.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Refer patients with functionally limiting visual impairment for vision rehabilitation and social services. Counseling, vocational rehabilitation, or peer-support referral should be considered according to the patient's needs.

rows: A Pilot Study of Laser Photocoagulation for Diabetic Macular Edema

In eyes with DME, an MMG photocoagulation technique was less effective at reducing OCT-measured retinal thickening over 12 months than the standard focal photocoagulation technique modified from the ETDRS.
A Randomized Control Trial Comparing Intravitreal Triamcinolone Acetonide and Laser Photocoagulation for Diabetic Macular Edema
Over 2 years, focal/grid photocoagulation for center-involved DME was more effective and had fewer adverse effects than 1-mg or 4-mg doses of preservative-free intravitreal triamcinolone.
Temporal Variation in Optical Coherence Tomography Measurements of Retinal Thickening in Diabetic Macular Edema

Although retinal thickening decreases slightly over the day on average, most eyes with DME have little meaningful change in OCT, CST, or visual acuity between the hours of 8 AM and 4 PM. A change in CST over 11% is likely to be real.
Evaluation of Vitrectomy for Diabetic Macular Edema Study

Vitrectomy reduces retinal thickening in most eyes with DME and vitreomacular traction. Although visual acuity outcomes improved by 10 or more letters in 38% of eyes, 22% lost 10 or more letters after vitrectomy
A Pilot Study of Peribulbar Triamcinolone Acetonide for Diabetic Macular Edema
In cases of DME where the patient has good visual acuity, peribulbar triamcinolone, with or without focal photocoagulation, is unlikely to be of substantial benefit.
An Observational Study of the Development of Diabetic Macular Edema Following Scatter Laser Photocoagulation
Clinically meaningful differences in OCT thickness or visual acuity are not substantially different when PRP is applied in one sitting compared with four sittings.

Approximately one quarter to one half of eyes diagnosed with subclinical DME will progress to more definite thickening or be judged to need treatment for DME within 2 years. Because CST is greater in men than in women, studies involving comparisons of retinal thickness to expected norms should consider different mean values for men and women.
A Phase 2 Evaluation of Anti-VEGF Therapy for Diabetic Macular Edema: Bevacizumab (Avastin)
Intravitreal bevacizumab can reduce DME in some eyes, but this preliminary study was not designed to definitively determine whether the treatment was beneficial.
Intravitreal Ranibizumab or Triamcinolone Acetonide in Combination with Laser Photocoagulation for Diabetic Macular Edema

At 2 years, intravitreal ranibizumab with prompt or deferred (≥24 weeks) focal/grid laser photocoagulation is more effective in increasing visual acuity compared with focal/grid laser treatment alone or intravitreal triamcinolone with laser photocoagulation for the treatment of center-involved DME. Focal/grid laser treatment at the initiation of intravitreal ranibizumab is no better, and possibly worse, for vision outcomes than deferring laser treatment for 24 weeks or more in eyes with center-involved DME with vision impairment.
Intravitreal Ranibizumab or Triamcinolone Acetonide as Adjunctive Treatment to Panretinal Photocoagulation for Proliferative DR

The addition of one intravitreal triamcinolone injection or two intravitreal ranibizumab injections in eyes receiving focal/grid laser photocoagulation for DME and PRP is associated with better visual acuity outcomes and decreased macular edema by 14 weeks.
The Course of Response to Focal Photocoagulation for Diabetic Macular Edema

Eyes that demonstrate a definite reduction in, but not complete resolution of, central DME at 16 weeks after focal/grid laser photocoagulation have a 23% to 63% likelihood of continuing to improve without additional treatment.
Evaluation of Visual Acuity Measurements in Eyes with Diabetic Macular Edema

Across nationwide sites using a variety of autorefractors, visual acuity tended to be worse and more variable with autorefraction than manual refraction, suggesting that autorefraction is not a good substitute for manual refraction for clinical trials with improved visual acuity outcomes as a primary endpoint.
Effect of Diabetes Education During Retinal Ophthalmology Visits on Diabetes Control

Use of a personalized intervention at ophthalmology visits, including HbA1c measurement and counseling about the importance of glycemic control in reducing diabetic complications was not effective in improving HbA1c levels.
An Evaluation of Intravitreal Ranibizumab for Vitreous Hemorrhage Due to Proliferative DR

Intravitreous ranibizumab versus saline did result in significantly different rates of vitrectomy by 16 weeks in eyes with vitreous hemorrhage from PDR. However, ranibizumab treatment resulted in improved short-term secondary outcomes including visual acuity improvement, increased PRP completion rates, and reductions in recurrent vitreous hemorrhage.
Comparison of Time-Domain OCT and Spectral-Domain OCT Retinal Thickness Measurement in Diabetic Macular Edema

This study of eyes with no to minimal nonproliferative DR developed conversion equations to transform CST values obtained on a spectral-domain OCT to a time-domain OCT scale for group comparisons. In addition, values were established for machine and gender-specific thresholds to determine DME presence in diabetic eyes.
A Pilot Study in Individuals with Center-Involved DME Undergoing Cataract Surgery

This small, observational study of eyes with DME undergoing cataract surgery revealed only a small percentage of eyes experienced substantial visual acuity loss or definitive worsening of DME after surgery.
An Observational Study in Individuals with DR without Center-Involved DME Undergoing Cataract Surgery

A history of DME treatment and presence of non-center-involved DME are risk factors for development of center-involved DME after cataract surgery in eyes with DR and no center-involved DME prior to surgery.
A Phase II Evaluation of Topical NSAIDs in Eyes with Non Central Involved DME
At 1-year follow-up in eyes with noncenter-involved DME, this study did not identify a difference between the effect of topical nepafenac 0.1% and placebo drops on OCT parameters or visual acuity.
Prompt Panretinal Photocoagulation versus Intravitreal Ranibizumab with Deferred Panretinal Photocoagulation for Proliferative DR

Ranibizumab injections are an effective alternative to PRP in treating PDR. At 2 years, visual acuity outcomes were noninferior to ranibizumab, whereas average visual acuity over the 2-year period was better and there was less peripheral field loss, reduced rates of DME onset, and fewer eyes that underwent vitrectomy.
A Comparative Effectiveness Study of Intravitreal Aflibercept, Bevacizumab and Ranibizumab for Diabetic Macular Edema

The 2-year clinical trial compared three drugs used to treat DME and found that gains in vision were greater for participants receiving the drug aflibercept than for those receiving bevacizumab, but only among participants starting treatment with 20/50 or worse visual acuity. At 1 year, aflibercept had superior gains to ranibizumab in this vision subgroup; however, a difference could not be identified at 2 years. The three drugs yielded similar gains in vision for patients with 20/32 or 20/40 visual acuity at the start of treatment.
A Comparative Effectiveness Study of Intravitreal Aflibercept, Bevacizumab and Ranibizumab for Diabetic Macular Edema – Follow-up Extension Study

After Protocol T ended, patients received standard care. Sixty-eight percent of patients received at least one anti-VEGF injection. Visual acuity remained improved from baseline but worsened in years 2 to 5. No changes in CST were seen in years 2 to 5.
Short-term Evaluation of Combination Corticosteroid + Anti-VEGF Treatment for Persistent Central-Involved Diabetic Macular Edema Following Anti-VEGF Therapy

In eyes with persistent DME and visual impairment despite previous anti-VEGF therapy, the dexamethasone + ranibizumab group experienced greater reduction of DME but no greater improvement in vision than sham + ranibizumab group over 6 months.

Effect of Initial Management With Aflibercept vs Laser Photocoagulation vs Observation on Vision Loss Among Patients With Diabetic Macular Edema Involving the Center of the Macula and Good Visual Acuity: A Randomized Clinical Trial

No significant difference in 1 or more lines of visual acuity loss at 2 years between eyes initially managed with aflibercept or eyes initially managed with laser photocoagulation or observation and given aflibercept only if there was worsening of visual acuity. But most eyes in the observation group did not receive aflibercept and had a median visual acuity of 20/20.
Effect of Intravitreous Anti–Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor vs Sham Treatment for Prevention of VisionThreatening Complications of DR: The Protocol W Randomized Clinical Trial

At 2 years, the proportion of eyes progressing from moderate to severe NPDR to PDR or CI-DME was lower with aflibercept treatment than with sham treatment. At 4 years, treatment with aflibercept did not improve visual acuity in eyes before developing PDR or CIDME compared with eyes receiving aflibercept after PDR or CI-DME developed but did reduce the probability of developing PDR or CI-DME.
Comparison of Early Treatment DR Study Standard 7-Field Imaging With Ultrawide-Field Imaging for Determining Severity of DR

Increased retinal nonperfusion was associated with worse DR severity and predominantly peripheral lesions on ultrawide field fluorescein angiography. Use of ultrawide field fluorescein angiography could improve prediction of worsening DR severity in eyes with NPDR and complement color fundus photography. At 4 years, greater baseline nonperfusion of the retina on ultrawide field fluorescein angiography was associated with higher risk of worsening Diabetic Retinopathy Severity Score.
Intravitreous Anti-VEGF vs. Prompt Vitrectomy for Vitreous Hemorrhage from Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy

There was no difference in the primary outcome of visual acuity at 24 weeks between intravitreal aflibercept and vitrectomy with PRP. However, there was faster clearance of the vitreous hemorrhage in the vitrectomy group (4 weeks) versus the aflibercept group (36 weeks).
Aflibercept Monotherapy versus Bevacizumab First Followed by Aflibercept If Needed for Treatment of Center-Involved Diabetic Macular Edema.

At 2 years, there was no significant difference between the visual acuity outcomes of eyes treated with bevacizumab first and then switching to aflibercept as needed versus eyes treated only with aflibercept. Risk factors for switching to aflibercept at any time were older age at baseline and, after 12 weeks, greater central subfield thickness.
A Pilot Study Evaluating Photobiomodulation Therapy for Diabetic Macular Edema
Photobiomodulation was not found to be effective in the treatment of DME in eyes with good vision. It was safe and well tolerated.

document_sections.heading: RETINA/VITREOUS PREFERRED PRACTICE PATTERN® DEVELOPMENT PROCESS AND PARTICIPANTS
document_sections.content: The Retina/Vitreous PPP Committee developed the guidance through discussion and review of successive drafts, including two in-person meetings and additional review by email, until it reached consensus. The Preferred Practice Patterns Committee discussed the document in June 2024, and revisions followed. A wider review in July 2024 sought feedback on recommendation quality, feasibility, applicability, patient preferences, and barriers and facilitators to implementation. The guideline is scheduled for formal reassessment in 2029.

document_sections.heading: OBJECTIVES OF PREFERRED PRACTICE PATTERN® GUIDELINES
document_sections.content: Preferred Practice Pattern guidelines identify features of high-quality ophthalmic care. Committees interpret the best available evidence; where evidence is less decisive, they also use collective judgment. The guidance concerns general practice rather than an individual patient's care, cannot guarantee success, and neither exhausts acceptable approaches nor excludes reasonable alternatives. Clinical decisions remain the physician's responsibility. Product references are illustrative rather than endorsements and can include uses outside approved FDA labeling or usual practice; physicians must determine regulatory status, obtain appropriate consent, and comply with applicable law. Guidelines undergo annual review or earlier review when warranted and remain valid for 5 years after approval unless replaced. The intended users of this guideline are ophthalmologists.

document_sections.heading: METHODS AND KEY TO RATINGS
document_sections.content: The guideline uses methods from SIGN and GRADE. Individual studies receive SIGN-based evidence ratings: I++ for high-quality meta-analyses, systematic reviews of RCTs, or RCTs with very low bias risk; I+ for well-conducted equivalents with low bias risk; I- for those with high bias risk; II++ for high-quality case-control or cohort evidence with very low confounding or bias risk and a high probability of causation; II+ for well-conducted case-control or cohort evidence with low confounding or bias risk and a moderate probability of causation; II- for such studies with high confounding or bias risk and a significant possibility that the relationship is not causal; and III for nonanalytic evidence. GRADE rates the overall evidence as Good quality when further research is very unlikely to change confidence in the effect estimate, Moderate quality when further research could importantly affect confidence or change the estimate, and Insufficient quality when further research is very likely to do so and any effect estimate is highly uncertain. A Strong recommendation applies when desirable effects clearly outweigh undesirable effects, or clearly do not; a Discretionary recommendation applies when the balance is less certain. Ratings accompany recommendations in the main text. Searches were performed in PubMed on March 6, 2023, January 23, 2024, and August 6, 2024. Systematic reviews were identified and assessed, and recommendations considered benefits, harms, and their balance. Final decisions used informal consensus, with voting for disagreements and abstention by members with direct financial relationships in the disputed area.

document_sections.heading: HIGHLIGHTED FINDINGS AND RECOMMENDATIONS FOR CARE
document_sections.content: Only 60% of people with diabetes receive the recommended annual DR screening. Dilated fundus examination is the screening reference standard, although validated digital imaging can also detect disease. People with type 1 diabetes should begin annual screening 5 years after onset; those with type 2 diabetes should be screened promptly at diagnosis and at least annually afterward. Patients should be advised that control of glucose and blood pressure reduces DR onset or progression, while rapid intensive glucose lowering can accelerate or precipitate DR, as observed with semaglutides and other newer agents. Pregnant women with pre-existing diabetes should be examined early and monitored closely; an examination during pregnancy is not required for gestational diabetes. Closer monitoring is needed during puberty because DR can progress faster. Intravitreal anti-VEGF agents, including agents that also address other targets, effectively treat CI-DME with vision loss and PDR and can reduce DR severity. PRP remains important for PDR. With CI-DME and good acuity, deferral until acuity is affected (20/30 or worse) is reasonable. The ophthalmologist and patient should choose the biological product together. Infectious endophthalmitis is the gravest ocular complication of intravitreal injections; topical povidone iodine is recommended because omission has been associated with an unacceptably high risk.

document_sections.heading: DISEASE DEFINITION
document_sections.content: DR is an ocular manifestation of diabetic end-organ injury in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Although traditionally considered a retinal microvascular disorder, evidence suggests early neurodegeneration may contribute to vascular abnormalities. OCT and psychophysical testing have identified neural changes before vascular lesions. Early visible findings include microaneurysms in mild NPDR and intraretinal hemorrhages in moderate NPDR. Capillary nonperfusion, cotton wool spots, hemorrhages, venous changes, and IRMA characterize more severe disease. Increased permeability can produce edema or exudates and impair central vision. PDR involves new vessels on the disc, retina, iris, or filtration angle and can cause vitreous hemorrhage, fibrosis, tractional detachment, or neovascular glaucoma. Macular edema or nonperfusion can markedly impair sight at either nonproliferative or proliferative stages.
