Experimental and clinical findings also implicate inflammation and leukocytes: chronic hyperglycemia increases adhesion molecules, including ICAM-1 and VCAM-1, promoting leukostasis; early blood-ocular barrier disruption and leukocyte accumulation contribute to endothelial-cell and pericyte injury. Inflammatory cytokines are elevated in aqueous and vitreous samples from advanced DR and DME.

document_sections.heading: PATIENT POPULATION
document_sections.content: The guideline encompasses all patients with diabetes mellitus.

document_sections.heading: CLINICAL OBJECTIVES
document_sections.content: Objectives are to identify people at risk of DR; coordinate systemic care among patients, primary care clinicians, and specialists, including attention to HbA1c, blood pressure, lipids, weight, renal and coronary disease, neuropathy, and smoking; monitor lifelong for onset and progression; treat existing or threatened visual loss; limit treatment-related effects on sight and vision-related quality of life; offer visual rehabilitation when needed; arrange ophthalmic follow-up for potentially reversible visual loss from cataract, glaucoma, or refractive changes; and develop improved telemedicine technologies.

document_sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
document_sections.content: An estimated three out of five people with diabetes in the United States have at least one associated complication. Type 1 diabetes involves autoimmune pancreatic beta-cell destruction and usually severe insulin deficiency. Type 2 diabetes ranges from insulin resistance with relative deficiency to predominantly impaired secretion with insulin resistance; affected people generally do not require insulin for survival even if they use it. Obesity is common and itself contributes to resistance. Type 2 accounts for 90% to 95% of diabetes and consequently a larger share of DR-related visual disability, although ocular complications are more frequent and severe with type 1.

document_sections.heading: Prevalence of Diabetes
document_sections.content: Diabetes prevalence is increasing worldwide. IDF projected 451 million affected people in 2017 and 693 million by 2045; projected worldwide type 1 prevalence rises from 8.4 million in 2021 to 13.5 to 17.4 million by 2040 (60%–107% higher than in 2021), with the largest relative rise expected in low-income and lower-middle-income countries. Estimates based on the 2020 U.S. census identified 133 million Americans aged 18 years and older with diabetes or prediabetes. For 2021, CDC estimated 38.4 million Americans 18 or older with diabetes (11.6% of that age group), of whom 22.8% were unaware; another 97.6 million (38% of U.S. adults) had impaired fasting glucose by glucose or HbA1c criteria. IDF estimated diabetes in 10.5% (536.6 million) of people aged 20 to 79 worldwide in 2021, with similar rates by sex and a peak at ages 75 to 79. Estimates were 12.1% in urban versus 8.3% in rural areas, and 11.1% in high-income versus 5.5% in low-income countries. Projected 2045 prevalences were 21% in middle-income and 12% in both high-income and low-income countries. Estimated global diabetes-related health expenditure was $966 billion USD in 2021 and is projected at $1,054 billion USD by 2045. In 2021, 44.7% (239.7 million) of adults aged 20 to 79 with diabetes were estimated to be unaware of it; proportions undiagnosed were 53.6% in Africa, 52.8% in the Western Pacific, and 51.3% in Southeast Asia. U.S. diagnosed diabetes affected 4.8% at ages 18 to 44, 18.9% at 45 to 64, and 29.2% at 65 or older. Among adults aged 18 or older, estimates were 16.0% for non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaskan Native, 12.5% for non-Hispanic Black, 10.3% for Hispanic, 9.2% for non-Hispanic Asian, and 8.5% for non-Hispanic White people. Prediabetes corresponds to HbA1c 5.7% to 6.4%; an estimated 38% of U.S. adults aged 18 or older (97.6 million) have prediabetes by fasting glucose or HbA1c. From 2019 to 2021, age-adjusted diabetes prevalence was 13.1% among people with less than high-school education versus 6.9% among those with more than high-school education. Diabetes and prediabetes among people under age 20 were reported at 35 per 10,000, with 86% having type 1. Another comparison reported diabetes prevalences of 12.6% among Americans of African descent, 11.8% among those of Hispanic ethnicity, 7.0% among Americans of European descent, and 8.4% among Asian Americans. Among Native American and Alaskan Native people, an approximate prevalence of 6.4 per 1000 was reported in 1990, and 9.3 per 1000 among those under 35 in 1998. Other research suggests high prevalence in Asia. Approximately one third of Americans are estimated to develop diabetes during their lifetime. Pediatric type 2 diabetes has become more frequent in several countries alongside childhood obesity. Evidence suggests earlier onset and more complications in racial and ethnic minority populations; social determinants also affect diabetes incidence and prevalence. Education and financial resources, along with demographics, access, and psychological distress, predict mortality among adults with diabetes.

document_sections.heading: Prevalence of Diabetic Retinopathy
document_sections.content: DR is a leading cause of new legal blindness among working-age Americans and of blindness in this age group worldwide. Among U.S. adults with diabetes aged 40 or older, estimated DR prevalence was 28.5% (4.2 million), versus 34.6% (93 million) worldwide; corresponding VTDR estimates were 4.4% (0.7 million) and 10.2% (28 million). In 2019, 11.8% of adults with diagnosed diabetes reported severe difficulty seeing or blindness. Data from 2021 estimated DR prevalence of 26.43% among people with diabetes and VTDR prevalence of 5.06%, representing 1.84 million people. A global meta-analysis estimated prevalences of 22.3% for DR, 6.2% for VTDR, and 4.1% for CSME; estimated worldwide adult counts in 2020 were 103.12 million, 28.54 million, and 18.83 million, respectively, with projections for 2045 of 160.50 million, 44.82 million, and 28.61 million. Regional DR prevalence was highest in Africa (35.9%), North America and the Caribbean (33.3%), and the Middle East and North Africa (32.9%), and lowest in South and Central America (13.4%). Relative to Asian patients with diabetes, prevalence was higher among Hispanic (OR, 2.92) and Middle Eastern (OR, 2.44) patients. The Asia Pacific region was estimated to account for more than 50% of worldwide DR-associated visual impairment or blindness: 51% of blindness (n = 424,400) and 56% of visual impairment. Reported DR prevalence among people with diabetes ranged from 10% in India to 43% in Indonesia. The number of U.S. youths with diabetes was projected to rise from 213,000 in 2017 (95% CI, 209,900–218,000; type 1 diabetes 185,000, type 2 diabetes 28,000) to 239,000 in 2060 (95% CI, 209,000– 282,000; type 1 diabetes 191,000, type 2 diabetes 48,000). A pediatric type 2 diabetes meta-analysis reported DR rates of 1.11% less than 2.5 years after diagnosis (95% CI, 0.04%–3.06%), 9.04% at 2.5 to 5.0 years (95% CI, 2.24%–19.55%), and 28.14% after more than 5 years (95% CI, 12.84%–46.45%). DR becomes more prevalent with longer diabetes duration. In the Chinese American Study, prevalence was 35.8% among Chinese American versus 42.0% among Latino people with type 2 diabetes; duration was more strongly associated with DR among Latino participants after adjustment for other predictors. A worldwide meta-analysis estimated DR in 13% of newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes.

document_sections.heading: RISK FACTORS
document_sections.content: Diabetes duration is a major DR risk factor. In type 1 diabetes, retinopathy affects approximately 25% after 5 years, almost 60% after 10 years, and 80% after 15 years. WESDR found PDR in approximately 50% of people aged 30 and younger after 20 years of type 1 diabetes. LALES and Proyecto VER found PDR in 18% of participants with diabetes for more than 15 years, without a difference between diabetes types. The Singapore Eye Disease Study identified Indian ethnicity, diabetes duration, HbA1c, serum glucose, and systolic blood pressure as independent predictors of any DR; lower diastolic pressure, total cholesterol, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol were associated with lower odds. In a Canadian First Nations study, elevated HbA1c predicted two-step DR progression (HR =1.42; P < 0.0001), as did systolic blood pressure (HR = 1.24 per 10 mmHg; P = 0.009). Among people older than 30 with type 2 diabetes of known duration less than 5 years, DR occurred in 40% using insulin and 24% not using it; with documented duration up to 19 years, corresponding rates were 84% and 53%. PDR developed in 2% with type 2 diabetes for less than 5 years and 25% with duration of 25 years or more. Differences between historical cohorts may reflect changing glucose and hypertension care. Glycemia and blood pressure are principal modifiable risks; once DR exists, glycemic control appears more predictive of progression than duration. An HbA1c target of 7% or lower is recommended for most patients, with possible benefit from 6.5% in selected patients. Higher HbA1c corresponds to greater DME risk. The VISS Study associated long-term weighted HbA1c from type 1 diagnosis to 30+ years with PDR and nephropathy and proposed HbA1c 7.0% (53 mmol/mol) or lower, as near normal as possible, to avoid PDR and macroalbuminuria. In a prospective cohort of 3322 people with type 2 diabetes followed for 10 to 25 years, diagnosis at ages 15 up to age 40 carried adjusted OR 2.8 for DR versus diagnosis at ages 60 to under 70. Hypertension treatment remains important. A meta-analysis found modest DR-prevention benefit from lowering blood pressure for up to 5 years, especially with hypertension and type 2 diabetes, but little evidence that lowering it slows DR progression without hypertension. Large studies suggest lipid management may reduce progression and treatment need; findings about age, diabetes type, clotting, renal disease, inactivity, inflammatory markers, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors are less consistent. Ophthalmologists should encourage adherence to care for all medical aspects of diabetes. DR is more prevalent among patients receiving dialysis; an association was reported with systolic, but not diastolic, pressure, fasting glucose, HbA1c, and high HDL cholesterol. A 2018 meta-analysis found lipid-lowering agents protective against DR progression and possibly DME onset, without an effect on acuity or hard exudates. A 2023 Cochrane review found that fenofibrate probably did not change DR progression across type 2 diabetes patients with and without existing DR but probably reduced progression in those with DR (I+, Moderate Quality). A later trial associated fenofibrate with a 27% reduction in progression or treatment among patients with early DR, with equivalent effects by diabetes type. A study suggested omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, docosahexaenoic acid, and eicosapentaenoic acid might relate to less severe DR; a systematic review found that nutraceutical evidence needs further research (III, Insufficient quality). Evidence on genetic and epigenetic explanations of differing progression is conflicting: one study found associations of longer duration and higher HbA1c with PDR in haplogroup H (P = 0.0001 and P = 0.011, respectively), but not haplogroup UK; a larger study did not reproduce that association. One study associated HMGA1 rs139876191 carriage with significantly lower PDR risk and proposed reduced VEGF A expression as an explanation. A meta-analysis of 13 studies associated VEGF variants rs2010963, rs833061, and rs699947 with NPDR or PDR. In a type 2 diabetes study, patients with metabolic syndrome versus those without it had more albuminuria (40.8% vs. 21.8%; P < 0.001), retinopathy (37.9% vs. 28.6%; P < 0.001), coronary disease (19.4% vs. 11.6%; P < 0.001), cerebrovascular disease (5.8% vs. 3.2%; P = 0.014), and ankle-brachial index less than 0.9 or 1.3 or higher (6.1% vs. 3.0%; P = 0.015). These outcomes tended to rise with the number of syndrome components (all P for trend < 0.05); screening may help identify higher-risk patients. In 50,254 eyes, baseline NPDR features predicted 5-year PDR progression: IRMA versus venous beading carried HR = 1.77; P = 0.0013 for PDR, and dot-blot hemorrhages in 4-quadrants carried HR = 3.84; P = 0.0095 for vitreous hemorrhage. Protocol S associated worse baseline PDR with worsening despite anti-VEGF or PRP (64% [high-risk PDR or worse] vs. 23% [moderate PDR or better]; HR = 3.97; P < 0.001). Within its PRP group, worsening was more frequent after pattern scan than conventional single-spot PRP (60% vs. 39%; HR = 2.04; P = 0.008), regardless of spot count. OCT and OCTA have identified additional progression biomarkers.

document_sections.heading: NATURAL HISTORY
document_sections.content: Without appropriate intervention, DR tends to advance from mild to severe disease. Clinical studies support treatment approaches described as 90% effective at preventing severe visual loss (acuity < 5/200). Nonproliferative findings include microaneurysms, intraretinal hemorrhages, venous enlargement, and cotton wool spots; vascular leakage may cause edema and hard exudates. CSME denotes retinal thickening or nearby exudates involving or threatening the macular center. Timely treatment should be considered when central involvement, nearby thickening or exudates, and associated or potential visual loss are present. CSME is categorized by whether the center is involved. Progressive vessel closure produces ischemia, venous changes, IRMA, hemorrhages, and exudation; defined severity thresholds establish severe NPDR, for which PRP or anti-VEGF should be considered. Table 1 presents the clinical severity scale: no apparent retinopathy, mild, moderate, and severe NPDR, and PDR, including U.S. and international severe-NPDR definitions. Two or more severe-NPDR features constitute very severe NPDR. PDR involves neovascularization and may cause hemorrhage, fibrosis, vitreoretinal traction, retinal breaks or detachment, and neovascular glaucoma. High-risk features include associated vitreous hemorrhage or NVD occupying greater than or equal to about one-quarter to one-third disc area even without hemorrhage; neovascular glaucoma or high-risk PDR calls for prompt anti-VEGF agents and PRP. Greater ETDRS severity predicts progression, and more severe baseline NPDR predicts incident DME. In a study of 2240 youths aged 21 or younger with type 1 and 1768 with type 2 diabetes, DR developed in 20.1% and 7.2%, respectively, over median follow-up of 3.2 and 3.1 years; type 1 onset was faster (P < 0.0001). A separate retrospective study of people under 22 reported, by 15 years after diagnosis, type 2 versus type 1 HRs of 1.9 (P = 0.02) for any DR, 2.3 (P = 0.048) for PDR, 1.5 (P = 0.50) for DME, 2.4 (P = 0.24) for visually significant cataract, and 4.1 (P = 0.007) for pars plana vitrectomy; its authors suggested at least equally frequent ophthalmoscopy for type 2. A systematic review suggested an association between DR and stroke (pooled risk ratio 2.04; 95% CI, 1.25–3.32).

document_sections.heading: CARE PROCESS
document_sections.content: DR care involves medical history, regular eye examination or high-quality photographic screening in previously untreated patients, and continued follow-up. Screening distinguishes patients needing retinal specialist assessment or treatment from those suitable for annual screening. Education should stress that important DR can exist without symptoms or impaired vision and that early detection, timely treatment, and at least annual retinal examinations matter. In a 10-year Joslin observational study, 89% with mild DR and 55% with VTDR reported no awareness of eye disease, while 25% with VTDR missed recommended follow-up; unawareness was associated with longer diabetes duration, an eye examination more than 1 year earlier, and no future appointment. An English screening-program analysis estimated that biennial rather than annual screening would delay identification by 1 year in 56.3% with sight-threatening DR and 43.6% with PDR, particularly among Black patients. Annual dilated examination is advised for type 2 diabetes without DR and, starting 5 years after onset, type 1 diabetes without DR. Table 2 sets out initial and subsequent examination timing. Near-normal glucose and blood pressure reduce DR onset or progression, and patients should understand the importance of HbA1c and pressure control; lipids may also matter. Aspirin prescribed for another indication need not be stopped out of concern for DR or vitreous hemorrhage.

document_sections.heading: PATIENT OUTCOME CRITERIA
document_sections.content: Outcomes encompass stable or improved visual function and vision-related quality of life, optimal control of glucose, blood pressure, and other risks through communication with primary care, and development of systemic diabetic complications.

document_sections.heading: DIAGNOSIS
document_sections.content: Initial assessment should include the comprehensive adult medical eye evaluation, with particular attention to DR. The clinical category in each eye, macular-edema status, and the level of diabetes control inform intervention and follow-up timing.

document_sections.heading: History
document_sections.content: Initial history should cover diabetes duration; prior HbA1c; medications; obesity, renal disease, hypertension, lipids, pregnancy, neuropathy, and cystic fibrosis; ocular trauma, other eye conditions, injections, and operations including retinal laser; and present visual symptoms and their rate of progression.

document_sections.heading: Examination
document_sections.content: Initial examination should assess acuity, anterior segment by slit lamp, IOP, pupils for optic-nerve dysfunction, posterior pole stereoscopically, and peripheral retina and vitreous. Before dilation, gonioscopy is indicated for suspected iris new vessels or raised IOP to detect angle neovascularization. Dilation is preferred: only 50% of eyes are classified correctly for DR presence and severity without it. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy with a 90 diopter (D) or 78 D lens is recommended for posterior pole and midperipheral assessment; indirect ophthalmoscopy or slit lamp is preferred for the periphery. Detailed evaluation should look for macular edema, potentially with OCT; severe-NPDR signs; NVD or NVE; vitreous or preretinal bleeding; and retinal evidence of hypertension.

document_sections.heading: Examination Schedule
document_sections.content: For type 1 diabetes, sight-threatening DR is rare before puberty, although substantial disease can emerge 6 to 7 years after onset. Begin ophthalmic examinations 5 years after diagnosis and repeat annually; education on early glycemic control should begin at disease onset. Type 2 diabetes may precede its diagnosis by years: up to 3% diagnosed at age 30 or later have CSME or high-risk findings at diagnosis, and about 30% have some DR. Refer for comprehensive examination at diagnosis and continue at least annually. People planning pregnancy with pre-existing diabetes should have an eye examination beforehand and counseling about possible DR development or progression. Examine during the first trimester and arrange repeat visits according to severity; systemic management during pregnancy should address glucose and blood pressure. Gestational diabetes arising during pregnancy does not require a pregnancy eye examination and does not appear to increase pregnancy-related DR risk. During puberty, DR progresses faster; reported relative risk is 4.8 versus prepubescent patients despite comparable diabetes duration.

document_sections.heading: Ancillary Tests
document_sections.content: Appropriately selected ancillary investigations can augment examination. The tests discussed are color or red-free fundus photography, OCT, FA, OCTA, and B-scan ultrasonography.

document_sections.heading: Color Fundus Photography
document_sections.content: Fundus photography, with or without dilation, reproducibly detects DR and helps record severity, NVD or NVE, treatment response, and future treatment requirements. Widefield images can document the overall retinal disease burden.

document_sections.heading: Optical Coherence Tomography
document_sections.content: OCT depicts the vitreoretinal interface, neural retina, and subretinal space at high resolution. It measures thickness, tracks edema, and identifies vitreomacular traction or other macular disease. Anti-VEGF trials have used OCT to monitor edema objectively; clinical decisions about injections, corticosteroids, laser, or vitrectomy often partly depend on it. Thickness does not consistently correspond to acuity. Spectral-domain OCT loss of inner foveal layers has been associated with visual loss in diabetic macular ischemia. Outer-retinal hyperreflective foci (P = 0.037), poor baseline vision (P < 0.001), absence of epiretinal membrane (P = 0.048), and baseline subretinal fluid (P = 0.001) were associated with improved logMAR acuity in a cited study. Intraretinal hyperreflective foci, outer-layer loss, and outer-retinal reflectance relate to acuity or photoreceptor status. OCT parameters can distinguish normal eyes, diabetic eyes without DR, and early DR. Table 3 outlines situations for its use. Phase 3 treatment decisions about maintaining or changing intervals use changes in CST against a reference or absolute threshold; assessment increasingly combines CST and acuity. Intraretinal fluid has shown a stronger association with acuity than subretinal fluid.

document_sections.heading: Fluorescein Angiography
document_sections.content: Routine FA is not indicated in regular diabetic eye examinations. As treatment with anti-VEGF and intraocular corticosteroids has reduced use of focal laser, localization of leaking microaneurysms by FA is less often needed. FA remains useful for distinguishing DME from other macular disorders, investigating unexplained visual loss, identifying macular nonperfusion that may explain treatment-resistant visual loss, and locating untreated ischemic retina when neovascularization persists after scatter laser. Widefield FA better detects peripheral ischemia and lesions. Protocol AA associated predominantly peripheral lesions detected by FA, but not by color imaging, with greater worsening risk over 4 years independently of baseline DRSS; its findings suggested ultra-widefield FA might improve risk prediction in NPDR. Table 4 describes clinical uses. Severe FA-related medical events, including death in about 1/200,000 patients, are possible; nausea occurs in 3%-15% and urticaria in 0.5%. Angiography facilities should have plans and protocols for emergencies and risk reduction. Fluorescein crosses the placenta and has been detected in breastmilk for up to 72 hours, although fetal harm has not been documented.

document_sections.heading: Optical Coherence Tomography Angiography
document_sections.content: OCTA is FDA approved, but screening and management indications for DR remain under development. It noninvasively depicts capillary-scale abnormalities by retinal depth, enabling quantitative macular-ischemia assessment and detection of preclinical microvascular changes and neovascular tissue. Studies associate measured nonperfusion with DR severity. It cannot depict leakage, although the absence of dye leakage can leave ischemia easier to see. Limitations include projection artifacts, no consensus segmentation algorithm, and restricted field for peripheral ischemia and neovascularization; montages or widefield OCTA can partly address the field limitation.

document_sections.heading: Ultrasonography
document_sections.content: When vitreous hemorrhage or another media opacity limits viewing, ultrasonography can assess the retina, quantify hemorrhage, characterize vitreoretinal traction, and identify diabetic retinal detachment.

document_sections.heading: Other Tests
document_sections.content: Electroretinography is used to assess neural retinal dysfunction even before visible vascular abnormalities and could help predict future microaneurysm locations. Visual fields can show dysfunction without visible DR; dark-adapted chromatic perimetry detects sensitivity loss in eyes without DR and with mild NPDR. AI is under evaluation to assist monitoring and progression prediction; distinguishing arteries from veins has aided AI-based OCTA analysis.

document_sections.heading: MANAGEMENT
document_sections.content: Untreated DR and visual loss impose economic burdens. Laser, anti-VEGF agents, and intravitreal corticosteroids offer varying degrees of cost-effective management. The patient and physician should individualize the choice of laser, anti-VEGF product, or approved intravitreal corticosteroid. Care combines healthy diet and lifestyle, systemic treatment, timely eye evaluation, and ophthalmic treatment; social, financial, insurance, family, employment, and cultural circumstances affect patients' ability to follow a plan. Coordination among clinicians and education about referral, surveillance, and repeated treatment visits are important.

document_sections.heading: Prevention of Diabetic Retinopathy
document_sections.content: Diet, exercise, and weight control may lower diabetes risk for some and can moderate its visual complications, but cannot prevent every complication. DCCT found that optimized HbA1c delayed DR onset and progression in type 1 diabetes. Ophthalmologists should collaborate with primary care and explain the value of bringing glucose, monitored by HbA1c, as close to normal as safely possible. Studies also support glucose, lipid, and blood-pressure control in type 2 diabetes. ETDRS found that aspirin 650 mg per day did not slow DR progression and that aspirin did not increase the severity, frequency, or duration of vitreous hemorrhage with PDR; DR therefore does not call for changes to aspirin prescribed for medical reasons.

document_sections.heading: Early Detection of Diabetic Retinopathy
document_sections.content: DR can remain asymptomatic for years, including when advanced; screening and appropriate referral are therefore essential. Table 5 summarizes initial management by DR severity and edema status, including follow-up and treatment options. For CI-DME with acuity 20/25 or better, observation or focal laser followed by aflibercept if vision declines did not differ from initial anti-VEGF treatment; deferral until acuity is worse than 20/25 is appropriate. Conditions that may aggravate edema include hypertension, fluid retention associated with heart failure, renal failure, and pregnancy; brief deferral of photocoagulation while medically addressing such conditions may be considered. NCI-DME treatment can also be deferred when acuity is better than 20/32, close review is feasible, and the patient understands the risk. Following anti-VEGF injection, reassessment may occur as early as 1 month. Trial analyses suggest treatment may prevent severe visual loss (acuity < 5/200) in 90%, yet referrals and screening remain inadequate; two community studies found 43% to 65% had no dilated examination at enrollment. Digital photographic screening, with or without dilation, can aid detection and referral where access is limited. OCT appears sensitive and effective for DME detection if other causes of cystoid edema are absent (I+, Good quality, Strong recommendation). Small studies have explored chromatic perimetry and electroretinography for early neural dysfunction. Photographic screening participation has been associated with later adherence to clinician-performed dilated examinations; programs should follow established guidelines. FDA-approved autonomous screening systems include LumeneticsCore™ in 2018, EyeArt® in 2020, and AEYE-DS in 2022. They use primarily nonmydriatic photographs, with dilation if needed for image quality, and software to determine whether more-than-mild DR or VTDR is present. Trials reported high sensitivity and specificity and nearly 100% negative predictive values; effects on visual outcomes remain unknown. DCCT observed early DR acceleration with rapid intensive glucose lowering. SUSTAIN 6 reported more vitreous hemorrhage, blindness, or events requiring intravitreal treatment or photocoagulation with semaglutide than placebo (HR = 1.76; 95% CI, 1.11–2.78; P = 0.02). A medication review associated PPARgamma agonists with worsening DME, semaglutide with slight DR worsening, and SGLT-2 inhibitors with more retinal-vein occlusions among older patients and those with advanced kidney disease. A retrospective comparison of 6065 SGLT-2 inhibitor initiators and 12,890 controls did not associate the inhibitor with NPDR progression. A meta-analysis of 23 trials involving 22,096 patients found 730 incident DR cases, including 463 with semaglutide and 267 in controls; overall relative risk was 1.14. Semaglutide versus placebo yielded relative risk 1.24; 95% CI, 1.03–1.50. With semaglutide, age 60 or older and diabetes duration of 10 years or more were risk factors (relative risk 1.27; 95% CI, 1.02–1.59 and relative risk 1.28; 95% CI, 1.04–1.58, respectively).

document_sections.heading: Medical and Surgical Management
document_sections.content: Management depends on DR severity and whether edema is CI-DME or NCI-DME; DME can occur at any DR stage. Treatment interactions matter: PRP can exacerbate DME, reports describe edema temporally associated with oral glitazones, and anti-VEGF treatment for DME can lessen DR severity. Table 5 presents severity-based management guidance, while Table 6 catalogues treatment adverse effects. Individual needs may differ.

document_sections.heading: Diabetic Macular Edema
document_sections.content: ETDRS defined CSME by retinal thickening at or within 500 µm of the macular center; hard exudates at or within 500 µm with adjacent thickening, excluding residual exudates after successful edema treatment; or thickening covering 1 disc area or larger with any part within 1 disc diameter of the center. DME is now classified as CI-DME or NCI-DME because central involvement carries greater risk of visual loss. OCT best detects and measures CI-DME and provides central-thickness changes for treatment-response monitoring. A DRCR.net study proposed a CI-DME threshold of central thickness two standard deviations above the reference population of diabetic eyes without edema.

document_sections.heading: Treatment Deferral
document_sections.content: Good acuity may coexist with CI-DME: an estimated 40% of DME eyes in ETDRS had acuity 20/20 or better. Trials establishing anti-VEGF benefit enrolled eyes with acuity 20/32 or worse. Protocol V found no difference in visual-acuity loss among initial aflibercept 2 mg, focal laser with aflibercept if acuity declined, and observation with aflibercept if acuity declined when baseline acuity was 20/25 or better. Rescue criteria were a decline of at least 10 letters (> 2 lines on an eye chart) at any visit or 5 to 9 letters (1 to 2 lines) at two consecutive visits. At 2 years, mean acuity was 20/20 in all groups and OCT CST had not changed significantly from baseline. Deferral until acuity reaches 20/30 or worse is reasonable in eyes with good acuity and CI-DME, with examinations every 2 to 4 months. Higher initial CST, worse DRSS, and DME treatment in the fellow eye predicted later anti-VEGF need.

document_sections.heading: Anti-Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor Therapy
document_sections.content: Multiple trials and reviews found anti-VEGF more effective than focal laser alone for visual improvement in CI-DME, making anti-VEGF first-line treatment. Ratings attached to the cited evidence include I+, Good quality, Strong recommendation; I-, Insufficient quality, Discretionary recommendation; and I+, Moderate quality, Discretionary recommendation.

document_sections.heading: Aflibercept
document_sections.content: Aflibercept 2 mg targets VEGF A, VEGF B, and PLGF. In the parallel phase 3 VIVID and VISTA trials, intravitreal treatment every 4 or 8 weeks produced greater visual improvement than macular laser at 52, 100, and 148 weeks; adverse-event findings were consistent with its known profile and similar to other anti-VEGF agents.

document_sections.heading: Bevacizumab
document_sections.content: Bevacizumab is an anti-VEGF A antibody. The phase 2 BOLT trial compared intravitreal 1.25 mg bevacizumab every 6 weeks with focal laser every 4 weeks for persistent DME with impaired vision. At 2 years, vision was substantially better with bevacizumab, including significantly more gains of 10 letters and 15 letters; no bevacizumab patients lost 10 or more letters versus 14% after laser.

document_sections.heading: Ranibizumab
document_sections.content: Ranibizumab is an anti-VEGF A Fab fragment. In the parallel phase 3 RISE and RIDE trials, monthly intravitreal 0.5 or 0.3 mg, with macular laser available if needed, improved vision rapidly and durably, reduced further visual loss, and improved edema, with low ocular and nonocular adverse-event rates. In February 2025, FDA approved a ranibizumab implant for DME after response to at least 2 anti-VEGF injections.

document_sections.heading: Brolucizumab
document_sections.content: Brolucizumab is a single-chain anti-VEGF A antibody fragment approved for DME in June 2022 following the phase 3 KITE and KESTREL noninferiority studies. Eyes received 5 brolucizumab loading doses every 6 weeks and then dosing every 8 or 12 weeks; the comparator received aflibercept 2 mg every 8 weeks after 5 monthly loading doses. Brolucizumab was noninferior for mean best-corrected acuity change at year 1. In that year, 55% in KESTREL and 50% in KITE remained on 12-week dosing; median exposure through week 52 was 7 injections of brolucizumab 6 mg. Fluid persisted at week 52 in 60.3% with brolucizumab 6 mg versus 73.3% with aflibercept in KESTREL and 54.2% versus 72.9% in KITE; significance was not tested. KESTREL intraocular inflammation affected 3.7% with brolucizumab 6 mg, including 0.5% retinal vasculitis, versus 0.5% with aflibercept 2 mg. KITE reported 1.7% in each arm and no retinal vasculitis. Occlusive retinal vasculitis cases were subsequently reported after approval.

document_sections.heading: Faricimab-svoa
document_sections.content: Faricimab-svoa is a bispecific anti-VEGF and anti-angiopoietin-2 antibody approved for DME in 2022. YOSEMITE and RHINE compared faricimab 6 mg with aflibercept 2 mg in treatment-naïve and previously treated patients, with the latter capped at 25% of the cohort. Faricimab every 8 weeks after six monthly doses, or personalized intervals up to every 16 weeks after four monthly doses, achieved noninferior acuity gains to aflibercept every 8 weeks after five monthly doses. In the personalized-interval arms, 73.8% and 71.1% reached intervals of every 12 weeks or greater at 1 year, and 52.8% and 51.0% reached every 16 weeks. At year 2, 78.1% and 78.1% reached every 12 weeks or greater, and 60% and 64.5% every 16 weeks. Personalized-interval patients received 3 faricimab injections in year 2 versus five with fixed every-8-week faricimab or aflibercept. Pooled faricimab groups had larger CST reductions through year 2, while more-than-two-step DRSS improvement was comparable across arms. Intraocular inflammation excluding endophthalmitis was 1.3% with faricimab versus 0.6% with aflibercept; otherwise safety was comparable, without new signals. FDA approved a single-dose prefilled syringe in 2024. In patients with baseline acuity 20/50 or worse, post hoc analysis found comparable acuity gains across treatments at years 1 and 2. Both faricimab groups had greater mean CST changes at year 1; at year 2 the difference from aflibercept 2 mg was significant for fixed every-8-week faricimab but not treat-and-extend faricimab.

document_sections.heading: Anti-Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor Therapy
document_sections.content: Aflibercept 8 mg was approved for DME in 2023. PHOTON compared aflibercept 8 mg every 12 or 16 weeks with 2 mg every 8 weeks after 3 monthly loading doses in all 3 groups, allowing prespecified shortening of 8-mg intervals after week 16. At week 48, both 8-mg groups achieved noninferior visual improvement, and 93% of 8-mg recipients maintained intervals of 12 weeks or greater. Mean central-retinal-thickness changes were -171.7 µm with 8 mg every 12 weeks, -148.3 µm with 8 mg every 16 weeks, and -165.3 µm with 2 mg. The safety profiles were comparable.

document_sections.heading: Biosimilars
document_sections.content: The 2021 FDA approval of ranibizumab-nuna 0.5 mg for retinal disease did not include DME, for which ranibizumab 0.3 mg is required. Ranibizumab-eqrn was approved in 2022 at 0.3mg and 0.5-mg and is interchangeable with ranibizumab 0.3 mg for DME and DR. Prospective comparative long-term data beyond 1 year are unavailable. The ophthalmologist and patient should choose among reference, biosimilar, and interchangeable products because individual responses can vary. Four aflibercept biosimilars received FDA approval for DR and DME in 2024: aflibercept-jbyf, aflibercept-yszy, afliberceptmrbb, and afliberceptayyh. A phase 3 study reported comparable efficacy and safety for afliberceptjbvf (MYL-1701P) and reference aflibercept.

document_sections.heading: Other Studies
document_sections.content: Protocol T showed that bevacizumab, ranibizumab, and aflibercept 2 mg improved CI-DME vision, without a statistically significant difference in serious adverse events at 2 years. At baseline acuity 20/40 or better, visual results were similar; at 20/50 or worse, aflibercept outperformed both comparators at year 1 and only bevacizumab at year 2. Combined ranibizumab and prompt or deferred laser produced better 2-year outcomes than laser alone. Anti-VEGF is the initial CI-DME choice; focal laser can subsequently be considered for persistent edema. READ-2 found better outcomes with ranibizumab alone or combined with laser than with laser alone. Protocol I found anti-VEGF with prompt or deferred laser better than laser alone or laser plus triamcinolone acetonide; prompt laser conferred no added benefit. About 30% received focal laser during 2 years in RISE and RIDE, while 46% received it before the 3-year visit in Protocol I. Protocol I reduced injection frequency in years 2 and 3 after moving to as-needed treatment at 6 months while preserving acuity. Focal laser for persistent edema might lessen injection requirements. Evidence favors ranibizumab and aflibercept over conventional laser for DME (I++, Good quality, Strong recommendation). In eyes with acuity 20/32 or worse from CI-DME, monthly or protocol-guided ranibizumab, bevacizumab, or aflibercept 2 mg produced around 2 lines of gain at 2 years versus visual stabilization with focal treatment; 30%–46% also received focal laser, and immediate versus delayed timing did not alter results. In Protocol T eyes starting at 20/50 or worse, 2-year mean gains were 18.3 letters with aflibercept, 13.3 with bevacizumab, and 16.1 with ranibizumab; only the aflibercept–bevacizumab difference was statistically significant. Second-year injections averaged about half as many as first-year injections. Over 2 years, focal laser for persistent edema was used in 41%, 64%, and 52% of the respective groups (all pairwise comparisons were P < 0.05). Two thirds of eligible participants completed year 5; from years 2 to 5, clinician judgment guided treatment, acuity remained better than baseline, and OCT thickness remained stable. The DRCR protocol begins monthly anti-VEGF injections for 4 to 6 months, permits withholding when vision or thickness stops improving or when 20/20 acuity and/or edema resolution is achieved, resumes treatment on deterioration, and doubles visit intervals after successive treatment-free visits up to 4 months. Treat-and-extend also adjusts intervals by response; a prospective study found similar 2-year anatomical and visual results to monthly dosing with fewer injections. Protocol AC found similar 2-year acuity with initial bevacizumab and aflibercept 2 mg rescue versus initial aflibercept in eyes starting at 20/50 to 20/320; 70% of bevacizumab-arm patients ultimately switched, with 57% of those switches between weeks 12 and 24.

document_sections.heading: Complications of Intravitreal Injections
document_sections.content: Infectious endophthalmitis is the most serious ocular injection complication, reported at 0.019% to 0.09% in trials. Topical povidone iodine is recommended because omitting it has been associated with unacceptably high risk. Routine antibiotic drops before or after injection are not recommended: they do not lower endophthalmitis risk and increase resistance in ocular flora. Retinal detachment, cataract, zonular or capsular injury, and sustained IOP elevation are rare. Review at 1 month after anti-VEGF injection may be appropriate. Systemic ATE and raised IOP remain theoretical risks for all anti-VEGF agents, with inconclusive trial results. A 2021 review found no increase in major cardiovascular events (I+, Moderate quality), and a Veterans Health Affairs analysis found no higher systemic adverse-event risk among patients with diabetes. A 2023 Cochrane review reported no increased mortality but could not exclude a clinically meaningful increase because mortality evidence had low to very low certainty (I+, Good quality). Another meta-analysis found no significant overall mortality effect from treatment intensity but marginal evidence of higher mortality with greater intensity in the DME subgroup (incidence rate ratio 1.17; 95% CI, 1.02–1.33, P = 0.03; I+, Moderate quality). Another meta-analysis suggested a possible modest increase in death and cerebrovascular events with monthly treatment for 2 years. A 2021 review found increased mortality among patients with DR despite no overall increase in major cardiovascular events. Pooled RISE and RIDE data reported deaths during the first 2 years in 4.4% (11 of 250) with ranibizumab 0.5 mg, 2.8% (7 of 250) with 0.3-mg, and 1.2% (3 of 250) in controls; by 3 years, corresponding treated-group figures were 6.4% (16 of 249) and 4.4% (11 of 250). A causal relationship cannot be excluded. At 2 years, ATE rates were 7.2% (18 of 250), 5.6% (14 of 250), and 5.2% (13 of 250), respectively, and stroke rates were 3.2% (8 of 250), 1.2% (3 of 250), and 1.6% (4 of 250). At 3 years, ATE rates were 10.4% (26 of 249) with 0.5-mg and 10.8% (27 of 250) with 0.3-mg ranibizumab; stroke rates were 4.8% (12 of 249) and 2.0% (5 of 250). In YOSEMITE and RHINE, baseline-to-week-100 ATE incidence was 5% (64 of 1,262) with faricimab versus 5% (32 of 625) with aflibercept 2 mg. Another report gave baseline-to-week-100 thromboembolic-event rates of 6.4% (37 of 578) in combined aflibercept 8 mg groups versus 4.2% (12 of 287) in controls. PHOTON reported ATEs through week 48 in 3.1% (15 of 491 patients) with combined aflibercept 8-mg groups versus 3.6% (6 of 167 patients) with aflibercept 2 mg. Real-world treatment often involves less care than trials and worse results. A review linked injection nonadherence to worse initial vision, deteriorating vision, age, and distance from the treatment center (II-, Moderate quality). One study found 25.4% of PDR patients lost to follow-up over 4 years, varying with age and regional income; another found 11% missed appointments at 1 year, associated with insurance status.

document_sections.heading: Laser Photocoagulation Surgery
document_sections.content: ETDRS found that focal laser lowers moderate-vision-loss risk with CSME; DRCR.net Protocols B and I also found benefit for CI-DME. Anti-VEGF has not been studied in NCI-DME, for which focal/grid laser is recommended. Modified ETDRS laser uses less energy and wider spacing, targets microaneurysms, and avoids foveal vessels within at least 500 µm of the center. A Cochrane review found that, versus no intervention, laser reduces visual-loss likelihood and increases partial or complete DME resolution at 1 to 3 years (I, Moderate quality, Strong recommendation). A 2024 review found subthreshold laser as effective as traditional laser but called for longer follow-up to assess safety. Before treatment, the ophthalmologist should discuss risks and adverse effects. FA can help identify leaking microaneurysms, capillary dropout, and enlargement of the foveal avascular zone for planning; OCTA shows dropout and zone enlargement but not leakage. Arrange reassessment within 3 to 4 months. Focal laser rarely causes choroidal neovascularization with subretinal fibrosis and possible permanent central visual loss; severe subretinal hard exudates and elevated pretreatment serum lipids are other important associated factors.

document_sections.heading: Corticosteroids for Diabetic Macular Edema
document_sections.content: Topical and periocular corticosteroids showed no significant DME benefit. Intravitreal triamcinolone acetonide reduced thickness at 4 months, but focal/grid laser produced better mean acuity by 24 months; within 2 years, half of phakic triamcinolone-treated eyes required cataract surgery and about 30% had an IOP increase above 10 mmHg from baseline. Findings were largely unchanged at 3 years. In a later study, intravitreal triamcinolone acetonide plus focal laser in pseudophakic eyes yielded gains comparable to anti-VEGF. A systematic review found low-to-moderate-certainty evidence of no significant acuity difference, lower thickness, and more IOP adverse events with intravitreal corticosteroids than anti-VEGF (I+, Moderate quality). A Cochrane review suggested a modest benefit of about 1 line of vision or less (I-, Moderate quality). MEAD compared a 0.7-mg dexamethasone implant with sham in treatment-naïve CI-DME and found improved acuity with a mean four to five injections over 3 years. Cataract-related events affected 67.9% of phakic implant eyes versus 20.4% with sham; approximately one third of implant recipients required treatment for increased IOP. In REINFORCE, 36% of dexamethasone-implant-treated eyes gained at least 15 letters; mean treatment interval was 5 months, without new safety concerns. A fluocinolone acetonide implant is approved for DME after corticosteroid treatment without IOP elevation. FAME found improved acuity with a 0.19-mg implant versus sham at 3 years, when 75% had received only one implant. Cataract extraction in phakic eyes occurred in 80.0% versus 27.3%, and incisional glaucoma surgery in 4.8% versus 0.5%. At 36 months in PALADIN, CST decreased 60.69 μm (P < 0.0001) and best-corrected acuity changed +3.61 letters (P = 0.0222) relative to baseline. IOP above 30 mmHg occurred in 10.89%, and steroid-attributable incisional surgery in 1.49%. Following implantation, numbers of eyes needing laser, anti-VEGF, or corticosteroid treatment declined 55%, 36%, and 78%, respectively (P < 0.0001), relative to before implantation. Dexamethasone or fluocinolone implants may migrate anteriorly, particularly with aphakia, an open posterior capsule, or damaged zonules. A migrated dexamethasone implant can damage corneal endothelium chemically or mechanically, causing edema and requiring urgent repositioning or removal to avoid decompensation and keratoplasty. Corneal edema is less common with fluocinolone, but mechanical endothelial injury or raised IOP can still require surgical removal. Because cataract progression and elevated IOP are concerns, intravitreal corticosteroids are generally second-line DME treatment, especially in phakic eyes. No large randomized trial has assessed them as rescue after anti-VEGF; visual and anatomical improvement may occur after inadequate anti-VEGF response, particularly in chronic edema.

document_sections.heading: Other Treatments
document_sections.content: In a DRCR.net phase 2 trial of eyes with persistent CI-DME after at least three anti-VEGF injections during the preceding 20 weeks, adding a dexamethasone implant reduced macular thickness but did not improve visual acuity overall. A prespecified subgroup analysis found improvement of at least 15 letters in 11% with anti-VEGF plus dexamethasone versus 2% with anti-VEGF alone (P = 0.03). A Cochrane review found no added benefit from combining corticosteroids with anti-VEGF rather than using anti-VEGF alone (I, Moderate quality, Strong recommendation), while describing the supporting evidence as low-certainty because few studies had long follow-up. Corticosteroids have repeatedly shown greater cataract and elevated IOP risks than anti-VEGF therapy. Pars plana vitrectomy may improve vision in selected patients with substantial vitreomacular traction and diffuse DME unresponsive to prior macular laser surgery and/or anti-VEGF. DRCR.net Protocol D found visual improvement in 38% of such eyes and visual loss in 22%; variation in factors affecting vision complicates randomized assessment, and most vitrectomy studies preceded anti-VEGF therapy. Some authors propose that micropulse laser causes less macular damage, but a meta-analysis found no visual-acuity difference from conventional laser surgery. A Cochrane review identified no randomized controlled trials of NSAIDs for DME (III, Insufficient quality).

document_sections.heading: Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy
document_sections.content: Management is described according to the degree of retinopathy, associated macular edema, risk of visual loss, and ability to attend follow-up.

document_sections.heading: Normal or Minimal NPDR
document_sections.content: Repeat examination yearly when the retina is normal or has only rare microaneurysms. Within 1 year, 5% to 10% of patients without retinopathy develop DR; existing retinopathy worsens in a similar proportion.

document_sections.heading: Mild to Moderate NPDR without Macular Edema
document_sections.content: Re-examine patients with microaneurysms and occasional blot hemorrhages or hard exudates within 6 to 12 months because progression is common. In WESDR, approximately 16% of patients with type 1 diabetes and mild retinopathy progressed to proliferative disease within 4 years. The 4-year incidence of CSME or less severe macular edema is approximately 12% with mild NPDR and 23% with moderate NPDR in patients with type 1 or 2 diabetes. Anti-VEGF therapy can change the clinically visible retinopathy level; closer surveillance may be needed when treatment stops after edema control, particularly with more advanced retinopathy.

document_sections.heading: Severe NPDR and Non-High-Risk PDR
document_sections.content: DRS found that PRP reduced severe visual loss in severe NPDR and non-high-risk PDR, while indicating that deferral until high-risk features arise is reasonable. ETDRS likewise allowed postponement in eyes with DME but suggested considering earlier PRP, especially for very severe NPDR and non-high-risk PDR, which carry a nearly 50% risk of high-risk PDR within 1 year. Very severe NPDR has two or more 4-2-1 characteristics. ETDRS considered severe NPDR and non-high-risk PDR together because their courses and treatment considerations were similar. Its reported progression findings were 45% developing very severe NPDR, 46% moderate PDR, 22% mild PDR, and 15% of those with severe NPDR developing PDR within 1 year. Re-examination is therefore advised within 2 to 4 months.

document_sections.heading: High-Risk PDR
document_sections.content: The DRS high-risk definition requires any three of four features: neovascularization anywhere; neovascularization on or near the optic disc; at least moderate neovascularization, meaning vessels within 1 disc diameter of the nerve head larger than one-quarter to one-third disc area or vessels elsewhere occupying at least one-half disc area; and vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage. DRS found substantial severe-vision-loss risk that PRP markedly reduced. Most affected patients should receive PRP promptly. DRCR.net Protocol S found ranibizumab injections noninferior to PRP for PDR at 2 years; injection-treated eyes had less worsening of macular edema at 2 and 5 years and less measured peripheral-field loss at year 2, but not year 5. Outcomes after loss to follow-up were worse with injections than after PRP; choosing anti-VEGF instead of PRP therefore requires caution, and anti-VEGF alone could be considered when follow-up is dependable. Consider additional PRP and/or anti-VEGF for neovascularization that fails to regress, increasing retinal or iris neovascularization, new vitreous hemorrhage, or newly formed neovascular areas. Vitreous traction on regressed vessels can cause hemorrhage without necessarily warranting further PRP, especially without venous dilation. Consider pars plana vitrectomy for visually or therapeutically obstructive vitreous opacity, severe fibrovascular proliferation, or tractional detachment involving or threatening the macula. Potential benefit from early vitrectomy rises with neovascularization severity; anti-VEGF in later proliferative disease remains under investigation.

document_sections.heading: Laser Surgery
document_sections.content: PRP reduces severe vision loss in PDR and severe NPDR. Full ETDRS PRP used 1200 to 1600 moderate burns, each of 0.1 second duration, separated by one-half burn width and placed at least 2 disc diameters from the fovea out to the equator. Full PRP is an established choice when laser is selected; partial or limited PRP is not recommended. FA is generally unnecessary for effective PRP, although assessment of nonperfusion and, potentially, visual fields beforehand can distinguish existing field deficits from changes perceived after laser. ETDRS analyses particularly support considering PRP before high-risk PDR in type 2 diabetes: early treatment reduced severe vision loss or vitrectomy by 50% (2.5% vs. 5%; P = 0.0001) compared with deferral. In type 1 diabetes, timing depends on follow-up adherence and the fellow eye's status and response. Impending or recent cataract surgery and pregnancy may influence timing in either diabetes type. Before PRP, assess macular edema, discuss risks and adverse effects, and obtain informed consent. A post hoc analysis found considerable visual-field loss at 1 year after PRP and additional loss subsequently; field loss also occurred with ranibizumab alone and needs further study. With PDR and CSME, perform focal laser and/or anti-VEGF before or alongside PRP when PRP might worsen edema and moderate vision loss. Do not delay PRP for high-risk PDR with extensive NVD or recent vitreous/preretinal hemorrhage; anti-VEGF may accompany it. Consider anti-VEGF plus PRP at the initial session when CI-DME coexists. A 2023 Cochrane review found that anti-VEGF with or without PRP regressed new vessels, reduced vitreous hemorrhage, and improved visual acuity, although the improvement relative to PRP alone did not appear clinically meaningful (I-, Moderate quality).

document_sections.heading: Anti-Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor Therapy
document_sections.content: DRCR.net Protocol S compared PRP with ranibizumab, given monthly for 6 months unless neovascularization fully regressed at 4 months and subsequently as needed. Approximately 11% of participants had mild to severe NPDR. Ranibizumab vision at 2 years was not more than 5 letters worse than PRP; mean vision, visual-field preservation, vitrectomy frequency, and new DME-associated visual loss favored ranibizumab, at the cost of more injections and visits. Visual-field changes did not differ at 5 years. In an adherence analysis, about half had a prolonged follow-up lapse despite study safeguards; median visual-acuity change was a loss of 2 letters with at least 1 long lapse versus a gain of 5 letters without one (P = 0.02). Another study found aflibercept 2 mg similar to PRP for PDR, with potentially better vision without CI-DME at 1 year. RIDE and RISE follow-up found more two-step or three-step retinopathy improvement with ranibizumab than after sham crossover. A 2021 review favored ranibizumab and ranibizumab plus laser for visual improvement (I+, Insufficient quality). Other reviews favored anti-VEGF over PRP for fewer adverse events, including moderate or severe visual loss (I-, Moderate quality, Discretionary recommendation), and associated anti-VEGF alone with better visual outcomes than PRP alone or anti-VEGF plus PRP (I-, Moderate quality, Discretionary recommendation). In another analysis, 22% of injection-treated PDR patients were lost to follow-up over 4 years. Long-term consequences of anti-VEGF alone require further study; reports raise concern about severe outcomes including increased neovascular glaucoma. Indications in mild or moderate NPDR remain unknown and depend partly on glucose control and follow-up reliability. In DRCR Protocol AB, monthly aflibercept 2 mg and vitrectomy with PRP produced no difference in visual acuity at 24 weeks for vision-limiting diabetic vitreous hemorrhage, but hemorrhage cleared in 4 weeks with vitrectomy versus 36 weeks with aflibercept (P < 0.001); approximately one third of each arm later received the alternative intervention. Severe PDR traction may appear or progress after anti-VEGF, although Protocol S found no statistically significant difference in tractional detachment versus PRP. DRCR.net studies found short-term reduction in PDR progression and improvements in retinopathy severity with anti-VEGF. In Protocol T year 1, improvement among 423 NPDR eyes occurred in 44 of 141 (31.2%) with aflibercept, 29 of 131 (22.1%) with bevacizumab, and 57 of 151 (37.7%) with ranibizumab. Adjusted differences were 11.7% for aflibercept versus bevacizumab (P = 0.004), 8.9% for ranibizumab versus bevacizumab (P = 0.01), and 2.9% for aflibercept versus ranibizumab (P = 0.51). At year 2, improvement persisted in 25%, 22%, and 21% of those respective groups despite fewer injections; worsening was uncommon with all three. RIDE and RISE reported DR progression at 2 years in approximately 11% of ranibizumab eyes versus 34% of sham eyes; at least two-step worsening was significantly more frequent with sham, and post hoc improvement was greatest with moderately severe to severe NPDR at baseline. In VIVID, two-step DRSS improvement with aflibercept 2 mg every 4 or 8 weeks was 29.3% and 32.6%, respectively, versus 8.2% with laser (P < 0.0004 and P < 0.0001, respectively). Corresponding VISTA findings were 37.0% and 37.1% versus 15.6% (P < 0.0001 for both comparisons). PANORAMA compared two aflibercept 2 mg schedules with sham for moderately severe to severe NPDR. At 24 weeks, two-step DRSS improvement occurred in 157 of 269 eyes (58.4%) across aflibercept arms versus 8 of 133 eyes (6.0%) with sham (adjusted difference, 52.3%; P < 0.001). At 52 weeks, it occurred in 88 of 135 eyes (65.2%) on aflibercept 2q16 (adjusted difference, 50.1%), 107 of 134 eyes (79.9%) on aflibercept 2q8/pro re nata (adjusted difference, 64.8%), and 20 of 133 eyes (15.0%) on sham (P < 0.001 for both comparisons). Through week 100, vision-threatening complications or CI-DME occurred in 22 of 135 eyes [16.3%] on 2q16 [adjusted difference, -34.2%], 25 of 134 eyes [18.7%] on 2q8/pro re nata [adjusted difference, -31.7%], and 67 of 133 eyes [50.4%] on sham (P < 0.001 for both comparisons). A post hoc analysis suggested reduced NPDR worsening using leakage and nonperfusion biomarkers. Protocol W compared preventive aflibercept 2 mg with sham in moderate to severe NPDR. At 2 years, CI-DME with vision loss or PDR occurred in 16.3% versus 43.5% (HR = 0.32; P < 0.001); PDR probabilities were 13.5% versus 33.2%, and vision-limiting CI-DME probabilities were 4.1% versus 14.8%. Mean (SD) visual-acuity changes were -0.9 (5.8) and -2.0 (6.1) letters (adjusted mean difference, 0.5 letters; P = 0.47), showing no vision difference. At 4 years, cumulative PDR or vision-limiting CI-DME probabilities were 33.9% versus 56.9% (adjusted HR = 0.40; P < 0.001), but mean (SD) vision changes remained similar: -2.7 (6.5) versus -2.4 (5.8) letters (adjusted mean difference, -0.5 letters; P = 0.52).

document_sections.heading: Other Treatments
document_sections.content: Vitrectomy is usually reserved for activity persisting despite anti-VEGF or PRP or disease unsuitable for medical treatment alone. Indications include nonclearing vitreous hemorrhage, tractional detachment involving or threatening the macula, combined rhegmatogenous and tractional detachment, and dense premacular subhyaloid hemorrhage. DRVS found better outcomes when vitrectomy for hemorrhage occurred within 1 to 6 months rather than at 1 year. Serial ultrasound during vitreous hemorrhage can assess for retinal tears and threatening tractional or rhegmatogenous detachment. Endolaser and small-gauge instruments have improved outcomes and reduced adverse events. A meta-analysis suggested preoperative anti-VEGF shortens surgery and reduces retinal breaks and operative bleeding (I+, Moderate quality, Strong recommendation); a Cochrane review suggested preoperative or intra-operative bevacizumab may reduce postoperative vitreous hemorrhage (I+, Moderate quality, Strong recommendation). Either anti-VEGF or vitrectomy is a reasonable initial choice for persistent vitreous hemorrhage alone; anti-VEGF can provide similar eventual visual and anatomical outcomes but takes much longer to improve vision. FAME reported that a fluocinolone acetonide implant delayed or reduced progression to PDR and lowered retinopathy severity through 18 months.

document_sections.heading: Follow-Up Evaluation
document_sections.content: At follow-up, review changes in symptoms, pregnancy, blood pressure, serum lipids, renal status, HbA1c, dialysis, and fenofibrates. Examine visual acuity, the iris by slit lamp, IOP, and the dilated posterior pole stereoscopically. Perform gonioscopy preferably before dilation if iris neovascularization is suspected or IOP is high; obtain OCT when appropriate and examine peripheral retina and vitreous when indicated. Recommended intervals are presented in Table 5.

document_sections.heading: PROVIDER AND SETTING
document_sections.content: The ophthalmologist performs examination and surgery, although trained personnel may carry out some examination tasks under ophthalmologist supervision and review. Given the complexity of DR care, treating ophthalmologists should know the relevant clinical-trial recommendations.

document_sections.heading: COUNSELING AND REFERRAL
document_sections.content: Refer patients with diabetes to primary care or endocrinology for systemic management and convey ocular findings to the clinician managing diabetes. Some patients lose substantial vision despite recommended treatment. When surgery fails or no further treatment is available, provide professional support and consider counseling, visual rehabilitation, or social services. Empathic discussion can identify concerns; consider counseling, vocational rehabilitation, or peer support for depression, anxiety, or loss of independence or employment. Refer functionally limiting visual impairment for visual rehabilitation and social services, since rehabilitation improves functional ability.

document_sections.heading: SOCIOECONOMIC CONSIDERATIONS
document_sections.content: A pre-anti-VEGF analysis from 1989 projected lifetime PDR requiring PRP in 72% of type 1 diabetes patients and macular edema in 42%. Its modeled costs were $966 per person-year of vision saved for PDR and $1,120 per person-year of central vision saved for edema, below annual Social Security disability payments; indirect productivity and suffering costs were greater. A 1996 analysis estimated diabetic eye screening and treatment at $3,190 per QALY saved overall, $1,996 with type 1 diabetes, $2,933 with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, and $3,530 with type 2 diabetes not treated with insulin. A 2013 analysis estimated laser plus bevacizumab versus laser alone at $11,138 per QALY for CSME; reported comparator cost-utilities were $3,101 per QALY for DME laser and $23,640 per QALY for laser treatment of extrafoveal choroidal neovascularization. A 1999 analysis projected recommended eye care would lower blindness prevalence by 52% and cost less directly than lost productivity and disability facilities. A PDR analysis estimated ranibizumab versus PRP without baseline CI-DME at $582,268 per QALY at 5 years and $742,202/QALY at 10 years, versus $65,576/QALY and $63,930/QALY, respectively, with CI-DME; anti-VEGF may be cost-effective when CI-DME is present but not otherwise. Pediatric point-of-care autonomous AI screening was assessed as effective and cost-saving if adherence reached at least 23%. In a claims study spanning 2007 to 2015, only 40% underwent screening. At 5 years, Medicare Advantage patients had fewer examinations than privately insured patients (OR, 0.79; P < 0.01) but less DR (OR, 0.71; P < 0.01). Compared with White patients, Hispanic patients had more DR (OR 1.60, P < 0.01) and fewer examinations (OR, 0.75; P < 0.01); compared with women, men had fewer examinations (OR, 0.84; P < 0.01) and more DR (OR, 1.17; P < 0.01). Higher education was associated with more examinations and less DR. Social determinants probably mediate many observed racial and ethnic differences.

document_sections.heading: APPENDIX 1. QUALITY OF OPHTHALMIC CARE CORE CRITERIA
document_sections.content: Quality ophthalmic care places patients' interests, dignity, and needs first. The ophthalmologist should maintain competence, communicate compassionately, support access and continuity, prevent disease where possible, and avoid exploiting vulnerability. Effective partnership entails listening, explaining prognosis and options, and involving patients in decisions. Clinical judgment guides testing, treatment, timing, and review according to urgency and individual needs. Clinicians should perform only procedures within their competence or obtain qualified assistance; arrange suitable preoperative, postoperative, and substitute care; make appropriate and timely referrals and consultations; maintain accurate records; review results promptly; and identify care providers to patients. When treatment cannot help further, offer accessible support and rehabilitation. Before invasive testing or treatment, obtain relevant history and examination and explain diagnosis, expected benefits and risks, alternatives, and consequences of no treatment to support informed choice. Adopt innovations according to demonstrated safety, effectiveness, benefit, and cost; assess personal performance, share important clinical findings and unexpected complications, maintain facilities prepared for urgent complications, and provide cost-conscious care without unacceptable loss of quality.

document_sections.heading: APPENDIX 2. INTERNATIONAL STATISTICAL CLASSIFICATION OF DISEASES AND RELATED HEALTH PROBLEMS (ICD) CODES
document_sections.content: The appendix tabulates ICD-9 CM and ICD-10 CM codes for background, proliferative, mild, moderate, and severe nonproliferative DR and diabetic macular edema, distinguishing diabetes types and edema status where applicable. Its coding notes specify that relevant ICD-10 CM characters distinguish the presence or absence of macular edema, that laterality rules vary by code series, and that unspecified codes should be used only when no more specific option exists.

document_sections.heading: APPENDIX 3. MAJOR STUDY RESULTS
document_sections.content: The appendix presents major clinical studies of DR and DME, including laser surgery, vitrectomy, intravitreal drugs, and systemic management. Its outcome tables summarize comparisons without repeating their individual cells here.

document_sections.heading: DIABETIC RETINOPATHY STUDY (1972–1979)
document_sections.content: DRS assessed laser photocoagulation for severe NPDR and PDR. Table A3-1 reports severe visual loss by baseline severity, treatment, and follow-up duration. Severe visual loss meant acuity worse than 5/200 at two or more consecutive completed visits scheduled 4 months apart.

document_sections.heading: WISCONSIN EPIDEMIOLOGIC STUDY OF DIABETIC RETINOPATHY (1979)
document_sections.content: WESDR began in 1979 to describe the frequency and incidence of ocular, renal, and amputation complications of diabetes and examine potential contributors, including glycemic control, smoking, and blood pressure.

document_sections.heading: EARLY TREATMENT DIABETIC RETINOPATHY STUDY (1985–1990)
document_sections.content: ETDRS studied photocoagulation in NPDR and PDR without high-risk features. Table A3-2 compares visual-loss outcomes by macular-edema location, treatment, and time. Visual loss meant at least a doubling of visual angle, such as 20/20 to 20/40 or 20/50 to 20/100.

document_sections.heading: Results of Early Scatter Laser Treatment in ETDRS
document_sections.content: For NPDR or non-high-risk PDR, early PRP provided benefit over deferral, but prospects for retaining vision were favorable with either approach. At 5 years, severe visual loss or vitrectomy occurred in 2% to 6% with early laser and 4% to 10% with deferral. Because early PRP sometimes slightly reduced acuity or visual field, ETDRS favored postponement at least until disease approached high-risk PDR. Such eyes had a 50% risk of reaching high-risk PDR within 12 to 18 months. Particularly in type 2 diabetes, considering PRP before high-risk PDR reduced severe visual loss or vitrectomy by 50% relative to deferral. For type 1 diabetes, treatment timing depends on follow-up adherence, fellow-eye status and response, impending cataract surgery, and pregnancy.

document_sections.heading: DIABETIC RETINOPATHY VITRECTOMY STUDY (1983–1987)
document_sections.content: DRVS evaluated vitrectomy for very severe PDR. Early surgery helped type 1 diabetes patients with severe vitreous hemorrhage but showed no analogous benefit for type 2 diabetes. Severe hemorrhage obscured the macula or major vessels for 3 disc diameters from the macular center. Early surgery benefited patients with acuity of 5/200 or worse and severe hemorrhage limiting vision for at least 1 month, without prior treatment or complications such as detachment or iris neovascularization. At 2 years, acuity of 20/40 or better occurred in 25% with early surgery versus 15% with deferral; the difference was most pronounced in type 1 diabetes (36% vs. 12%) and was not statistically significant in type 2 diabetes. DRVS also supported early surgery for acuity of 20/400 or better with specified combinations of severe neovascularization, fibrous proliferation, and moderate hemorrhage: at 4 years, 44% after early surgery versus 28% with observation reached 20/40 or better. Subsequent surgical advances limit direct application of historical results. Early vitrectomy should be considered for selected type 2 diabetes patients, particularly when severe hemorrhage prevents laser treatment of active neovascularization.

document_sections.heading: FENOFIBRATE INTERVENTION AND EVENT LOWERING IN DIABETES (FIELD) STUDY (2005)
document_sections.content: FIELD randomized 9795 people with type 2 diabetes to assess long-term fenofibrate and cardiovascular events. Fenofibrate did not significantly lower the primary coronary-event outcome, but reduced total cardiovascular events, mainly through fewer nonfatal infarctions and revascularizations. More placebo recipients began statins, potentially obscuring a moderately larger benefit.

document_sections.heading: DIABETIC RETINOPATHY CLINICAL RESEARCH NETWORK (DRCR.NET) (2002–PRESENT)
document_sections.content: DRCR.net coordinates multicenter research into DR, DME, and related disorders, emphasizing trials while also supporting other research. Established in 2002, it includes over 115 sites and over 400 physicians in the United States. Its studies address anti-VEGF, laser, corticosteroids, PDR, hemorrhage, and education; Table A3-3 summarizes individual protocols. Protocol T found improved vision at 1 year with each of ranibizumab, aflibercept, and bevacizumab and similar safety. For baseline acuity of 20/50 or worse, aflibercept produced better mean acuity at 1 year; at 2 years it remained superior to bevacizumab but no longer to ranibizumab. Protocol I found that adding focal/grid laser promptly to initial ranibizumab was no better, and possibly worse for vision, than deferring laser for ≥24 weeks; ranibizumab with either laser timing outperformed prompt laser alone through 2 years. In pseudophakic eyes, triamcinolone plus prompt laser appeared comparable to ranibizumab approaches but increased IOP risk. Protocol S randomized 394 eyes of 305 adults with PDR to PRP or ranibizumab 0.5 mg, which could be administered as often as every 4 weeks; either arm could receive ranibizumab for DME. At 2 years, ranibizumab was noninferior for acuity. Mean improvement was +2.8 letters with ranibizumab versus +0.2 with PRP (P < 0.001). Peripheral-field reduction was -23 dB versus -422 dB (P < 0.001); vitrectomy occurred in 4% versus 15% and DME in 9% versus 28%, respectively (P < 0.001 for both). Neovascular activity and regression rates were similar.

document_sections.heading: STUDY OF RANIBIZUMAB INJECTION IN SUBJECTS WITH CLINICALLY SIGNIFICANT DIABETIC MACULAR EDEMA WITH CENTER INVOLVEMENT SECONDARY TO DIABETES MELLITUS (RISE AND RIDE)
document_sections.content: These parallel phase 3 randomized, double-masked, sham-controlled studies tested monthly intravitreal ranibizumab 0.5 or 0.3 mg, with macular laser available if needed. Published phase 3 findings in 2012 indicated sustained vision improvement, less subsequent vision loss, and reduced DME, with low reported ocular and nonocular adverse-event rates.

document_sections.heading: RANIBIZUMAB FOR EDEMA OF THE MACULA IN DIABETES (READ-2)
document_sections.content: This phase 2 multicenter randomized trial compared ranibizumab 0.5 mg, focal laser, and their combination over 2 years. Ranibizumab began at baseline and months 1, 3, and 5 in one arm; laser was given at baseline and, if needed, month 3 in another; the combination arm received both at baseline and month 3. From month 5, participants could receive ranibizumab every 2 months and/or maintenance laser every 3 months. At 24 months, between-group differences were not statistically significant and vision improved in every group; combined treatment required fewer injections than ranibizumab alone.

document_sections.heading: BEVACIZUMAB OR LASER THERAPY (BOLT) STUDY
document_sections.content: In this phase 2 randomized 2-year trial for persistent, vision-impairing DME, bevacizumab 1.25 mg was injected every 6 weeks and focal laser delivered every 4 weeks. At 2 years, vision favored bevacizumab substantially, including significantly more gains of 10 and 15 letters. No bevacizumab recipient lost 10 or more letters, versus 14% of laser-treated patients.

document_sections.heading: DIABETIC MACULAR EDEMA AND VASCULAR ENDOTHELIAL GROWTH FACTOR TRAP-EYE: VIVID AND VISTA
document_sections.content: These trials compared intravitreal aflibercept 2-mg injection with macular laser for DME. Aflibercept yielded better visual improvement at 52, 100, and 148 weeks, with adverse events consistent with its established safety profile.

document_sections.heading: DIABETIC RETINOPATHY CLINICAL RESEARCH NETWORK PROTOCOL T
document_sections.content: At 1 year, aflibercept had a greater overall mean visual improvement than bevacizumab or ranibizumab, with effects dependent on baseline vision. With milder visual loss, gains were 8.0, 7.5, and 8.3, respectively (P > 0.50 for each pairwise comparison). With baseline acuity of 20/50 or worse, gains were 18.9, 11.8, and 14.2, respectively (P < 0.001 for aflibercept vs. bevacizumab; P = 0.003 for aflibercept vs. ranibizumab; P = 0.21 for ranibizumab vs. bevacizumab). Adverse-event rates did not differ significantly. At 2 years, mean vision was similar with aflibercept and ranibizumab but remained significantly better with aflibercept than bevacizumab. Antiplatelet Trialists' Collaboration events were slightly more frequent with ranibizumab at 2 years. All three improved vision, and injections were fewer in year 2 than year 1.

document_sections.heading: YOSEMITE AND RHINE
document_sections.content: These randomized, double-masked DME trials compared faricimab 6.0 mg every 8 weeks, faricimab 6.0 mg on personalized treatment intervals, and aflibercept 2.0 mg every 8 weeks through 100 weeks. At 2 years, faricimab intervals extending to every 16 weeks provided noninferior vision gains and anatomical improvement; ocular adverse-event incidence was similar among arms.

document_sections.heading: PANAROMA
document_sections.content: PANORAMA randomized eyes with DRSS level 47 or 53, no DME, and acuity of 20/40 or better to two aflibercept 2 mg schedules or sham. One aflibercept schedule used every 16 weeks after three monthly doses and one 8-week dose; the other used every 8 weeks after five monthly doses, followed by pro re nata treatment at week 56. At 100 weeks, aflibercept-treated moderately severe to severe NPDR eyes more often improved at least two DRSS steps and less often developed center-involved DME or vision-threatening complications than sham eyes.

document_sections.heading: FAME AND PALADIN
document_sections.content: In phase 3 FAME, sustained-release intravitreal fluocinolone acetonide 0.19 mg improved DME vision versus sham at 3 years but increased cataract extraction and incisional glaucoma surgery. In prospective, nonrandomized PALADIN, treated eyes had mean CST change of -60.69 µm and mean best corrected visual-acuity change of +3.61 letters at 3 years. Among eyes retaining the implant at 36 months, about one quarter needed no rescue therapy and mean IOP appeared stable.

document_sections.heading: MEAD
document_sections.content: In phase 3 MEAD, a dexamethasone 0.7-mg implant improved vision compared with sham for CI-DME at 3 years but increased cataract and IOP rises requiring treatment.

document_sections.heading: PHOTON
document_sections.content: PHOTON randomized DME patients to aflibercept 2 mg every 8 weeks or aflibercept 8 mg every 12 or 16 weeks after initial monthly treatment. Extended-interval aflibercept 8 mg gave noninferior best corrected visual-acuity gains and a similar frequency of ocular adverse events to aflibercept 2 mg every 8 weeks.

document_sections.heading: APPENDIX 4. GLYCEMIC CONTROL
document_sections.content: DCCT found that improved glucose control delayed DR onset and progression, as well as nephropathy and neuropathy, in type 1 diabetes. Each 10% relative decrease in HbA1c, illustrated by 9% to 8.1%, corresponded to a 39% reduction in retinopathy-progression risk; no threshold above the nondiabetic HbA1c range of 4% to 6.05% eliminated risk. DCCT ended after 6.5 years. EDIC followed 95% of its participants, with 1294 to 1335 examined annually. Over EDIC's first 4 years, further DR progression was 66% to 77% lower after prior intensive treatment than after conventional treatment; benefit persisted at 7 years and included severe DR, CSME, and need for retinal laser. Changes toward approximately 8% HbA1c in either former arm did not immediately erase or reproduce differences, suggesting lasting effects of earlier glycemic exposure. Four-year retinopathy incidence and progression remained related to glycosylated hemoglobin after adjustment for baseline factors. Rapid correction of prolonged poor control can transiently worsen retinopathy during the first year: about 10% of type 1 diabetes patients with baseline retinopathy in DCCT had increased progression, potentially including more cotton wool spots.
