Frequent ocular monitoring is important during improved metabolic control. DCCT intensive regimens caused a threefold rise in severe hypoglycemia and excess weight gain. Irregular eating, failure to check glucose before vigorous exercise or driving, and excess alcohol increase hypoglycemia risk; diabetes-nurse and dietitian education may mitigate it. The document reports that semaglutide can produce rapid glycemic improvement and severe hypoglycemia and has been associated with significantly more retinopathy complications. In UKPDS, 3867 newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes patients were studied. Intensive treatment with sulfonylureas or insulin reduced microvascular complications but not macrovascular disease; retinal photocoagulation need was 29% lower than with conventional care (relative risk, 0.71; 95% CI, 0.53–0.96; P = 0.003). ACCORD enrolled 10,251 high-cardiovascular-risk adults with type 2 diabetes at 77 sites; participants were aged 40 to 79, averaged 62 years of age and 10 years of diabetes, and entered trials of glucose, blood-pressure, and lipid strategies. The intensive-glucose arm stopped in 2008 for safety: over an average 3.5 years, 257 died versus 203 in standard care, a difference of 54 deaths, or about three additional deaths per 1,000 participants treated for a year, representing a statistically significant 22% higher death rate. A nonsignificant trend toward 10% fewer primary cardiovascular events did not outweigh harm. Intensive versus standard blood-pressure treatment did not significantly differ on the primary cardiovascular outcome, although stroke fell significantly with small event numbers. Fibrate plus statin did not improve the combined cardiovascular endpoint overall versus statin alone; possible benefit among men and the 17% with lowest HDL and highest triglycerides contrasted with a trend toward more events among women. An American College of Physicians guidance review described the ideal HbA1c target as uncertain and emphasized individualizing goals by benefits, harms, preferences, and life expectancy. It suggested 7% to 8% for most nonpregnant adults with type 2 diabetes, with potentially stricter targets for life expectancy > 15 years; several reviewed guidelines considered 7% particularly applicable to newly diagnosed patients without substantial complications.

document_sections.heading: APPENDIX 5. CLASSIFICATION OF DIABETIC RETINOPATHY IN THE EARLY TREATMENT OF DIABETIC RETINOPATHY STUDY
document_sections.content: Table A5-1 presents ETDRS ophthalmoscopic criteria for mild, moderate, and severe nonproliferative retinopathy and for early and high-risk proliferative disease. Its criteria distinguish lesion types, retinal fields, standard photographs, new-vessel location and size, and associated vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage.

document_sections.heading: APPENDIX 6. ANTI-VEGF AND CORTICOSTEROID AGENTS FOR PATIENTS WITH DIABETIC RETINOPATHY AND DIABETIC MACULAR EDEMA
document_sections.content: Table A6-1 lists anti-VEGF injections, biosimilars, corticosteroid injections and implants, and a ranibizumab implant used for DR or DME, together with their formulations, doses, brand names, and manufacturers; bevacizumab intravitreal injection is identified as off-label.

document_sections.heading: GLOSSARY
document_sections.content: The glossary defines clinical and trial terminology. CSME includes retinal thickening at or within 500 µm of the macular center, nearby hard exudates with adjacent thickening, or thickening covering 1 disc area with some portion within 1 disc diameter of the center. Diabetes diagnostic criteria presented there are fasting plasma glucose ≥126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) after at least 8 hours without calories; hyperglycemia symptoms with casual glucose ≥200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L); or glucose ≥200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) at 2 hours after an oral load equivalent to 75 g anhydrous glucose. The cited expert committee did not recommend routine oral glucose tolerance testing. DME denotes macular fluid from leaking vessels; NPDR lacks retinal neovascularization, whereas PDR features new vessels at the disc and/or elsewhere. Mild NPDR has at least 1 microaneurysm without meeting moderate criteria; moderate NPDR includes more extensive hemorrhages or microaneurysms and/or other specified lesions without reaching severe criteria. Severe NPDR follows the 4-2-1 rule: severe hemorrhages and microaneurysms in 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2 or more quadrants, or moderate IRMA in 1 or more quadrants. High-risk PDR is defined by specified disc or other neovascularization extent, with or without accompanying vitreous/preretinal hemorrhage. Moderate visual loss means at least 15 letters lost or a doubling of visual angle; severe visual loss means acuity worse than 5/200 at two successive visits scheduled 4 months apart. The glossary also distinguishes focal from grid laser, describes PRP as peripheral scatter treatment intended to regress neovascularization, and defines OCT and key vascular findings.

document_sections.heading: LITERATURE SEARCHES FOR THIS PPP
document_sections.content: PubMed searches took place on March 6, 2023, with limited updates on January 23, 2024 and August 6, 2024. Filters targeted human, English-language randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews published since June 1, 2019. The committee assessed 4,112 studies and included 111; searches on patient values and preferences yielded 50 studies. Searches on economic evaluation and treatment costs supplied 94 studies, of which 5 were included. The section lists search strategies for costs, diagnosis, epidemiology, genetics, natural history, preferences, quality of life, risk factors, and treatment, and diagrams identification, screening, exclusions, and inclusion.
